author: Alicia Houser
title: Tanzania’s Peace Was Never Peaceful
content:
One year ago, on October 29, 2025, the sound of bombs and bullets rang out around Dar es Salaam and several other cities across Tanzania. Before last year’s election, Tanzania had enjoyed an international reputation as a peaceful haven in an often tumultuous region. Foreign governments and tour companies certainly helped craft this image, but so did Tanzania’s government and population. Since I started visiting the country in 2017, people have often cited

amani

 (peace) as one of Tanzania’s best attributes. People attributed this purported peace not to satisfaction with the government or living conditions, but to fear.

Watanzania ni woga

 (Tanzanians are cowards), my friends tell me self-deprecatingly. This fear belies the peaceful image Tanzania has cultivated overseas. 


Histories, or perhaps more accurately colonial histories, place Tanzania in the category of African countries that peacefully acquired independence. To consider Tanzania’s transition to independence as peaceful is to take a short view of history. This narrative ignores the Hehe killed during seven years of fighting against the Germans, which ended in 1898 with

Chief Mkwawa

 killing himself rather than surrendering and his skull being taken to Germany. It ignores the organized resistance that involved the entire southern half of Tanzania, the

Maji Maji

 war of 1905–1908, which some consider the first Pan-African anticolonial resistance movement. The Tanzanian historian Gilbert Gwassa estimated that 300,000 Africans died in this movement, most of them from starvation. The narrative of peaceful transition also ignores the roughly 600,000 Africans who died as a result of

World War I

 military incursions on Tanzanian soil. In these three events alone, almost one million would-be Tanzanians lost their lives to colonization. 


I was in Dar es Salaam last year during the election. The internet cut out at about noon, and the sounds of bombs and bullets started around 1 pm and continued off and on for another four days. Without internet, radio, or television, I got my news the old-fashioned way: through other people. My friends in Arusha and Moshi sent frequent messages, and I went out to my courtyard and sat with my neighbors who were connected to other cities across the country. We exchanged what we had heard: someone’s niece had stepped outside her apartment in Dar and encountered a body, Muhimbili Hospital was overflowing; bodies were being stacked outside mortuaries; ballot boxes had been burned. There would be no votes to count. By day three of the lockdown, rumors were circulating that the government was preparing for a prolonged battle, and that Dar’s drinking water might be poisoned. By day five, the store next door to me had sold out of airtime, water, sodas, and milk. Amid the fear, though, was excitement.


Watanzania wameamka, one of my neighbors said proudly. Tanzanians have woken up. A neighbor who stopped by noted that

hakuna mafanikio bila

 sacrifice. No success without sacrifice. Another neighbor said she was going to give 10,000 shillings to any

bodaboda

 and

bajaji

 drivers (the motorcycle and three-wheeler taxi drivers who ferry much of urban Tanzania) she saw; they were the ones leading the protests.


On day six, Mama Samia—as President Samia Suluhu Hassan is popularly known—was sworn in as president at a ceremony closed to the public. The sounds of bombs and bullets had fizzled out over the days, and the morning marking one week since the election radiated with the usual city sounds of buses,

bajajis

, and

bodabodas

 that had gone quiet for so long. The halt in violence did not result from any recognition by Samia of the illegitimacy of the election, which did not include any candidates from the country’s main opposition parties. The electoral commission barred CHADEMA, the largest of them, and disqualified the candidate of ACT-Wazalendo. After days of police shooting

live rounds

 into crowds and indiscriminately killing

civilians

 caught in the wrong place at the wrong time, the protests stopped. Tanzanians decided they did not want to die. After the election, there was a general feeling of “Where do we go from here?”


Months before the election, in March of last year, I attended a memorial event on the slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro in Old Moshi, remembering the 19 area chiefs whom the Germans hanged on March 2, 1900, on accusations of subversion. One of the elders recalled a phrase he heard often growing …

author: WoMin
title: Women Unite to Defend the Congo Basin Against Extractivism – A Call for Climate Justice at COP31
content:
As world leaders gather in Antalya, Türkiye, for the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), taking place from 9–20 November 2026, women from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the Republic of Congo and Cameroon are raising an urgent message: there can be no climate justice without defending the Congo Basin, protecting community territories and recognising the leadership of women on the frontlines of environmental struggles.


The Congo Basin is one of the world’s most important ecological treasures, acting as the “

second lungs

 of the Earth”, after the Amazon, which is being decimated. Spanning over four million square kilometres across six countries, its forests, rivers and peatlands play a vital role in regulating the global climate, protecting biodiversity and sustaining millions of people. For Indigenous Peoples and local communities, the forest is not simply a natural resource; it is their home, heritage, identity and source of life.


Yet this vital ecosystem faces growing threats from mining, logging, oil and gas extraction, deforestation and expanding infrastructure. Across the Congo Basin, rising demand for minerals is increasing pressure on forests and community territories.


Recent investigations have

documented

 mining concessions overlapping with community forests in the DRC, gold-mining-related

forest destruction and water pollution

 in the Republic of Congo, and

concerns over the impacts

 of the Lobé-Kribi iron-ore project on forests and livelihoods in Cameroon.


This exposes a growing contradiction: while governments promote renewable energy as a solution to the climate crisis, the extraction of minerals needed for the energy transition can create new threats to forests, water resources and the communities that depend on them.


For women in the Congo Basin, this is not an abstract debate. It means polluted rivers, disappearing food sources, loss of agricultural land and declining access to forests.


Women on the frontlines expose the cost of extractivism


To strengthen collective resistance, women and community organisations from the DRC, the Republic of Congo and Cameroon came together for a

cross-border solidarity exchange

 to share stories of resistance, expose the impacts of extractivism and develop strategies to defend the Congo Basin.


Over three days, organisations including

Centre d’Encadrement pour la Promotion de la Femme et la jeune fille

 (CEPF),

Dynamique des femmes pour le développement

 (DYFED),

Green Development Advocates

 (GDA), and the Association pour le Respect des Droit des population autochtones et du développement rural et du Droit de l’homme (ARPA2DH)

shared their experiences and struggles. Testimonies from women in Lessoukou, Mayoko, Mangi, Bongonde and Bandzonko revealed the devastating impacts of mining and forest exploitation.


In Lessoukou, 17 of the community’s 24 villages are reportedly occupied by mining companies, threatening access to ancestral lands and traditional livelihoods. Élisé Matsanga, an Indigenous woman from Lessoukou, shared:


“

Agriculture once enabled us to feed our families and send our children to school. Today, because of corporate activities and the loss of access to our lands, we can no longer farm as we used to. We have lost our livelihoods

.”


In Mangi, Tshopo Province, Nyota described how communities are excluded from decisions affecting their territories while rivers become increasingly polluted.


“

We are forced to walk up to three kilometres to find safe drinking water, and sometimes even our children have no choice but to drink polluted water. Our lands, forests and rivers are our sources of livelihood, yet we watch helplessly as they are destroyed

.”


In Bandzonko, Republic of Congo, Odile, the village chief,

described how mining pollution

 has forced women to walk up to 15 kilometres in search of water, exposing families to serious health risks. In Bongonde, Équateur Province, Annie Mboyo, a community woman,

highlighted the disappearance

 of mushrooms, caterpillars, wild fruits and fish, resources that have traditionally sustained community food systems. Meanwhile, in Mayoko, Oko Jeanine, another community woman, denounced the lack of consultation and the destruction of agricultural fields by mining companies.

These lands belong to us. They are our heritage, our livelihoods and our identity. How can companies demand that we obtain permits to cultivate our own land while they extract …

author: Mada Masr
title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.


Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.


After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.


The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.


The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.


The judge then abruptly asked for a lawyer unknown to any member of the defense counsel to be brought in, “in a move that astonished all those present,” said Bahgat, and announced that the court decided to appoint a lawyer for Attalah.


At that point, all members of the defense counsel cried out to reject the court’s appointment of a lawyer when the eight chosen lawyers were present. Attalah herself spoke to say she did not accept the court-appointed lawyer acting on her behalf, an objection the judge refused to have recorded in the session’s minutes.


“In an even more shocking move,” said Bahgat, the judge himself began to log down the requests of the court-appointed lawyer, without the lawyer having said a word. The judge then read out the conviction amid shouts and protests from the defense counsel.


The judge sentenced Attalah to the maximum possible penalty: a LE3 million fine, the closure of Mada Masr’s website and the confiscation of its property.


Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse.

Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure

Mada Masr

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Western Cape hit with tighter water restrictions
content:
The water and sanitation department has issued a warning to residents and businesses in the Western Cape that it will implement a 7% reduction in domestic and industrial water allocations as well as a 15% reduction in water for irrigation. Addressing the media on Monday, Minister of Water and Sanitation, Pemmy Majodina said that the current water in storage in the province is below the preferred operational threshold of 80%.


“While the major dams remain at acceptable levels overall, some key components of the system have recorded significant declines compared to the previous year. Storage levels remain significantly above those experienced during the severe drought period of 2016-2017; yet, the current water storage is below the preferred operational threshold of 80% and approximately 11.9 % points below the ten-year average of 84.49%,” Majodina said.


According to the minister, the decline in stored water resulted from below-average winter rainfall in the province while the looming El Niño event is increasing temperatures and evaporation.


Municipalities are expected to restrict water supply to residents and can impose further restrictions, but by no more than the 7% that the national government has imposed. The department is expected to write a submission to the director general who will approve the restriction and get it gazetted.


“Modelling undertaken by water resource specialists reveals that if water users continue to utilise their full allocations without intervention, the risk of water shortages and mandatory restrictions will increase substantially from 2027 onwards,” said Majodina.


The City of Cape has announced that it will introduce level 1 water restrictions from 1 December 2026.


Rural taps already dry


The Kannaland Local Municipality that covers Ladismith, Calitzdorp and Zoar are already on level 4 water restrictions. Water in the municipality is available for human consumption only.


Carmelitta Juries lives on a farm near Ladismith. While the farm dam is full, the water isn’t safe to drink without first disinfecting it with bleach. Carmelitta said they have no choice but to rely on the unsafe dam water as the municipality offers no alternative. “The municipality promised that they would put up water tanks. One tank could sustain a couple of homes. For example, 10 homes can use one tank, but to date we haven’t heard anything further,” she said.


Zoar resident, Irene Isaacs said that it is harder for the village to access water in summer. Community members without water storage tanks must wait for municipal trucks to deliver water. Elderly residents are especially vulnerable in these circumstances, she said, and depend on members of the community to carry water in buckets to their homes.


Kannaland Municipality is already on level 4 restrictions. File photo by Mandla Mnyakama


Bergriver, Swartland and Saldanha Bay municipalities have been flagged as key areas where water scarcity and aging infrastructure pose significant constraints to future growth unless supply and bulk infrastructure are urgently upgraded. Hendrix Van Wyk from Vredenburg, which falls under Saldanha Bay Municipality, told

Elitsha

 that in poor neighbourhoods like Hopland, Louwville, Selbou and Yskor, the water pressure in the taps is low. “It takes up to 30 minutes to fill up a 5-litre bucket and a 20-litre bucket takes about 2 hours to fill up,” he said.


According to Majodina, construction of the Clanwilliam Dam, which will increase water availability for the West Coast District Municipality, is 40% complete.


Partnership, not privatisation of water

 insists DWS


A

new amendment to the Water Plan

 states that if a municipality is not delivering a clean, safe supply of water, the national government can hand that function over to the private sector. The government has already implemented this in the City of Tshwane where a public-private partnership is taking effect. According to

BusinessTech

, Coca-Cola has partnered with the government to invest R500-million in municipal water infrastructure to stop service delivery from collapsing.


During Cape Town’s severe drought between 2015 and 2018, marked by the

Day Zero Campaign

, water rights groups protested against water guzzlers, and the soft drink manufacturer was one of their targets. At the time, Coca-Cola drew about 530-million litres of water annually from the City of Cape Town to manufacture its products. A litre of Coke requires about 2 litres of …

author: Jessica Holdman
title: South Carolinians Resist Proposed Dominion Energy/NextEra Mega-Merger
content:
The merger would create the world’s largest regulated utility across four states.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

About 30 South Carolinians spoke in opposition to the $67 billion merger of Florida-based NextEra Energy and Virginia-headquartered Dominion Energy during a public hearing Tuesday in Columbia.

The hearing was one of three held by state utility regulators across the Lowcountry and Midlands as they weigh whether to approve the takeover that would create the world’s largest regulated utility. One more set of meetings are scheduled for Dec. 8, from 9 a.m. to noon and 5-9 p.m., both virtual and in person at the Public Service Commission in Columbia.

A final decision is expected by Jan. 29 under a schedule accepted by the commission in August.

If approved, the newly combined company would serve a total of 10 million customers across four of the nation’s fastest-growing states — Florida, North Carolina, Virginia and South Carolina, where Dominion has 820,000 customers.

Opponents of the merger, who protested outside ahead of the hearing, called NextEra’s promise of $2.25 billion worth of monthly bill credits — $10 per every 1,000 kilowatt hours used, lasting two years — “a joke.”

By comparison, the companies offered Virginia four years of credits and $100 million in bill assistance and energy efficiency programs for low-income, disabled and elderly customers. Virginia’s governor is pushing for $29 monthly credits and a six-year rate freeze.

But for many who spoke, even that would not be enough to change their minds.

“No amount of credits or benefits that they promise us makes this a good deal,” said Anjani Moro, a member of the South Carolina Tenant Union and co-founder of the grassroots Stop NextEra SC Coalition. “A mega monopoly, the world’s largest utility company, will not have our interests at heart.”

Even under Dominion, Moro said she’s struggled.

Dominion expanded to South Carolina in 2019 after SCANA, parent company of South Carolina Electric & Gas, abandoned its joint effort with state-owned utility Santee Cooper to expand the V.C. Summer nuclear plant.

SCANA spiraled toward bankruptcy and Dominion Energy bought what was the only Fortune 500 company based in South Carolina.

“Ever since then the points of contact for people have diminished,” Moro said. “I know people that used to be able to pay in person can’t pay in person. And the rates have continued to go up.”

In May, regulators approved Dominion Energy South Carolina for a nearly 8% rate hike — the company’s second increase in two years.

Moro was among those who testified in opposition to the increase, which took effect in July.

“My electric bill was almost $200 when I testified,” Moro told the commissioners Tuesday. “Now it’s almost $400.”

“I’m a mother of a small child,” she added. “I live in a 1,000-square-foot house. When I testified in May, I told y’all that I had to withhold paying health insurance to make sure I could keep up with my rent and my electric bills.”

Then, days after her May testimony, Dominion and NextEra announced their merger intentions.

“Their shareholders get $360 million,” Moro said. “We get $10 a month for two years.”

Others who spoke also shared their monthly Dominion bill amounts: more than $300 in a high energy usage month, $450 when temperatures drop, $387 for natural gas near Florence.

They went on to cite numbers from California-based Energy and Policy Institute, showing NextEra’s Florida Power & Light as having some of the highest profit margins in the country.

The numbers, which come from Federal Energy Regulatory Commission filings, put Florida Power & Light’s net income at $5 million in 2025.

The institute estimates 27% of customers’ monthly bills go to pay for that — the highest of the 79 utility companies analyzed nationwide.

Dominion Energy South Carolina ranked 41st, with 15% of customers’ bills going to company profits.

“They (NextEra) are a company that comes and just tries to acquire other utilities, and their goal is to make as much money as possible,” Moro said.

NextEra has sought for years to expand by acquiring other utilities, though with little success.

Deals to purchase Hawaiian Electric, Texas-based Oncor and Duke Energy all fell through, as did NextEra’s bid to buy South Carolina’s state-owned utility Santee Cooper in the wake of the failed V.C. Summer …

author: Randi Beers
title: News quiz Nov. 21 | Old traditions and new beginnings
content:
The holidays are again approaching and there’s lots to remember: gifts, Christmas parties, cards, holiday concerts, family visits — and don’t forget the turkey. But do you remember the events of last week? Let’s find out.


1.

 The public got a chance to see inside Nunavut’s new Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre during an open house on Nov. 14. The centre will offer various services to assist residents recovering from addiction. Which amenity is not included at the facility?


A.

 A daycare


B.

 A country food processing area


C.

 An Olympic-sized swimming pool


2.

 The Qikiqtani Inuit Association opposes a finding by the Nunavut Impact Review Board that a planned hydro project for Iqaluit does not need a full public review. Which company is behind the project?


A.

 Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp.


B.

 Arctic Fresh Projects Ltd.


C.

 Qulliq Energy Corp.


3.

 Iqaluit-born artist Aija Komangapik helped paint a new mural at the University of Ottawa. What did she illustrate?


A.

 A number of sea creatures, real and mythical, including narwhal, a grey seal and Sedna.


B.

 Traditional practices being passed down through generations.


C.

 A map of Inuit Nunangat that shows how all the regions are culturally connected.


4.

 What new powers would proposed Bill S-8 give police?


A.

 The authority to search people’s luggage before boarding regional northern flights.


B.

 The authority to intercept mail.


C.

 The authority to open anybody’s Christmas presents without a search warrant.


5.

 Speaking of police, an investigation in Ottawa led to the seizure of five kilograms of cocaine alleged to be destined to Nunavut. How many doses of cocaine did police estimate they kept off the streets?


A.

 5,000


B.

 50,000


C.

 500,000


Nunavut Justice Minister George Hickes, left, and Nunavut RCMP commanding officer Chief Supt. Kent Pike discuss drug-trafficking routes into Nunavut during a news conference in Iqaluit on April 15. (File photo by Arty Sarkisian)


Answers:


1.

 C — The $83.7-million Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre

will have a little something

 for everybody — a sewing room, daycare, area for processing country food and a group therapy room. But there is no pool.


2.

 A — Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp. is behind the $500-million proposal to build a hydro plant for Iqaluit. The company is owned by Qikiqtaaluk Corp., which is owned by QIA. This means QIA is

requesting

 a full public review of its own project.


3.

 B — Artist Aija Komangapik’s portion of the mural includes a seal, narhwhal, blue whale and walrus. “The creation for all the animals starts in the ocean, and for Inuit, it starts with Sedna,” she said to Nunatsiaq News

in an interview

.


4.

 B — Don’t worry, nobody is going through your presents without a search warrant. But if passed, Bill S-8 would give police the

power to intercept mail

 if they believe a package holds illicit items such as alcohol or drugs. (They would still need a search warrant.)


5.

B — Police

estimate

 a cocaine seizure they executed in August kept 50,000 doses of cocaine out of the territory. No charges have been announced in relation to the seizure.

author: Brittany Boschman, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Guardians of the Buffalo: New bison-care guide supports efforts to bring iconic species home
content:
The three authors behind a new bison-care manual,

Guardians of the Buffalo

, speak about their book at ‘Fort Qu’Appelle, Sask.’ in September during this year’s Treaty 4 Gathering. From left: the book’s photographer Johane Janelle, and co-writers Wes Olson and Cody Spencer.

 Photo by Brittany Boschman


Under the bright September sun, school buses arrived and departed from the valley as an announcer’s voice carried across the powwow grounds.


Youth chatted, learned and moved between tipis for hands-on demonstrations during the 40th Annual Treaty 4 Gathering in Fort Qu’Appelle, Saskatchewan.


Inside one of the canvas tipis, a Buffalo hide lay near the entrance, where co-authors Wes Olson and Cody Spencer sat with photographer Johane Janelle to introduce a new book on bison care.


The presentation was part of a September book tour for

Guardians of the Buffalo: The Essential Guide to Bison Care

, which offers practical guidance for Indigenous communities, farmers and others interested in restoring and caring for bison herds


Spencer himself was first introduced to bison — and inspired to work as a rancher and herd manager — thanks to Olson’s first book,

Portraits of the Bison

, which was co-written with Janelle, his spouse.


“I just caught the bug,” Spencer recalled, “and I just had to figure out ways to get involved with the species.”


He said the book grew out of the questions he and Olson have received from people interested in starting their own bison herds.


“One of the most frequent questions I’ve had during that time was from people who want to get into the industry: How do I start?” Olson said. “Where do I even begin?”


The Fort Qu’Appelle event took place on Sept. 17, during the

annual gathering

 to honour the 1874 treaty’s spirit and intent, bringing communities together to celebrate culture and share teachings with the next generations. Youth from surrounding communities attended the week-long gathering for its education days.


Decades of bison stewardship


Olson spent 32 years working in national parks, much of that time focused on bison management and establishing new wild populations. Spencer is a bison rancher from southwest Alberta who has managed several herds in Alberta and Texas.


“We’ve also been in the bison industry, raising bison in captivity for a long time,” Olson said. “Between us, I think we calculated 87 years of bison stewardship.”


Spencer grew up on a farm where his family raised grain and cattle. He said his lack of experience with bison initially allowed him to approach the animals without bringing assumptions about cattle management into his work.


“I didn’t have direct experience with bison, which can be a benefit for a lot of people,” Spencer said. “You’re not coming into management with preconceptions about how you need to be managing cattle and applying that to buffalo.”


He said his work has focused on finding management practices that benefit both the animals and the land.


READ MORE:


In Manitoba, a growing herd of bagwaji-bizhikiwag offers lessons in community


“We’re just always committed to finding out what are the best ways that we can manage these animals and caretake them for their own health,” Spencer said, “but also the health of the land.”


The book is intended to help readers understand the responsibilities involved in establishing and managing a herd. Its opening chapter includes a questionnaire to help readers consider the responsibilities involved in establishing and managing a herd.


“This is a manual,” Spencer said. “This is

the

 manual.”


The remaining chapters combine technical information about bison management with cultural, ecological and conservation perspectives. Topics include animal care, fencing, water systems, handling facilities, herd management and land restoration. 


“There’s a lot that you need to know, and so it’s all in the book,” Spencer said.


One section of the book compares the physical characteristics of wood and plains buffalo, helping readers understand how to tell the two types apart. It also explains why maintaining genetic integrity is important when establishing and managing herds.


Guardians of the Buffalo

 explains differences between wood and plains bison, including why preserving their genetic integrity is important.

Image courtesy International Buffalo Relations Institute


‘How to care for life’


The book is intended for a broad audience, including ranchers, conservationists, Indigenous …

author: Jaharra Anglin Stubbs
title: Family Caregivers Month: The Economic Burden of Unpaid Care
content:
Every November, National Family Caregivers Month recognizes the millions of Americans who provide care to their loved ones. Caregivers are adult children, spouses, partners, and other loved ones who complete daily tasks and maintain their quality of life. While caregiving is often an expression of love and family responsibility, it also comes with high financial, physical, and emotional costs that frequently go unrecognized.

More than 63 million Americans provide ongoing care for adults or children with complex medical conditions or disabilities. Of these, 59 million care for adults. Around 10% of U.S. adults are caregivers for parents aged 65 or older, while another 3% care for an aging spouse or partner.

The financial burden is particularly pronounced among lower-income households. Among adults with an aging parent, spouse, or partner, 39% of those with lower incomes identify as caregivers, compared with 23% of middle-income adults and 16% of upper-income adults. For caregivers whose household income is less than $40,000, nearly one-third of their income goes toward out-of-pocket expenses related to their loved ones’ needs.

The financial demands of caregiving can be substantial. Every year, $1 trillion in family caregiving services goes unpaid. Housing and household needs account for the largest share of expenses, at 42%, with home modifications for safety making up 29%, and 37% going to insurance premiums, co-pays, and other medical expenses not covered by insurance.

Yet 65% of working caregivers experience work-related disruptions. These can include needing time off and finding extra work to cover these expenses. These disparities also vary dramatically across racial and ethnic minority groups and by region.

These financial burdens are not distributed equally across racial and ethnic groups. AAPI caregivers report an average cost of $16,716. Black caregivers spend a high share of their household income, averaging 52%, while Hispanic and Latinx communities report the greatest financial strain among the racial and ethnic groups surveyed by AARP. By comparison, White caregivers spend about 24% of their household income on caregiving.

Regionally, caregivers in the Mid-Atlantic spend twice as much on average as caregivers in the West North Central region, reflecting the cost-of-living crisis. However, costs are not the only issue to consider as we reflect on the holistic effort of caregiving.

Beyond these financial costs, caregiving remains a deeply gendered responsibility. Women are more likely than men to identify as caregivers. In the U.S., 28% of women with aging parents or spouses or partners consider themselves caregivers, compared with only 23% of men. Forty-seven percent of women, versus 30% of men, experience a negative impact on their emotional well-being, and 38% of women experience negative impacts on their health while serving as caregivers for their loved ones. Outside formal caregiving, women provide most informal caregiving, often becoming hands-on health providers, care managers, care advocates, companions, and decision-makers.

As we recognize National Family Caregivers Month, it is important to acknowledge not only the dedication of caregivers but also the financial sacrifices and inequalities they face. Caregiving is rooted in love, but it is also sacrificial. If you or anyone you know is serving as a caregiver, show them a little more love this month so they know they are cared for.

author: By Sean Summers, Unicorn Riot
title: Two Palestine Solidarity Activists Refuse to Testify Before a Grand Jury
content:
Merrimack County, NH — In November 2023, Sophie Ross and Bridget Shergalis approached a large industrial building in Merrimack, New Hampshire. The structure houses Elbit Systems of America, the domestic branch of an Israeli weapons manufacturer that’s a key supplier of drones and ground equipment used in the country’s ongoing

genocide in Palestine

.


The two were participating in an action organized by Palestine Action U.S. Some blockaded the road leading to the facility while Shergalis and Ross, along with others, continued to the building.


A few protesters stayed on the ground and sprayed the facade with red paint, sealed doors shut with a bike lock, and broke windows. Shergalis and Ross made their ways to the building’s roof and lit flares to announce their presence while attempting to damage the building’s HVAC system.


Both women were arrested that day, along with Calla Walsh. Paige Belanger, another participant, was arrested days later. All four were

charged with multiple felonies

 that could have brought decades in prison if convicted. After a legal battle, and a series of victories, Shergalis, Ross, Belanger and Walsh were

sentenced to 60 days jail time

 for misdemeanor convictions.


See all of our Palestine coverage


Nearly three years after that action, Shergalis and Ross have been subpoenaed to testify in front of a federal grand jury. The reason for the subpoena isn’t clear, but one thing is: both women are refusing to cooperate.


On October 5, Bridget woke up to strangers knocking on her window. When her partner answered, he found people dressed in unassuming clothes. Only after he asked what they wanted did the couple realize what was happening. The strangers were FBI agents there to serve her a subpoena to testify before a grand jury.


She told the agents to leave their contact info and expect to hear from her attorney, Kira Kelly. Ross was spared the door knock after agents delivered a subpoena to Kelly, the attorney representing both of the women.


The document simply ordered both women, individually, to appear in the U.S. District Court in Concord, New Hampshire on October 21, only 16 days out from the delivery of the subpoena.


No other details that clarify the target or goals of the investigation appear in the subpoena, and both Shergalis and Ross, along with their lawyer, are unclear about the reason behind the order. While Kelly told Unicorn Riot an assistant U.S. attorney told them it’s in relation to the 2023 action, no more information was made available to them, leaving everyone but prosecutors to speculate about the motivation behind the investigation.


While details are sparse, reporting from the time of the action and recent developments suggest the grand jury may be related to the Cox Media heir and controversial left-wing benefactor James Cox “Fergie” Chambers Jr.


Chambers participated in the November 2023 Elbit protest where Shergalis and Ross were arrested. In a 2024

profile in Rolling Stone

, Chambers told a reporter he had fled the country after the action for fear that he may be implicated in a racketeering case for his involvement. Chambers insisted in that interview that he wasn’t doing anything wrong by moving to Tunisia, but that he was scared of facing RICO charges.


In July, Chambers was arrested in Ibiza, Spain and he’s been held in the country since while awaiting the

outcome of an extradition order under consideration

 by the Spanish government. The U.S. has asked authorities in Spain to send Chambers back to this country to face charges on a still-sealed indictment.


Related:

Anarchist Hacker Jeremy Hammond Summoned to Testify in Front of Grand Jury


More important to Shergalis and Ross than the who or why of the grand jury’s convening, though, is the principle behind the practice and the pair’s moral objection to the process. The thought of betraying a political movement both say they’re committed to is unacceptable to them.


“I would like to be able to, like, look other people in the eye and sleep at night and all of that good stuff,” Shergalis told Unicorn Riot. “And that’s, that isn’t possible with testifying. It just isn’t, it wouldn’t be.”


By openly opposing the subpoena from the start, both hope to establish that they cannot be coerced into testifying. That’s a key distinction in how things may play out.


Under the

law

, people who refuse to testify after being subpoenaed to a

grand jury

 might be sentenced to jail time for being …

author: Valerie Anne
title: LGBTQ+ Representation in Television Hits Devastating Lows
content:
As I’m sure you’ve noticed, LGBTQ+ representation in media is at the lowest it’s been in over a decade.

GLAAD’s latest Where We Are in TV study showed some bleak results that reflect the state of the country due to the hateful administration we live under and the wealthy conservatives who own most of the media conglomerates. Trans representation took the biggest hit, going from 33 characters to a measly SEVEN, and since three of them were on shows that were cancelled and four are from limited series, none of those seven will be returning next season. NONE. Devastating.

Twenty-five percent of LGBTQ+ characters have left our screens since last year, which brings the stats to their lowest point in over a decade. Cable television hit a 16-year low. BLEAK.

Streamers have more queer representation than cable and broadcast characters put together, but we have lost almost 100 characters from streamers as well, so even that isn’t great news. And combining streaming, cable, and broadcast, of all LGBTQ+ characters, 44% of them are characters of color, which is the lowest percentage since GLAAD’s 2017-2018 report.

Pride points out that it seems wild to imagine because some of the buzziest shows of the last few years feature queer characters: The Hunting Wives, Hazbin Hotel, Pluribus, Stranger Things, Heated Rivalry. I don’t think this show made it into the count, but we also have Sterling Point and now The Body. Queer people show up for shows that feature them, and queer people are great at telling unique stories. Alas, too many higher-ups lean on outdated Christian ideals and won’t invest in us in an effort to silence us.

This is especially wild because, while it reflects what the political times want you to believe (that queer people are outsiders, among other things), it doesn’t reflect the actual statistics. Every generation reports identifying as gayer than the last, so representation should also be at a steady increase to reflect reality, not a drastic decrease.

The actual numbers of LGBTQ+ characters on broadcast and cable shows are harrowing to look at. There are dozens of characters on any given TV show, and dozens of shows on each network, and yet the highest number among them is HBO with 15 characters. The second-highest is a big drop down, with Fox and Starz coming in with 10 characters each.

The numbers start off a little more promising for streaming, with 116 on Netflix, but then they also start dropping dramatically, with 68 on Prime Video and then again a steep drop to Hulu with 24.

I’m sure you, like I have, felt the shift even before you saw these numbers. Here at Autostraddle, we used to have to have a weekly TV roundup because there were so many queer characters on cable and broadcast shows that we couldn’t keep up with individual recaps. We used to do Pop Culture Fix twice a week to keep up with the news coming at us from all angles. And now there aren’t enough recurring characters for a weekly roundup and barely enough news for 10-15 links a week in a pop culture roundup.

It’s disheartening to see these numbers go down more and more every year when we were in such a steady incline for so long, but the fact is: We’re still here. We’re still out here writing well-rounded characters and telling our stories and watching and supporting the LGBTQ+ characters we DO still have on TV. We will not go quietly into the night. We will keep shouting and keep showing up for the queer shows doing it right until these numbers make sense again.

More queer pop culture news (that’s less depressing)

+ Phoebe Bridgers was the musical guest on this weekend’s SNL

+ Former wee lesbian (on Derry Girls) Nicola Coughlan doubles down on her pro-trans, anti-Harry Potter stance and we love her for it

+ Rapper Young Miko has been dubbed the “Sexiest Lesbian Alive” by Curve magazine

+ Aspyn Ovard exposes fellow ex-Mormon socialites to the …

author: Gaurav Kumar
title: How India’s Cockroach movement maintains nonviolent discipline
content:
This article

How India’s Cockroach movement maintains nonviolent discipline

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


On Nov. 7, the eve of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, the leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP, including founder Abhijeet Dipke, were not at home. They were marching in Kochi, a port city in the southern state of Kerala, nearly 1,300 miles from Delhi. 


The march echoed the two demands the movement had been shouting in Delhi’s streets since the first week of October: Scrap the nationwide recheck of voter rolls that began in June 2025, and sack the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. 


The Cockroach movement came into being in May of this year and won its first victory in July, pushing India’s education minister out of office over a leaked national medical entrance exam. The open question then was whether

a movement with no one leader and no office

 would still be around after winning its first fight. It is, and while it still has no office, it has picked a much bigger fight. Not an exam this time, but the vote itself.


The Election Commission, which runs India’s elections, is rechecking every one of India’s nearly one billion voters. In the name of clearing the rolls of the dead, the duplicated, people who have moved and what its

June 2025 order

 called “foreign illegal immigrants,” it has

purged more than 130 million

 voters. In Delhi alone, the cleanup has knocked 4.76 million people, nearly a third of the city’s electorate, off the voter list. 


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, strongly backs the recheck, saying that it’s necessary to strike undocumented migrants from neighboring Bangladesh, particularly Muslims, who have slipped onto the rolls. Amit Shah, Modi’s home minister and most powerful lieutenant, has defended the recheck as a way to “detect, delete, deport” what he calls infiltrators.

But critics charge

 that the rolls are being manipulated to benefit the BJP. They say the recheck shifts the burden of proof onto voters, and that the people least likely to have the required documents are the ones being dropped. 


Human Rights Watch found

 that the purge has disproportionately affected women, the poor and Muslims; in one area of West Bengal that is nine percent Muslim, more than 92 percent of those deleted were Muslim.

Opposition leaders

 have called the recheck a backdoor version of the National Register of Citizens, a citizenship list the BJP promised in 2019 to extend across India.


Presiding over it all is Kumar, whose commission both referees India’s elections and runs the recheck. He was handpicked by Modi in February 2025 under a new law giving Modi more power over the selection, in a decision announced late at night over the written dissent of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi.


In late September, the national daily

The Indian Express


reported

 that two of the election commission’s three members, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had objected on record at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions and orders tied to the recheck that they say were issued in the commission’s name without their knowledge. (In an official statement, the commission maintained that all of its decisions on the recheck were unanimous.) 


Previous Coverage


What India’s Cockroach Party won — and what’s next


The Cockroach movement, which had been pressuring the government since July over broken promises, responded by calling Kumar the biggest threat to India’s democracy and giving him 48 hours to resign.


When Kumar ignored the movement’s deadline, it took to the streets of Delhi and other cities on Oct. 2, the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, who led India’s nonviolent struggle for independence.


Unlike most Indian police forces, Delhi’s police do not answer to the city’s elected government but to the federal Home Ministry, run by Shah. It answered the protests the way it did in July, only harder. On Oct. 10 police detained more than 2,000 people in Delhi, opposition leaders and journalists among them, while about 600 were detained in Mumbai, India’s financial capital, and mobile internet went dark in the heart of Delhi.


Two days later

, Jantar Mantar — a square just a short walk from Parliament that has been Delhi’s main protest site for decades and was occupied by the movement for five weeks this summer — was …

author: David S. D'Amato
title: La Via Libertaria all’egalitarismo
content:
Di

David S. D’amato

. Originale:

The Libertarian Road to Egalitarianism

, del 14 novembre 2014. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Secondo uno

studio recente di Emmanuel Saez e Gabriel Zucman per l’Ufficio nazionale per la ricerca economica

, “

lo 0,1% delle famiglie [americane] possiede tanta ricchezza quanto il 90% meno ricco

”. Sempre secondo lo studio, la tanto declamata “ripresa” non ha raggiunto la classe media; i benefici sono andati alla cima della piramide.


Mentre una piccola frazione della popolazione ammassa gran parte della ricchezza nazionale, esperti e accademici accusano e offrono soluzioni. Com’è facile immaginare, si accusa il libero mercato di causare differenze crescenti di ricchezza e reddito. Fautori delle liberalizzazioni e del libero mercato, i libertari sono spesso accusati di vivere in un mondo di fantasia, di ignorare il problema della disuguaglianza.


Siamo noi stessi a farlo: quando si arriva al dunque, troppi si sentono a disagio, si difendono sostenendo che la disuguaglianza

non è

 un problema, e che bisogna invece vedere lo stile di vita o qualche altro parametro. “Il capitalismo è un bene per i poveri!” Invece i libertari dovrebbero accettare il semplice fatto che la disuguaglianza è un grosso problema.


Non dobbiamo vedere nella disuguaglianza un punto debole del discorso sulla libertà economica, o una questione irrisolvibile. Le attuali relazioni economiche non sono il risultato della libertà di scambio o della legittima proprietà privata. In fatto di disuguaglianza, la ragione sta dalla parte dei libertari. Libertà e eguaglianza sono di fatto complementari, si rafforzano reciprocamente: dalla prima deriva la seconda.


Anarchici individualisti come Lysander Spooner sostenevano che “ricchezza e povertà estreme” sono il risultato del “diritto positivo”, sostituiscono il diritto naturale con un diritto arbitrario, “danno vita a monopoli e privilegi”. Sotto il capitalismo, spiega, chi possiede un certo capitale ha un particolare potere economico che non ha niente a che vedere con la libertà di produrre, scambiare e competere. In un’ottica generale, l’intervento dello stato beneficia chi è ricco e ha appoggi politici, oltre alle élite che possono influire su chi scrive e applica le regole che tutti dobbiamo rispettare.


Il meccanismo non è perfetto, e per questo sopra il capitalismo monopolistico troviamo tutto uno strato di misure chiaramente intese a proteggere i lavoratori, i consumatori e i poveri. Ma nessuna di queste misure riesce a intaccare l’obiettivo di fondo dell’intervento statale, il quale espropria i legittimi proprietari e mette le masse al servizio dei datori di lavoro. L’obiettivo storico dello stato, in breve, è la lotta di classe permanente, l’uso del proprio potere per tenere al sicuro un’aristocrazia socioeconomica.


La sinistra istituzionale ha certamente ragione sull’uguaglianza, ma tende a sbagliare in fatto di libertà, diritti individuali e mercato. L’anarchismo di mercato è per la libertà

ma anche

 per l’uguaglianza, e vuole una società senza stato in cui la legge ultima sia la parità di libertà e autorità.


La vera competizione aperta è una forza che ha il potere di dissolvere e disperdere. I libertari dovrebbero smettere di giustificare le attuali sconcertanti disuguaglianze come se fossero il risultato del

laissez-faire

 e della sovranità individuale.


Le nostre traduzioni sono finanziate interamente da donazioni. Se vi piace quello che scriviamo, siete invitati a contribuire. Trovate le istruzioni su come fare nella pagina

Sostieni C4SS

:

https://c4ss.org/sostieni-c4ss

.

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: 6- Cuttings will regrow – Sitting-in for Grandmother Cottonwood
content:
On July 27th, 2026 the U.S. government and Fisher industries cut down three ancient cottonwood trees in a small town called Lochiel, Arizona in order to build not just one but two border walls. This area is the habitat of the endangered Mexican Wolf as well as jaguars, bears, foxes and many other bizarre, beautiful bugs and animals. It is also the home of the Tohono O’odham people, important to many indigenous tribes on both sides of the border. When the three grandmother cottonwoods were cut, one brave comrade stood in front of construction equipment, preventing the destruction of the last ancient tree and the construction of the border wall. In that last tree, we began our tree sit. With the support of hundreds of activists, the land owners, nearby towns and tribes, and even the local sheriff department, we halted construction of the walls for 75 days.

For 75 days, activists sat in the remaining cottonwood as ground support grew into a sprawling camp. It was the first tree sit to stop border wall construction and was briefly the first binational tree sit in history, with a sit erecting on the Mexican side for three days in August. During these 75 days, O:shad camp, jaguar in O’odham, held morning ceremony in the easement, the road which enforced the border. Ceremony frequently extended to effectively halt all construction vehicles for the day, or days at a time. People fell in love, they danced in the mud, cooked communal meals, all while defending the land. Utopia felt nearby.

Then, on October 5th, hundreds of border patrol officers, accompanied by turning point usa, invaded O:shad camp. They cut down the grandmother cottonwood and forcibly removed the tree sitter without a proper extraction team, risking her life. Activists on the ground circled the trunk to protect the tree and continue their resistance against the wall. More than 10 activists were arrested and many more brutalized. Though on private property and with no warrant, they ransacked the camp and destroyed our belongings.

Indigenous and non-white activists were singled out and beaten much worse than white comrades. Border Patrol violently pushed, pulled and dragged, but also kneeled on throats, punched eyes, pushed skin into barbed wire. They specifically targeted our medic (who is Indigenous) to be violently dragged, beaten, and arrested. They prevented our media team from capturing what happened, while escorting Turning Point USA to film the day in order to spread their right wing propaganda.

The next day, as Border Patrol expanded their boundaries further into private property to make way for the wall, five more of us were taken, and lawyers were unable to find them in the system while border patrol ignored calls from their lawyers, friends and family.

A day later, my comrade locked herself to a cement truck and stayed in a stress position without food or water for 7 hours while Border Patrol covered her with an emergency blanket despite the hot climate. One officer told her and the other officers that they should drive her to the middle of nowhere where no one would be able to hear her scream. They began to move the vehicle with her still above the tire; we all thought she would be killed. Two comrades who ran towards her, worried for her life, were tackled, brutalized, and arrested – one was sexually assaulted during her arrest. Finally they brought in an expert extractor who took her out of lockdown and she was taken to detention and then federal prison. She is now facing federal assault charges.

The rest of us were shot with pepper balls, tear gassed, leaving us vomiting, injured, bruised and emotionally exhausted. After the tree sitter was removed from the grandmother tree in Lochiel, a comrade reinstated the sit on the mexico side. Cut off from ground support by border patrol, she went over two days without food or water. When mexican firefighters and Fisher construction workers went to pull her out, she free climbed further up the tree. They destroyed her platform and life sustaining materials, leaving her to perch in the cottonwood branches without a platform or supplies. She suffered dehydration and starvation in high heat but still managed to keep a backpack on her, which she filled with clippings of the Abuela tree so that no matter what happened, the trees offspring could be replanted.

The following day the wall continued.

In total 30+ of us have been arrested, and many more brutalized, injured, and traumatized. We are the …

author: Admin101
title: Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago
content:
We’re thrilled to announce the formation of three new Locals of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN)! From the Texas Hill Country, to the Great Lakes, to the Northeast, our organization is growing deeper roots and expanding our capacity to organize, struggle, and build popular power in communities across the country.


As you will read below, each new local grows out of its members’ deep involvement in the popular struggles of their neighborhoods, workplaces, and broader communities. What follows are brief introductions in their members’ own words — including their contact info and social media handles.


Austin, TX


The Austin Local has officially re-formed! Our members are primarily focused on labor and tenant organizing, as well as rapid response to ICE. We are also making preparations for an open reading group to discuss

BRRN’s Program

.


We welcome those with interest to contact us.


Email:

 austin@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_atx


Chicago, IL


The Chicago local is back! Our logo honors the Haymarket Martyrs Memorial — a symbol of the organizers who made anarchism a powerful current in immigrant and women workers’ struggles of their time, as well as the place we gathered for our first event all together as a local. 


We carry their memory with us alongside others as we work in the social movements where we are rooted. These include tenant struggles on the South and Northwest sides, as well as labor organizing in the Chicago Teachers Union. We look forward to deepening our connections with comrades in our movements and others through collective study and struggle.


Email:

 chicago@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_chicago

 


New York City, NY


Members of the New York City Local organize with tenants, neighbors, youth, coworkers, and parents to build Black, Brown, and working-class popular power throughout the city. Sites of social insertion include the Astoria Tenant Union in Queens, anticarceral youth and parent programs in Manhattan, immigrant defense coalitions in Brooklyn, the American Association of University Professors, and more. True to BRRN’s internationalist character, we also organize within the Palestinian and Sudanese solidarity movements.


From the Young Lords to Occupy Wall Street, we recognize the integral role that revolutionaries in NYC have played in past freedom struggles and look forward to reviving organized anarchism in the especifista tradition across the five boroughs.

BRRN’s Program

 serves as a blueprint for renewed efforts to confront imperial and capitalist violence as anarchist militants living at the nexus of US empire and global capital .


Email:

 nyc@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:

 @blackrose_nyc


Are you organizing at your workplace, on your campus, or in your neighborhood? Looking for a political home in which you can strategize with others about how to build power, force concessions, and push our mass movements in a revolutionary direction?


Black Rose/Rosa Negra could be right for you.


Read our

Join

 page and send us a membership inquiry!

Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago

Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation

author: Joshua Davis, Whitney K. Taylor
title: Federal Government Is Targeting Officials Who Are Trying to Hold ICE Accountable
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


In the months leading up to the 2026 midterm elections, congressional Republicans and federal prosecutors have targeted dozens of local officials in cities and counties across the country that have adopted some sanctuary policies. The investigations have increasingly focused on prosecutors and law enforcement officers, many of whom have publicly announced plans to go after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents who commit crimes in their jurisdictions or refuse demands to cooperate with federal immigration policing.


In total, 65 officials in 16 states have been targeted since January, according to a review of documents released by the

House Judiciary


Committee

 and the

Department of Justice

 (DOJ), as well as interviews with senior officials who have direct knowledge of individual investigations. The House Judiciary Committee has issued subpoenas and other demands for testimony, documents, and records to more than 40 officials, 15 of them local prosecutors. Alongside that, the DOJ has initiated investigations into 50 local or state officials since 2025, including five involving local prosecutors. In all, 17 local prosecutors have been swept up in House Judiciary or DOJ investigations and lawsuits related to immigration policies.


House Judiciary Committee Chair Rep. Jim Jordan said in a recent

report

 that “Democrats’ open-borders policies at the federal level and sanctuary policies at the state and local level allow millions of illegal aliens to pour into the country and ensure that criminal aliens, after encountered by local law enforcement, are released back into American communities,” echoing language the committee has commonly used in its investigations.


Many experts describe these investigations as unprecedented, and view the move as retaliation against local officials who refuse to cooperate with federal immigration agents or threaten legal action against ICE officers.


“These [prosecutors] are being intentionally intimidated by congressional and federal authorities,” said Mona Sahaf, the director of the Reshaping Prosecution initiative at the Vera Institute of Justice. “The use of [the] DOJ to target perceived political opponents is new. It’s busting norms, and it’s highly dangerous.”


The targeting of local prosecutors appears to be a matter of policy in the second Trump administration. “

Sanctuary Jurisdictions Directives

” issued by the attorney general’s office on February 5, 2025, held that the DOJ Civil Rights Division should “identify state and local laws, policies, and practices that facilitate violations of federal immigration laws or impede lawful federal immigration operations,” and “where appropriate, take legal action to challenge such laws, policies, or practices.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up


The DOJ, in a June 18

press release

 announcing an investigation into local officials in Philadelphia — including District Attorney Larry Krasner — concerning a policy prohibiting federal agents from wearing masks, said that its “series of lawsuits brought by the Civil Division” targeted “illegal policies designed to thwart federal law enforcement across the country.”


Rebecca Roiphe, the Joseph Solomon Distinguished Professor of Law at New York Law School, said the investigations into local prosecutors represented “a wholesale abandonment” of the principle of separation between the DOJ and the political branches of government. “This administration has pretty openly suggested that it is normal and appropriate and even laudable for the political branches to have some degree of control over the Department of Justice,” she said.


Referring to the DOJ investigations, Roiphe said, “The bottom line is that these federal prosecutions can end up threatening local prosecutors to fall in line with federal priorities, and that’s illegitimate in our system.”


These overlapping investigations, reports, and the DOJ directives follow the Heritage Foundation’s

Project 2025 threat to “initiate legal action against” prosecutors

 who refuse to adhere to the priorities of the Trump administration. For many of the targeted prosecutors, the political influence has become impossible to ignore.


Among the targeted is Parisa Dehghani-Tafti, the top prosecutor in Arlington, Virginia, who drew the ire of Representative Jordan’s …

author: anred
title: Ya son cuatro los obreros muertos por la explosión y crece la responsabilidad empresarial y estatal
content:
La explosión ocurrida el 13 de noviembre en Remedios de Escalada se cobró otras dos vidas. Matías Leguizamón y Juan José Servín, trabajadores de la empresa tercerizada Exgadet, fallecieron como consecuencia de las graves heridas sufridas durante el estallido. Ya son cuatro los trabajadores muertos. Una tragedia que expone la precarización laboral, la tercerización de tareas estratégicas, la falta de controles y una política de desregulación que coloca las ganancias empresariales por encima de la vida. Por ANRed


La tragedia de Remedios de Escalada suma dos nuevas víctimas. Este sábado se confirmó el fallecimiento de Matías Leguizamón y Juan José Servín, ambos operarios de Exgadet, la empresa contratada por MetroGAS para realizar trabajos de renovación de la red de distribución de gas. Los dos permanecían internados desde la explosión del viernes 13 de noviembre.


Sus muertes se suman a las de Marcelo García, de 47 años, y Néstor Julián D’Alessandro, de 44, trabajadores de MetroGAS que también perdieron la vida como consecuencia del estallido. De esta manera, asciende a cuatro el número de obreros fallecidos en un siniestro que dejó además decenas de heridos, viviendas y comercios destruidos y familias que todavía no saben cuándo podrán regresar a sus hogares.


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida de Agencia de Noticias Red Acción (@anredaccion)


No se trata de una fatalidad ni de un accidente inevitable. Lo ocurrido es un crimen social ligado al modelo de prestación de servicios públicos en el que las empresas concesionarias delegan tareas de riesgo en contratistas, fragmentan las responsabilidades y trasladan los costos de la reducción de gastos a quienes ponen el cuerpo en el trabajo y a las comunidades que viven alrededor de las obras.


La tercerización como negocio y como riesgo


La investigación deberá determinar las responsabilidades penales y técnicas, pero hay elementos que ya permiten dimensionar la gravedad de lo ocurrido. La explosión se produjo durante trabajos con una tuneladora que habría perforado una cañería de gas. La máquina pertenecía a Exgadet, contratista de MetroGAS.


Uno de los puntos centrales es qué sucedió después de la rotura. Según la propia presentación de MetroGAS ante la Justicia, un inspector de la distribuidora informó sobre el daño de la cañería a las 9:44, y reiteró el aviso a las 9:51. A las 10:06, una vecina también alertó sobre la pérdida de gas. La explosión y el incendio se produjeron posteriormente.


La Justicia investiga si se incumplieron los protocolos de emergencia y secuestró la máquina perforadora para realizar peritajes. Hasta el momento, la investigación busca establecer las responsabilidades de las empresas y de quienes intervinieron en las tareas.


La tercerización no es un detalle administrativo. Es una modalidad empresarial que permite reducir costos, fragmentar responsabilidades y precarizar las condiciones de trabajo en actividades que requieren experiencia, capacitación y controles permanentes. En este caso, cuatro trabajadores terminaron muertos.


La Asociación del Personal Jerárquico de la Industria del Gas (APJ GAS) había advertido sobre estos problemas incluso antes de que se conociera la magnitud de la tragedia. En un comunicado del 14 de noviembre denunció que la tercerización sistemática profundiza la precarización, fragmenta los controles, dificulta la aplicación de normas de seguridad y debilita la capacitación continua de los trabajadores.


El sindicato también señaló que había denunciado anteriormente las irregularidades y los métodos de trabajo de empresas contratistas como Exgadet, que presta servicios para MetroGAS y Naturgy Ban. Según la organización, ni las concesionarias ni el Estado escucharon esas advertencias.


Desregulación: el Estado que se retira y las empresas que avanzan


Lo sucedido en Remedios de Escalada tampoco puede separarse del contexto político y económico. El gobierno de Javier Milei impulsa una política de desregulación, flexibilización laboral y reducción de los controles estatales que presenta como una condición para favorecer las inversiones y liberar las fuerzas del mercado.


La reforma laboral promovida por el Gobierno, el debilitamiento de los organismos de control y la transferencia de responsabilidades hacia el sector privado forman parte de una misma orientación política: garantizar mejores condiciones para la rentabilidad empresarial, aun cuando eso implique deteriorar …

author: La Zarzamora
title: Comunicado Público de pu weichafe que siguen defendiendo la Mapu
content:
Damos a conocer un pensamiento, un actuar de individuos personas convencidas, comprometidas en las luchas dignas de zonas, territorios a lo largo de esta franja de tierra que denominaron Chile.

Queremos hacer un llamado a todas las personas, agrupaciones, comunidades, hogares, a los familiares de los presos políticos, a los que defienden la naturaleza, la ñuke mapu, contra este gobierno y sistema fascista, que solamente busca conseguir sus propios objetivos y privilegios sin importar el daño que hacen en general.

También enviamos este mensaje por la preocupación que tenemos hacia los territorios que están amenazados por la destrucción del monstruo capitalista, que no se cansa de destruir los espacios naturales y espacios donde viven personas que habitan en armonía con su entorno.

Desde acá decimos que avanzaremos hacia la unidad de los distintos pensamientos de lucha y métodos, que aplican y desarrollan un caminar de esfuerzo y sacrificio para llegar a vivir en una sociedad digna y autónoma. No nos canzaremos de organizar para pelerarle a estas bestias hambrientas del poder económico (de la elite nacional e internacional), porque estamos convecidos que podemos avanzar hacia una liberación en el Wall Mapu, una lucha de siglo en siglo, que resiste y se reconstruye año a año, década tras década.

Somos parte de un movimiento que ha optado por la lucha de autodefensa, la lucha armada legítima y ancestral, continuando el caminar con los costos que sean necesarios. Sabemos que el sabotaje y los ataques a sus infraestructuras, los debilita, los preocupa, les duele ser tocados por personas que entregan sus vidas por el camino que eligen, preparándose y articulándose para encontrar nuevos objetivos, como lo son quienes colaboran con el enemigo y venden sus almas al capitalismo.

Entregamos nuestra voluntad a los procesos que nos preparan para no equivocarnos, para no caer en sus garras, que aprietan y no sueltan fácilmente.

Debemos tener mucho cuidado, ellos están modificando y preparando sus leyes para hacer temer a la gente que lucha, aunque sabemos que ni eso frenará nuestro avance, ya que la unidad es más fuerte y hermosa a la vez. Contamos con experiencia, la que compartiremos y entregaremos en su momento a las nuevas generaciones.

A las personas que que quieren luchar les damos ánimo, sigan estudiando lo que sea para aportar a una fuerza futura, que destruya toda expresión capitalista.

Ejemplo de ello ha sido la franja Lafkenche, la zona de Malleco y otros territorios en donde sus weichafes tomaron las armas para defenderse del avance del monopolio capitalista, forestales de Angelini, Matte y el latifundio.

Ante esto, el estado vió con preocupación como perdían el territorio que nos usurparon, por lo que decidió nuevamente realizar un avance militar para obtener el control absoluto. Pero esto no nos asusta, ya que sabemos que en algún momento se le dará frente y este retrocederá, tal como lo han hecho anteriormente en lugares donde estuvieron instalados y fueron expulsados por la fuerza de la gente que decide luchar.

Hoy encarcelan a personas de estos territorios, a personas que han participado de la lucha por la tierra y todo lo que esto conlleva.

En el caso conocido como “Caso Grollmus” ocurrido el año 2022, detuvieron a varios integrantes de comunidades mapuche lavkenche y les condenaron en su conjunto a mas de 1000 años de prisión, en un hecho de racismo histórico sin antecedentes. Sabemos que no hay pruebas materiales, que se basan en relatos de testigos protegidos y que tienen presa a gente totalmente inocente. Esperamos su pronta libertad.

Sabemos también que la justicia está condenando al mapuche por luchar y a todos los que deciden enfrentar al gran capital; a los poderosos les decimos que tengan mucho cuidado porque nos levantaremos con mas odio y venganza hacia su sistema represivo, tanto dentro como fuera de las diferentes cárceles chilenas, en donde nuestros hermanos mapuche y de lucha, se mantienen custodiados por gendarmería.

A los funcionarios de gendarmería les decimos: No se equivoquen con nuestros presos comuneros mapuche, compañeros anarquistas, subversivos y comunistas reales. A todos les tenemos inmenso cariño y respeto por sus trayectorias. Reaccionaremos, cobraremos a altos y bajos mandos por sus decisiones. Nos dejaremos caer en sus casas, porque contamos con información de ellos.

Que estas palabras lleguen al CP Biobío, El Manzano, Temuco, Angol, Valdivia y Santiago.

Algunos actos …
