author: CMI Argentina
title: Fiyi: El niño, la crisis hídrica y el negocio millonario del agua
content:
Fiyi está siendo golpeada por una gran sequía asociada al fenómeno de El Niño y vuelve a poner en emergencia a miles de ciudadanos de este archipiélago del Pacífico. Pero mientras 6 de cada 10 habitantes no tienen acceso al agua potable, la empresa Fiji Water explota una fuente subterránea de aguas, considerada entre las más puras del mundo. El objetivo: abastecer mercados internacionales.


Por Adrián Flores para Red Eco


Este conjunto de Islas suelen aparecer en las postales turísticas como un paraíso de playas y aguas transparentes. Sin embargo, lejos de esa imagen, miles de personas atraviesan una situación muy diferente: conseguir agua segura se ha convertido en un problema cotidiano.


La sequía que afecta al archipiélago, está llevando al límite al precario sistema de abastecimiento. Los datos permiten ver la magnitud el problema. Según UNICEF y la Organización Mundial de la Salud, en 2022 solamente el 42 % de la población de Fiyi tenía acceso a servicios de agua potable gestionados de manera segura. Esto significa que casi seis de cada diez habitantes no alcanzaban ese estándar. Aunque una proporción mucho mayor contaba con algún servicio básico, eso no necesariamente garantizaba agua segura y sin contaminación.


Los informes difundidos durante noviembre muestran la gravedad del actual escenario. El periódico The Fiji Times, publicó el 1 de noviembre que 19 de las 44 fuentes de abastecimiento monitoreadas por la Autoridad del Agua de Fiyi se encontraban en niveles críticos.


El Gobierno realiza operativos de emergencia con camiones, plantas de tratamiento y embarcaciones para abastecer a las comunidades insulares. Los pronósticos tampoco son alentadores: si continúa la falta de lluvias, hasta el 82 % de las fuentes monitoreadas podría alcanzar niveles críticos.


La crisis ya golpea la salud. En la isla de Batiki se registró un aumento de casos de diarrea que motivó la intervención del Ministerio de Salud. Los productores agrícolas enfrentan pérdidas de cultivos y dificultades para mantener el ganado.


La crisis climática golpea sobre una estructura que no estaba preparada para responder. Y mientras miles de familias dependen de operativos de emergencia para acceder al agua, en el mismo territorio funciona una industria que convirtió ese recurso en un producto de exportación.


Fiji Water, el gran exportador de agua para las élites del mundo


En el valle de Yaqara, sobre la isla de Viti Levu, se encuentra la planta de Fiji Water. Desde allí se extrae agua que luego es embotellada y comercializada en distintos países.


La empresa pertenece a The Wonderful. Su negocio se construyó alrededor de una característica que funciona como argumento comercial: el origen natural del agua y su procedencia de un acuífero de Fiyi.


No hay elementos para atribuirle a Fiji Water la responsabilidad directa por toda la crisis hídrica del país. Los problemas de infraestructura, la desigualdad en el abastecimiento y las condiciones climáticas tienen una historia propia. Pero resulta inevitable preguntarse por las prioridades que establece el modelo capitalista donde una actividad industrial puede expandirse para abastecer mercados internacionales mientras una parte de la población sigue sin contar con agua segura.


Desfinanciamiento mas sequía


Las dificultades del sistema público no se explican únicamente por la sequía. Según datos del Departamento de Comercio de Estados Unidos, alrededor del 47 % del agua se pierde por filtraciones en las redes de distribución antes de llegar a los hogares, en un país donde miles de personas padecen interrupciones del servicio.


En este contexto, la información sobre las regalías de Fiji Water resulta particularmente significativa. La empresa matriz declaró en 2025 que sus operaciones en Fiyi, junto con las de su compañía hermana de transporte marítimo, aportaban anualmente en regalías al Estado, el equivalente a unos 43 millones de dólares estadounidenses. Esto representa un tercio de lo que el Estado destina al mantenimiento de la red pública de agua.


La comparación permite observar – y no de manera caprichosa – que el negocio privado aprovecha un recurso natural del territorio y obtiene ingresos de su comercialización internacional de centenares de millones (aproximadamente 500 millones de dólares en el 2023) mientras que paga regalías en una suma que ni siquiera sirve para mantener la precaria red de distribución.


Cuando la escasez abre negocios


La apropiación comercial del …

author: Rizomatica
title: En línea y gratis: Película inspirada en la vida de Matías Catrileo está disponible en OndaMedia
content:
Con dos años de recorrido nacional e internacional, premios a Mejor Película en festivales de Barcelona, Arica, Tierra del Fuego y Aysén y cerca de 70 muestras gratuitas en distintas regiones de Chile, el largometraje de ficción “Algún día las raíces” se incorporó este 18 de noviembre a la plataforma de cine chileno


OndaMedia

. Inspirada en la vida de Matías Catrileo, joven mapuche de 23 años asesinado por Carabineros de Chile el 2008.


Por Morín Ortiz. 


Cada comienzo de año gregoriano, el pueblo mapuche recuerda a Matías Catrileo, joven mapuche que el 3 de enero del 2008 fue asesinado en una acción de control territorial de la que fue parte junto a la Coordinadora Arauco Malleco. Se probó que Matías estaba desarmado y que recibió un disparo por la espalda, perpetrado por el cabo segundo Walter Ramírez de Carabineros de Chile. 


El 2011, la Corte Suprema ratificó la sentencia de la Justicia Militar que lo declaró culpable de violencia innecesaria con resultado de muerte. La condena: tres años y un día en libertad. El 2012 la familia Catrileo Quezada presentó el caso en la Corte Interamericana de Derechos Humanos y siguen a la espera. Un año después, Ramírez fue desvinculado de su cargo “por ser un desprestigio para la institución”, pero la familia de Matías sostiene que esto se logró a causa de la presión social. 


Fue en Temuco en enero del 2024, en la 16º conmemoración por la vida y muerte de Matías Catrileo, que se exhibió por primera vez el largometraje “Algún día las raíces” (65 min.), tras ocho años de que comenzara a gestarse por un joven equipo de estudiantes de Cine de la Universidad Mayor: Alejandro Valdeavellano Ramaciotti en dirección, guion y montaje; Catalina Saavedra Reyes en producción ejecutiva y Cristóbal Díaz en dirección de foto y montaje. 


Cuando propusieron la idea de hacer esta película a la familia Catrileo Quezada, aceptaron su condición: realizarla desde la autogesión, dadas las responsabilidades del Estado chileno en el asesinato de Matías. Fue gracias a una campaña de recolección de fondos y las voluntades de diversas personas que se logró. 


El rodaje fue el 2018 y duró tres semanas. Una de sus principales locaciones fue en la comunidad de Rucañanko, en el Lago Lleu Lleu, territorio mapuche en cuyo proceso de recuperación participó Matías. Angélica Ñancupil y Tania Antileo, fueron grandes apoyos en áreas de la investigación, producción y actuación. 


En palabras de Catalina Catrileo, la única hermana de Matías, Algún día las raíces

“logra denunciar a las forestales y deja en claro que hay una pérdida territorial, la necesidad de las comunidades por recuperar nuestro territorio y cómo eso es criminalizado y reprimido”.

Por esto recibe como una buena noticia que la obra pueda ser vista de manera gratuita en la plataforma de OndaMedia:

 “es bueno para ir transmitiendo la historia entre nosotros mismos y para dársela a conocer a gente que no la conoce”. 


Los procesos de realización de cine son largos, más aún si no se cuenta con el financiamiento necesario. Por lo que su director, Alejandro Valdeavellano recibe con goce la incorporación al catálogo de OndaMedia:


“significa seguir llegando a más imaginarios mapuche y no mapuche a través de la memoria de Matías Catrileo. Estoy muy contento de que la película pueda seguir apreciándose y muy agradecido de que la familia Catrileo Quezada estuvieran de acuerdo con exhibirla en esta plataforma”. 


Su productora general, Catalina Saavedra, destacó que la película:


 “llegue a otros públicos sin que el acceso económico sea una barrera. El cine también tiene que ver con generar encuentros, abrir conversaciones y permitir que las historias circulen”. Después de tantos años de trabajo colectivo “la película puede expandirse, ser mirada, interpretada y de alguna manera, aportar su granito de arena en la preservación de la memoria”. 


Entre otros logros de “Algún día las raíces”, están el ser la película más vista del Festival Internacional de Cine por los Derechos Humanos de Colombia el 2024 y la nominación a Mejor Actor en los Premios Caleuche para su protagonista, Felipe Arce, quien comparte elenco junto a Rallen Montenegro, Manuel Díaz y Nicolás Aliaga.

Desde el 18 de noviembre del 2026, “Algún día las raíces” está disponible para ser vista en Chile de manera online y sin costo en OndaMedia, plataforma de streaming de cine chileno. Quienes quieran verla desde el extranjero, pueden hacerlo en la plataforma Mirada Nativa, que …

author: Darío Aranda
title: Mapuches defienden el territorio, mientras la política de Estado es negar los derechos indígenas
content:
Por Susana Lara


Desde Río Negro


La ocupación tradicional indígena en tierras fiscales es una fuente permanente de conflictos en la provincia de Río Negro, a pesar de que tiene cuarenta años una ley específica que contempla la protección de la población rural originaria. En el centro de la provincia, en plena estepa, la cuarta generación de una familia mapuche fue despojada de la posesión de un campo de mil hectáreas por la Dirección Provincial de Tierras, órgano local que administra y adjudica las tierras fiscales, pero no resuelve sobre territorios indígenas, según la legislación vigente.


Todo en un contexto donde

el Senado Nacional aprobó la llamada "Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada"

, que mantiene límites para la compra de empresarios extranjeros pero

facilita los desalojos, donde comunidades indígenas y familias campesinas serán las más perjudicadas

.


Un siglo de presencia mapuche


Vicente Maliqueo y Francisca Coñohuepán se asentaron a principios del siglo XX en el paraje Guada Niyeu, a mitad de camino entre la ciudad de Fiske Menuco (General Roca), al norte, y Sierra Colorada, al sureste. Allí nacieron sus hijos y vivieron de la cría de animales. Con el tiempo levantaron una ruka (hogar) de adobe, crecieron los álamos y ampliaron las pircas (corrales de piedra), todo cerca de una vertiente de agua dulce. Su hijo Francisco Eufemio y su nieto Vicente sostuvieron la ocupación tradicional de esa fracción del territorio hasta el final de sus días, ocurridas en 2022 y 2021 respectivamente.


Ahora, el Estado provincial desconoció a sus descendientes y otorgó la tierra a un tercero ajeno al Pueblo Mapuche, un empleado público radicado en Cipolletti. En concreto, no permiten que la familia originaria ingrese a su territorio. La decisión es una práctica estatal históricamente ejercida en contra de la gente mapuche y los criollos pobres, en violación a la

Ley Integral del Indígena (2287)

 vigente desde 1988.


La parcela de mil hectáreas es parte de una fracción fiscal de 12.500 hectáreas, sin mensura ni planos aprobados todavía, según el catastro público oficial. Gran parte de esa tierra fiscal está dentro del área de permiso de exploración minera de GRG Resources Corp, proyecto de oro, cobre y plata como consta en la última versión del Catastro Minero e informa la propia empresa.


Foto: María e Hilda Maliqueo


La maquinaria administrativa


Eufemio Maliqueo nació en 1921 en Guada Niyeu. Formó familia con Matilde Ángel. Cuando ya tenían varios hijos, en 1960 se formalizó el inicio del trámite de reconocimiento de 1250 hectáreas ante la Dirección de Tierras y Colonias, según consta en la copia del expediente administrativo al que se accedió para esta nota. Con el correr de los años, se sumó a la petición su hijo Vicente.


Recién en 1984 la Provincia le otorgó un reconocimiento formal por mil hectáreas, cuando tanto él como su compañera tenían 64 años. En 2007 una inspección de Tierras vuelve a constatar la presencia del padre e hijo en el lugar, en un predio totalmente alambrado, con hacienda propia. Al año siguiente, la Provincia les otorgó el Permiso Precario de Ocupación (PPO), como si el anterior no existiera.


Luego del fallecimiento de su abuelo y su tío, en 2022, José Luis Llarenas Maliqueo se presentó formalmente ante las autoridades de la Dirección de Tierras para continuar la ocupación del campo conservando la marca y señal para los animales. El responsable del organismo le confirmó la recepción del pedido. Inmediatamente comenzó a hacer presentaciones en ese mismo expediente Pablo Melinguer, de Cipolletti, manifestando interés en el lugar argumentado sus trabajos hechos durante la esquila y asistencia personal a los ancianos durante sus últimos años. Una inspección de Tierras aseguró haber constatado la ocupación de Meliguer y dando por ciertos su presencia en una década. A la vez, denunció en la Comisaría a Llarenas y su familia por acceder al campo. En 2024, una nueva inspección certificó que ocupaba el lugar desde 2014, cuando todavía estaban con vida los ocupantes tradicionales. En ese mismo documento oficial consta que residía en Cipolletti donde presta servicios como enfermero del servicio penitenciario.


La tierra fiscal no está libre de ocupantes necesariamente. Más bien todo lo contrario. Sin embargo, en numerosas ocasiones el Estado provincial decide como si así fuera, desconociendo derechos de posesión ejercidos por décadas bajo la figura de “permisos precarios de …

author: Ariel Giagio
title: Mulheres negras na diplomacia: avanços e desafios dentro do Itamaraty
content:
Marise Ribeiro Nogueira foi a primeira mulher negra a ingressar na diplomacia brasileira como bolsista pelo Programa de Ação Afirmativa em 2003. Em entrevista à

Agência Pública

, ela conta que durante uma reunião em Washington D.C, capital dos Estados Unidos, foi abordada por um homem negro, de terno elegante. Era o representante do arquipélago caribenho São Cristóvão e Neves, que ocupava, naquela situação, o cargo de decano dos diplomatas.


“[Ele] me disse que ficava muito satisfeito por ver uma pessoa negra na delegação brasileira, porque era a primeira vez que via uma diplomata negra na delegação do Brasil”, recorda Nogueira que ainda atuava como terceira-secretária, o cargo inicial na carreira diplomática.


A partir deste momento, uma aliança se formou. Nogueira afirma que no fim da reunião conseguiu colocá-lo em contato com o representante alterno da missão brasileira junto à ONU em Nova York “e esse contato colaborou com a parceria entre o Brasil e a OEA na questão negra”, explica.


Hoje, ela é ministra de segunda classe e chefe da Assessoria Especial de Assuntos Internacionais do Ministério da Saúde. “Para mim foi uma honra ter sido a primeira bolsista do programa de ação afirmativa do Instituto Rio Branco a ser aprovada no concurso de admissão à carreira diplomática em 2023. Então lá se vão 23 anos de carreira diplomática”, declara a diplomata que também foi conselheira da embaixada do Panamá e a primeira mulher negra a trabalhar na Embaixada do Brasil nos Estados Unidos.


Marise Nogueira faz parte de um grupo de mulheres negras pouco conhecidas pelos brasileiros, mas que já deixaram seus nomes na diplomacia do país, reconhecida como uma das mais respeitadas do mundo. Entre elas estão Dulce Maria Pereira, Mônica de Menezes Campos e Isabel Heyvaert. São nomes que acabam servindo de referência para profissionais do Ministério das Relações Exteriores (MRE) mais jovens como Flávia Medeiros, ou a

primeira mulher quilombola

 a entrar na carreira diplomática, Helen Borgens.


Em 2026, o Itamaraty conquistou o maior número de mulheres diplomatas aprovadas pelo Concurso de Admissão à Carreira Diplomática (CACD) da história do Instituto Rio Branco e do Itamaraty. A diplomacia, que já foi por lei uma profissão exclusivamente masculina, terá na nova turma de 2026-2028 um grupo 45% feminino.


Se o número de pessoas negras que tomaram posse ainda é baixo, o crescimento já é significativo: 18 diplomatas negros foram aprovados no CACD. Foram 15 aprovados na reserva de vagas para pessoas negras, uma na reserva de vagas para pessoas quilombolas e duas pela ampla concorrência.


“As mudanças que temos hoje são fruto de muita luta coletiva, de movimentos sociais e de políticas de inclusão, como as cotas e bolsas de vocação.

Também carregam o legado de quem veio antes e enfrentou barreiras quando quase ninguém falava sobre isso”, avalia a oficial de Chancelaria e secretária executiva adjunta do Comitê Étnico-Racial do MRE, Flávia Medeiros.


“O papel das primeiras mulheres negras na diplomacia, como Mônica de Menezes Campos, foi muito além de serem pioneiras. Ao ocuparem espaços onde quase nunca se via pessoas como elas, desafiaram padrões e mostraram que mulheres negras também pertenciam àqueles lugares”, complementa.


A diplomata Isabel Heyvaert, , ministra de segunda classe e ex-embaixadora do Brasil na República da Sérvia, em Montenegro e na Etiópia, conheceu Mônica Campos. “Quando ela ingressou na carreira diplomática, eu já integrava o Itamaraty, como Oficial de Chancelaria, carreira distinta da diplomática. O pioneirismo de Mônica demonstrava que mulheres negras também podiam conquistar espaço em uma carreira historicamente marcada por uma representação social bastante restrita”, diz Heyvaert.


As conquistas, entretanto, não garantiram imunidade aos preconceitos raciais e de gênero. Como oficial da Chancelaria, Isabel Heyvaert ouvia que a “casa” era dos diplomatas, e não dos oficiais – assistentes que “não deviam se acomodar”. “Compreendi que, se desejasse ampliar meu campo de atuação e assumir responsabilidades para além das atribuições daquela carreira, precisaria prestar um novo concurso”. Ela foi aprovada em 1982 e oficializada como terceira-secretária em 1984.


Questionada pela

Pública

 sobre os momentos mais marcantes da carreira, Heyvaert relata uma visita ao Sudão em 2011, meses antes da independência do Sudão do Sul, durante graves conflitos que geraram uma dura crise humanitária. Embaixadora do …

author: anred
title: La Bonaerense al banquillo: arranca el juicio por el crimen de Alejandro Martínez en la comisaría de San Clemente del Tuyú
content:
Alejandro Martínez es retirado del Hotel Fontainebleau | Captura de video


En noviembre de 2021 el hombre de 35 años fue detenido en el hotel donde se hospedaba. Dos horas después yacía muerto en un calabozo de la Comisaría Tercera. Sergio Berni lo culpó de su propio deceso. Kicillof bancó a su ministro y a su policía. El martes en Dolores arranca el juicio contra tres de los asesinos. “Están todas las pruebas, tienen que ser condenados a perpetua”, dice la familia querellante. El juicio comenzará el martes 24 y tiene fecha de finalización pautada para el 4 de diciembre. Las audiencias se harán en el Edificio Central de los Tribunales de Dolores, de Alberdi 137. La causa lleva el número 903-9719. A cargo del Tribunal Oral Criminal 2 está el juez Juan Martín Enzagaray.

Por Daniel Satur (La Izquierda Diario).


La madrugada del 18 de noviembre de 2021

Alejandro Martínez

, trabajador de 35 años oriundo de Brandsen,

murió a golpes

 dentro de la

Comisaría Tercera de San Clemente del Tuyú

, Partido de la Costa. Hasta allí había sido trasladado por una patota de efectivos de la

Policía Bonaerense

, después de que desde el

Hotel Fontainebleau


llamaran al 911 por “ruidos molestos” en la habitación

707

, donde se hospedaba.


El

Fontainebleau


está en Costanera y calle 3 de esa ciudad balnearia. La noche anterior

Martínez

 se había alojado en esa habitación del séptimo piso. Llevaba pocas ropas, sus lentes (sin los que prácticamente no veía) y una mochila con bastante dinero. Esa plata, producto de una indemnización laboral, él se la iba a transferir al día siguiente a

Laura Lagana Santillán

, la madre de su pequeño hijo.


Según la reconstrucción de los hechos, tras el llamado telefónico llegaron al hotel

dos patrulleros

 de la

Comisaría Tercera

. Los efectivos de

La Bonaerense

 subieron y encontraron a

Martínez

 fuera de su habitación,

sentado

 en la escalera del pasillo. Poco después, según muestra el video de seguridad del hotel,

se lo llevaron caminando

. Él iba

con las manos atrás

,

descalzo

 y

sin sus indispensables anteojos

. No se le veía herido ni quejándose.


Tras la detención, el personal del hotel juró que en la habitación

no había quedado nada de Martínez

. Pero la

Policía

 nunca informó, al menos formalmente, que entre los elementos del detenido se había incautado una

importante suma de dinero

. Difícil saber si esa plata tiene que ver con el móvil del crimen, pero lo cierto es que

 a Martínez le robaron

 esa indemnización. Y los policías tienen todos los boletos.


Menos de dos horas después de ser sacado vivo del hotel,

el cuerpo inerte de Martínez

 yacía en uno de los calabozos de la seccional ubicada en San Martín entre 7 y 8. A su alrededor, la patota discutía nerviosa qué hacer con él. Y empezaron los llamados desesperados buscando “instrucciones”.


Martínez murió por

asfixia mecánica

. Tenía varias

costillas rotas

,

golpes

y

heridas

en todo el cuerpo. Otro detenido, desde un calabozo contiguo, escuchó la secuencia. Afirmó que varios policías tiraron al piso a

Alejandro

 y

le dieron una feroz paliza

. Los oficiales

José Pereyra

,

Christian Rohr

y

Maximiliano Munche

 estuvieron al frente de las acciones. Sus “camaradas”

Laura Chiarullo

,

Evelyn Garófalo

,

Jaqueline Mansilla

,

Carla Cantarella

,

Sandro Mujica

 y

Miguel Boulos

, de una u otra manera, participaron.


En 2022 se cerró la instrucción y la causa contra los nueve fue elevada a juicio. El próximo martes 24, más de cuatro años después, comenzará la primera parte del proceso.

Pereyra

,

Rohr

y

Munche

se sentarán en el banquillo, acusados de ser coautores de “

homicidio triplemente agravado

 por

alevosía y ensañamiento

 por el concurso premeditado de

más de dos personas

, por haber sido cometido por

miembros integrantes de una fuerza de seguridad

,

abusando

de sus funciones o cargos”.


Según el artículo 80 del Código Penal, la expectativa de pena por ese delito es de

reclusión perpetua

. Sin embargo, los tres acusados gozan del beneficio de la

prisión domiciliaria

 y llegarán al juicio habiendo estado poco tiempo tras las rejas. Por elección de los imputados, el juicio será por

jurado popular

 y las audiencias estarán presididas por

Tribunal Oral Criminal 2 de Dolores

.


Axel Kicillof, Sergio Berni y la Policía Bonaerense | Foto Prensa PBA


El rol de Berni, el aval de Kicillof


Cuando el hallazgo del cuerpo en la

Comisaría Tercera

 se hizo …

author: La Zarzamora
title: Comunicado y llamado Internacional del Frente en Defensa del Guaíba y contra la CMPC
content:
Como Frente en Defensa del Guaíba y contra la CMPC hacemos un llamado de solidaridad para enfrentar a la ofensiva ecocida de la multinacional fascista $hilena Celulosa CMPC, comandada por los Matte, en el territorio ancestral Guaraní M’Byá y lafken Guaíba, Barra do Ribeiro, sur de Bra$il.

El pasado miércoles 11 de noviembre se realizó una manifestación y marcha en el centro de Porto Alegre, donde se reunieron más de 300 personas para exigir la retirada total de dicha empresa y su nefasto «Projeto Natureza».

El «Projeto Natureza» es una planta procesadora de celulosa que pretende instalarse a las orillas del Rio Guaíba, en el fundo Barba Negra y en la Ponta da Formiga, territorio sagrado Guaraní M’byá. Su objetivo es duplicar la capacidad de producción total de celulosa de la CMPC. Hoy, cuentan con 44 plantas de procesamiento de celulosa en el continente, 3 de ellas en territorio $hileno, sumado a la planta que ya está instalada a las orillas del Guaíba en el municipio del mismo nombre. CMPC tiene la capacidad de producir 4,5 millones de toneladas de celulosa al año. Con el Projeto Natureza, su capacidad de producción podría llegar a 7,5 millones de toneladas de celulosa al año. Las consecuencias a largo plazo son difíciles de dimensionar, pero es sabido que el proyecto incluye el dragado del Guaíba, deforestación del bosque nativo, cambios en las leyes de protección ambiental, contaminación del agua y, sin dudas, la expansión masiva de plantaciones de eucalipto en Brasil, Uruguay y Argentina.

Al finalizar la marcha se realizó una acción directa coordinada en contra de la FEPAM, órgano del gobierno que otorga los permisos ambientales y de instalación a la CMPC. Manifestantes hicieron okupación de la institución, rayaron las paredes exigiendo «FUERA CMPC» y denunciando el actuar corrupto de la FEPAM, quienes ignoran por completo decenas de informes y cuestionamientos técnicos de diversas áreas sobre el impacto real de este proyecto en el territorio. Marcaron las paredes pulcras de ese actual antro de mafiosos que solo sirve como pantalla, ya que sin escrúpulos aprueban cualquier proyecto extractivista que se les ponga en frente.

El río Guaíba es parte medular de la vida en la ciudad de Porto Alegre y la región metropolitana. Es el horizonte con el que nos relacionamos cada día y gran parte del agua potable proviene de las aguas tratadas de este rio. Cuando protestamos contra la CMPC necesitamos que se entienda que esta empresa pretende derramar más desechos en el rio que toda la ciudad en su conjunto. Es un proyecto que básicamente contaminará el agua de consumo público de la región.

El actual gobierno de Lula, que basó su propaganda en ser una “alternativa al fascismo”, apoya y fomenta abiertamente el proyecto de la Familia Matte y la CMPC, que además de usurpar sistemáticamente territorio mapuche, apoyaron la dictadura de Pinochet y promovieron la Masacre de Laja en la que 19 trabajadores de la CMPC fueron fusilados por militares chilenos. El presidente Lula concedió a la CMPC una terminal portuaria de exportación en el puerto de Río Grande, en este puerto la empresa está asociada a Ultramar, empresa de la família Von Appen con infame trayectoria nazi.

Esta concesión transforma al rio Guaíba y a la Laguna dos Patos en hidrobia de madera y celulosa, impactando drásticamente la naturaleza y la pesca artesanal. Todo esto sin respetar y seguir los protocolos Guaraní y menos la convención 169 de la OIT que se supone consulta de manera previa, libre e informada a las comunidades indígenas afectadas. Esta maliciosa colaboración entre el gobierno y la CMPC se logra a través de la entrega de millones de pesos a algunas autoridades ancestrales para otorgar el visto bueno al gobierno, dividiendo a las comunidades y generando rupturas entre ellas.

Sobre la familia Matte es importante hacer memoria de que no es solo dueña de la celulosa CMPC, sino que también es dueña de Colbún, responsable por secar el Lago Chapo en la Región de Los Lagos en $hile, y de la Forestal Mininco, vieja empresa forestal conocida robar tierra mapuche, devastar bosque nativo, secar la tierra y por el asesinato de Alex Lemún de 17 años y de Pablo Marchant de 25, ambos asesinados en contexto de recuperación territorial y defensa de la tierra.

También, en 2021 se hizo famoso Fernando Puga Matte, uno de los integrantes de dicha familia, dueño del condominio de lujo Riñimapu donde trabajaban los «jardineros» que asesinaron a Emilia Milen, la Bau …

author: Unknown
title: Jiyan Tosun: State rhetoric of violence fuels social violence
content:
Individual gun ownership and incidents of violence involving firearms are steadily increasing in Turkey. According to data from the Umut Foundation, approximately 70 percent of violent incidents and murders committed in the country over the course of a year involve firearms. The majority of these weapons are unlicensed.


It is reported that 80 to 90 percent of the weapons used in firearm attacks and murders are unlicensed. Data from the Ministry of Interior also reveal the widespread prevalence of unlicensed firearms in Turkey.


According to the ministry, operations carried out throughout 2025 resulted in the seizure of 110,104 unlicensed weapons, including 50,216 handguns, 35,724 shotguns, 22,669 blank-firing pistols and 1,492 long-barrelled firearms.


Figures released by the Ministry of Interior for the first three months of 2026 show that the proliferation of firearms has continued. According to the data, 25,580 unlicensed weapons were seized during the first quarter of the year.


Demand for unlicensed firearms has increased


The proliferation of unlicensed firearms is raising concerns about individual gun ownership and firearm-related violence. In Turkey, where the activities of criminal gangs have also become a prominent issue, public trust in security institutions and the extent to which individuals feel safe have come under scrutiny.


According to a survey conducted by ASAL Research in July 2025, one in four people in Turkey said they did not trust any institution. The police ranked third in the trust survey, with a rate of 10 percent.


Concerns about personal safety are among the factors driving individuals to seek their own means of protection. One significant factor behind the growing demand for unlicensed firearms is that these weapons remain outside registration and oversight mechanisms.


Social media platforms, messaging applications and sales networks established by criminal organisations are reportedly playing a role in the supply of firearms. Weapons are reportedly traded through closed online groups, while correspondence and screenshots included in court files concerning certain criminal organisations have also exposed these networks.


How are unlicensed firearms obtained?


Social media and messaging applications have increasingly become prominent channels in the illegal firearms trade. In sales conducted through closed groups, membership is reportedly obtained through referrals, while information about the characteristics and prices of weapons is shared among members.


Firearms are also reportedly traded through open groups. Some groups resembling the accounts of officially registered firearms dealers allegedly direct people who make contact with unlicensed weapons.


Beyond online trading, weapons held by criminal organisations are reportedly circulated through unregistered sales networks. These transactions involve direct, in-person delivery, while some businesses allegedly facilitate the networks under the guise of legitimate commercial activity.


How are unlicensed firearms classified?


In the unlicensed firearms trade, weapons are classified into different categories according to their characteristics and history. Whether a weapon has previously been used, whether it has been linked to a crime and how it was manufactured are determining factors in these classifications.


Terms used in the trade include "original", "clean", "dirty", "homemade" and "converted from blank-firing weapons". These descriptions are used to determine the commercial value of firearms.


The conversion of blank-firing weapons into live firearms is a particularly concerning aspect of the unlicensed firearms market. The technical characteristics and reliability of such weapons vary, while their circulation outside official registration systems creates serious security risks.


A report prepared by the Umut Foundation in 2025 stated that the number of unlicensed firearms in Turkey had exceeded 30 million. Easier access to weapons and the spread of individual gun ownership remain major concerns for public safety not only in Turkey but also in Kurdistan.


 


'Violence is being normalised through the media'


Jiyan Tosun, Co-Chair of the Istanbul Branch of the Human Rights Association (IHD), said that one of the main reasons for the increase in individual gun ownership is the authorities' tolerance of firearms entering Turkey. She pointed out that a significant proportion of these weapons come from countries in …

title: Serok Nêçîrvan Barzanî Pêşwaziyê li Serokê Desteya Heşda Şe'bî Kir
content:
Êvara îro şemiyê 21.11.2026, rêzdar Nêçîrvan Barzanî, Serokê Herêma Kurdistanê, di hevdîtinekê de bi birêz Falih El Feyaz, Serokê Desteya Heşda Şe'bî re, rewşa siyasî ya Iraqê û pêşhatên dawî yên herêmê gotûbêj kirin. Di hevdîtinê de ku birêz Dr. Fuad Huseyîn Wezîrê Derve yê Iraqê amade bû, peywendiyên Hewlêr - Bexda mijareke din a hevdîtinê bû. author: rti_admin
title: Class Interests in Casteless Disguise: Can Caste Be Disowned Without Surrendering Property and Lineage?
content:
‘I don’t believe in caste. I have no caste. Let’s build a casteless society.’ One hears this all the time now, from people who call themselves progressive, rationalist, liberal. On the face of it, there’s nothing to argue with. Who could object to that?

But look at the Indian socio-economic structure honestly, and the slogan starts to look less like idealism and more like a sleight of hand. Because you can’t abandon caste in your speech while quietly holding on to the wealth and advantages caste handed you. That isn’t annihilation of caste. It’s a way of protecting the hierarchy while pretending to be above it.

Louis Althusser, in Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses (1970), made a point worth taking seriously here: ideology always exists in an apparatus, in practices—its existence is material. Caste is no different. It isn’t just a mental delusion people can shrug off. It has a material life, and in India that life runs through what we might call PPP: Property, Parents, Privileges.

Property means land, urban real estate, commercial capital—concentrated over generations in dominant-caste hands. Parents means lineage: hereditary prestige, ancestral standing, social capital kept carefully inside kin groups through endogamous marriage. Privileges means the leverage that comes from all of it—the networks that open doors in elite schools, boardrooms, professions, and commerce.

So when someone says they’ve “given up caste” because they dropped their surname, while still inheriting the family estate, the legacy networks, and the generational cultural capital—what exactly have they given up? You cannot disown caste while safeguarding the material lineage and property that caste produced. The two don’t come apart that easily.

Ambedkar: Annihilating Caste Means Annihilating Class

Ambedkar saw this clearly in Annihilation of Caste (1936). The caste order, he insisted, is not some innocent functional division of labour: “The Caste System is not merely division of labour. It is also a division of labourers.”

To the socialists of his day who thought economic reorganization alone would dismantle caste, he put the question squarely: can you have economic reform without first reforming the social order? If that order is graded by caste, what guarantee is there that Indian proletarians—divided into watertight caste compartments—will ever combine against their exploiters?

And on the myth of individual merit, he was blunt: those who benefit from birth, education, family name, business connections, and inherited wealth will win the race. But that isn’t a selection of the able. It’s a selection of the privileged. For Ambedkar, annihilation of caste was never about nominal changes in personal conduct. It demanded structural equality across economic, educational, political, and material life. Keeping the assets inside dominant groups while claiming caste is abolished runs directly against everything he argued.

The Biography of the “General Category”

Sociologist Satish Deshpande, in “Caste and Castelessness: Towards a Biography of the ‘General Category'” (2013), gave this rhetoric its proper name. Upper castes, he showed, have systematically laundered historical caste capital into the secular language of “merit” and individual competence. They shed the overt markers of caste, settle comfortably into the constitutionally unmarked “General Category,” and reinvent themselves as casteless modern citizens.

The burden of caste then gets shifted entirely onto SC, ST, and OBC communities—who are caricatured as “casteist” or backward for invoking affirmative action. Constitutional certificates become a badge of sectarian identity, while upper-caste generational capital passes as unmarked merit. That’s the strategy of the General Category, and Deshpande names it for what it is.

Lately there have been petitions before high courts—Telangana, Madras—asking for a “No Caste / Casteless” column in census forms, school transfer certificates, state applications. These deserve a closer look, because they tend to come in two flavours.

One is misguided cluelessness: well-meaning but politically naive people, from oppressed or liberal backgrounds, who imagine that leaving a box blank on a form dissolves structural violence. It doesn’t.

The other is more deliberate: an upper-caste design to escape structural accountability. If caste disappears from the census and public records, surveys can no longer measure how land, corporate wealth, and …

author: Brian Hioe
title: KMT Passes Cash Handouts, Leans into Attacks on Solar Energy Before Elections
content:
THE KMT PASSED a 20,000 NT cash handout to the general public yesterday in the legislature, shortly before elections. This would continue a familiar tactic of the party–to distribute cash handouts to the public in order to affect election outcomes. The TPP, unusually, broke from the KMT when it came to the cash handout at the last minute, but because insufficient DPP legislators were present in the legislature, it still passed.

Indeed, this has proven to be a useful electoral tactic in the past. While President Lai Ching-te called for opposition to the cash hand-outs, one notes that on other occasions the DPP first resisted cash hand-outs and then pivoted toward trying to take credit for the move after seeing that it was popular with the public. At other times, it has been the DPP itself that sought to move for cash hand-outs with the claim that this was distributing the dividends of Taiwan’s AI windfall to the public.

At the same time, one notes that, both last year and this year, the KMT pushed a drastic, far-reaching set of cuts to the government budget. This includes not only the defense budget but social services. While the KMT has claimed that such budgets were necessary for fiscal balance, the cuts it currently calls for would be at the expense of social services.

The KMT has historically leaned into vote buying to win elections, and this is perhaps no different. One notes that practices regarding vote buying continue, especially in rural areas of Taiwan, with young progressive candidates reporting that voters were paid 6,000 NT to vote for anyone but them.

In the meantime, the KMT is also leaning into what has increasingly been a recurrent theme for the party in past years–attacks on solar energy and an attempt to frame it as dangerous. Even as much of the world has sought to boost development in the renewable sector in order to offset the impact of climate change, the KMT has increasingly alleged that solar power is new, untested, and dangerous. By contrast, nuclear power is the only clean and safe alternative, and the DPP only advances solar energy projects because of corruption.

In the past, one has observed the circulation of AI-generated disinformation online claiming that solar panels are radioactive and showing birds seeming to die after drinking water near solar panels damaged by a typhoon–never mind that the species of bird depicted in the video does not exist in Taiwan.

As such, issues regarding solar panels have become contentious in several local races. In Tainan, KMT candidate Hsieh Lung-chieh has hit out at floating photovoltaic solar farms in the Wushantou Reservoir to suggest that chemicals used to clean the panels will be dangerous for the water supply.

Members of the Chiang mayoral administration have also hit out at suggestions to install solar panels on historic buildings such as the National Palace Museum, leading to an unusual spat between the Chiang mayoral administration and the National Palace Museum after Taipei Cultural Affairs division director Tsai Shih-ping published AI-generated images of solar panels being installed on the museum. The museum has since demanded a policy. Such controversies have also led Chiang to be criticized for not knowing his own mayoral administration’s policies, in that it was policies under his mayorship that have led solar panels to be installed on historic buildings such as the Longshan Temple in Wanhua.

Indeed, the KMT’s advocacy for nuclear energy was never rooted in science, but in historic nostalgia for a period in which the KMT was the sole ruling party of Taiwan, the economy was booming, and Taiwan was much more dependent on nuclear energy in its energy mix. The KMT, then, would be suggesting that the restoration of nuclear energy could bring back this period of greater order and economic prosperity. By contrast, any newer form of energy must be framed as potentially a threat to traditionalist reliance on nuclear energy. But it may be a sign of how the KMT has sought to mobilize its voters along traditional party issues to see this recent wave of attacks on the DPP over solar power.

author: Dae-Oup Chang
title: International Labour Solidarity from Below: Reflections on Inter-Asian Solidarity Building of Asia Monitor Resource Centre
content:
Since its establishment in 1976, the Asia Monitor Resource Centre (AMRC) has served as a regional hub for labour solidarity in Asia. This article reflects on the AMRC’s half-century journey towards building inter-Asian labour solidarity. It discusses not only what AMRC has achieved, but also what it has failed to achieve, why it has failed, and what these experiences might tell us about the future of inter-Asian labour solidarity. This is a personal reflection, drawing on my 23 years of involvement with the AMRC in various capacities: as a full-time activist, a member of the Board of Directors, a member of the Regional Council, and Chair of the Board of Directors.


International labour solidarity has long occupied a prominent place in the political imagination of labour movements. Almost every major trade union has declared its commitment to internationalism. However, there is a considerable distance between internationalism as a declared principle and internationalism as an actual process of movement building. Affiliation to international trade unions, participation in international conferences, and occasional solidarity campaigns do not necessarily generate lasting solidarity among workers across national borders.


This distinction between international solidarity as a dead principle and as a living practice was central to an experiment in building bottom-up inter-Asian labour solidarity in which I participated during the 2000s as an AMRC activist coordinating the Asian Transnational Corporation Monitoring Network (ATNC Network). As  one of the regional labour networks AMRC initiated, the ATNC network sought to connect grassroots workers’ organisations across Asia. Its broader ambition was to build an alternative foundation for international labour solidarity in Asia. 


Building a Network from Below


When I joined AMRC in 2003, the ATNC Network already existed as a pilot initiative, with a substantial emphasis on

corporate codes of conduct

. Such an approach was becoming increasingly popular in international labour advocacy, particularly following the emergence of consumer campaigns targeting major international brands during the late 1990s and early 2000s.

1


We were sceptical of the political consequences of this prevailing model of north–south labour solidarity. Our scepticism concerned the underlying structure of solidarity that this approach

reproduced

. Northern organisations possessed the resources, connections, and influence required to pressure major brands, while workers and their organisations in Asian production sites were primarily positioned as

recipients of assistance

. The political focus often shifted from workers’ collective struggles to consumer organisations’strategies and their relationships with corporations.


Such campaigns sometimes achieved meaningful results. They can generate international attention, provide protection to workers, and force employers to negotiate. We did not deny their practical value. However, they had little to do with building the larger collective power of workers. For us, workers’ power was something to be built collectively by workers in and beyond workplaces rather than granted by individual employers’ moral behaviour. 


Therefore, we sought to reverse the direction of the network’s activities. Instead of beginning with corporations and their codes of conduct, we wanted to begin with workers’ struggles, their own organisations emerging from such struggles, and solidarity-based relationships built  between such organisations. 


These relationships developed through practical engagement. A group of workers or worker organisations might initiate a strike or an organising campaign. AMRC and its local partners could support the struggles on the ground. Over time, this process allowed us to include more organisations, whether unions or NGOs. Through such activities, new relationships emerged between organisations participating in the same struggles. 


Our criteria for partnership were therefore not primarily based on size, institutional recognition, or formal representativeness. We were interested in organisations with real connections to workers’ struggles. This frequently meant working with small but independent unions and grassroots NGOs rather than established national trade union centres.

author: John David Parol
title: Trump Out, dumagundong sa Maynila sa kulminasyon ng protesta
content:
Sinalubong ng military honors ni Ferdinand Marcos Jr. si US President Donald Trump sa Malacañang kaninang umaga, Nobyemre 18, para sa kanilang bilateral meeting.

​Sa kabilang banda, kilometro lang ang layo mula sa palasyo, dumagundong ang panawagan ng sambayanan sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na protesta kontra sa Pax Silica at sa imperyalistang Estados Unidos.

​Taliwas sa mainit na pagtanggap sa loob ng Malacañang, dahas at harang ang sumalubong sa mga nagpoprotesta sa lansangan.

Sa kahabaan pa lang ng Recto Avenue, hinarang na ang hanay ng mga raliyista at hindi pinayagang makapagmartsa patungong Mendiola. Hinarang din ng mga pulis ang mga delegasyon ng Gitnang Luson at Timong Katagalugan na nagmantini sa kampuhan sa Liwasang Bonifacio.

Hindi na napigilan ng galit na bulto ang magbulalas ng “Pax you, Trump” kasabay ng panawagang itigil ang Pax Silica at Trump Out.

Noong Nobyembre 17, pinuri ni Trump si Marcos Jr. sa pagsasabing mayroon itong “very good genetics” sa kanyang talumpati sa hapunan para sa mga lider ng ASEAN at Estados Unidos sa Maynila. Inalala rin ni Trump ang matagal na niyang pagkakakilala sa mga magulang ni Marcos Jr. bago pa siya naging pangulo ng Estados Unidos.

Para sa mga progresibong grupo, tumatagos sa katotohanan ang papuring ito, ngunit hindi bilang karangalan, kundi bilang patunay na manang-mana si Marcos Jr. sa kanyang ama at ina bilang masugid na papet ng Estados Unidos.

Hindi lingid sa kaalaman ng nakararami ang pagpapatayo ni Imelda Marcos ng mga pader upang itago ang kahirapan ng mga maralita noong idinaos ang Miss Universe sa bansa noong 1974. Sa kasalukuyan, gumastos ng humigit-kumulang ₱22.9 bilyon ang administrasyong Marcos Jr. kaugnay sa 49th ASEAN Summit. Ayon sa Defend Jobs Philippines, libo-libong maliliit na manininda at manggagawa ang pinatigil sa paghahanapbuhay sa tabing ng paglilinis sa daraanan ng mga dayuhang lider.

Sa isinagawang program sa Recto Ave., binatikos ni Bayan Secretary-General Raymond Palatino ang pag-host ni Marcos Jr. ng kauna-unahang leader-level QUAD meeting sa Pilipinas kahit hindi naman miyembro ng nasabing alyansang militar ang bansa.

Aniya, manang-mana rin si Marcos Jr. sa diktadurya ng kanyang ama sa paggamit ng makinarya ng estado at kapulisan upang supilin ang lehitimong pagkilos ng taumbayan.

Bago pa man buksan ang ASEAN summit, tatlong kabataang estudyante na ang inaresto sa University of Makati na lumahok sa ikinasang kilos-proteta laban sa Pax Silica noong Nobyembre 13. Habang may higit 200 indibidwal ang marahas na dinampot sa malawakang pag-aresto sa Muntinlupa at Kamaynilaan noong Nobyemre 15. Dagdag pa rito ang sa marahas na pagharang, panggigipit, paniniktik at iba pang porma ng brutalidad na ipinatupad ng Philippine National Police.

Inihalintulad naman ng National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) sa kalagayan noong Martial Law at pagkakaroon ng concentration camps noong World War II ang pagtrato sa mahigit 200 indibidwal na inaresto sa kasagsagan ng mga protesta kaugnay ng 49th ASEAN Summit.

“Ang pagtrato sa kanila bilang mga detinido ay hindi nalalayo sa pagtrato ni Marcos Sr. sa mga protesters noong Martial Law at pagtrato ni Hitler sa mga Hudyo noong World War II,” ani Atty. Arman Hernando ng Pro-Labor Legal Assistance Center (PLACE), isa sa mga abogadong tumayong legal counsel ng mga inaresto sa Muntinlupa.

Nanawagan ang NUPL sa agarang pagpapalaya sa lahat ng inaresto at pagpapanagot sa Philippine National Police (PNP), Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), at administrasyong Marcos Jr. sa paghahasik ng dahas at brutalidad laban sa mga aktibista.

​Wala mang 24 oras ang itinagal ng pagbisita ni Trump sa bansa, babala ng mga grupo na habambuhay namang pasanin ng sambayanang Pilipino ang epekto ng anumang hindi pantay na kasunduan o lihim na napag-usapan sa bilateral meeting nina Marcos Jr. at Trump.

Sa kabila ng maagang pahayag nina Marcos Jr. at Trump sa harap ng media na hindi muna pipirmahan ang Pax Silica sa biyaheng ito, bigla namang ibinida ni Trump sa state luncheon sa Malacañang na nakapagkasundo na sila sa tinawag niyang “very big trade deal—the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far.”

Nagsara naman ang programa sa Mendiola sa pamamagitan ng simbolikong pagsunog sa watawat ng Estados Unidos habang dumadagundong sa mga sound system ang kantang “Trump Out” ng Switchbitch na sinabayan ng sigaw at indak ng bulto.

Sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na kilos-protesta, iginiit ng mga progresibong …

author: Binoy Kampark
title: Floods add to severe humanitarian crisis in Gaza
content:
Palestinians in the Gaza strip continue to live in precarious conditions, accommodated in makeshift, overcrowded shelters and tents brought about by a war waged with catastrophic consequences.

Israeli authorities are resisting efforts to improve living conditions in Gaza, even as they advance the demarcated Yellow Line that is shrinking the already diminished territory.

Heavy rainfall since November 6 has added to the misery for Gazans, 65% of whom live in tents or rudimentary shelters. Just under 1 million people live in areas prone to flooding, with 400,000 living in areas determined by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as “extremely high risk”.

Tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians have been flooded.

Instances of respiratory illnesses are on the rise. “The numbers already show the pressure,” Dr Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said. “Acute respiratory infections are 33,000 cases higher than at the same time last year.”

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the rains “damaged displacement sites, shelter and humanitarian facilities, and disrupted services across all five governorates”.

The damage caused within 24 hours was formidable, affecting 26,000 households. (That number has since risen to 46,000.) More than 6000 family shelters were destroyed in that time, with 17,400 damaged. Damaged buildings have collapsed, and the rains have added to existing structural and environmental risks.

Adding to this are the problems of exposed ordnance buried under the debris or shifted to other areas, endangering the lives of residents and humanitarian personnel.

The November 13 humanitarian situation report from OCHA is evenly grim. Between November 3–9, Israeli airstrikes, shooting and shelling continued, killing 22 Palestinians and injuring 90.

This brought the total number of reported deaths since the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement to 1613, with 5833 suffering injuries. The Ministry of Health in Gaza retroactively added 12 fatalities once their identification details were verified.

But there has not been a rise in humanitarian supplies to cope with the rain-borne crisis — rather the opposite. Between November 2–8, 228 of the 262 United Nations and partner trucks intended for entry into Gaza were offloaded on the Israeli side of Kerem Shalom; 128 from Ashdod, 25 from Egypt, 44 from Israel, 12 from the West Bank and 18 from Jordan.

The OCHA reported that the number of trucks offloaded constituted a fall of 42% from the previous week. Israel suspended the Egyptian corridor, citing concerns over smuggling. Between November 3–8, no trucks were offloaded.

The overall figures also fell due to, in the UN agency’s words, “reduced aid volumes available to partners amid funding constraints”.

The Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), responsible for coordinating aid, says otherwise. The crisis is being addressed; poor sanitary conditions were being improved prior to the rain, an effort coordinated with international bodies. More than 93,000 tents and over 8600 trucks holding tarpaulin sheets, blankets and winter clothing have entered Gaza since the winterization plan was launched by the Board of Peace, UN agencies and NGOs.

But the Haaretz newspaper obtained data which revealed a growing decline in food deliveries to Gaza, to add to severe shortages of medical supplies, tents and materials to repair crippled infrastructure.

Under the ceasefire deal, Israel had pledged that it would permit 4200 vehicles carrying essential humanitarian aid and commercial items, including food, fuel, vital medical equipment and supplies, shelter materials and equipment for repairing essential infrastructure into Gaza each week.

COGAT’s own figures supplied to the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) show totals well short of the promised monthly rate of 18,200 vehicles allowed into the Strip: 4700 in March, 5300 in April and over 9600 in May.

In June, the number rose to 12,000, only to fall again to 10,000 for the months of July and August. September proved to be the high point with 13,000, while in October only 6500 vehicles were allowed in. (Seemingly caught out by this unusual affliction of verisimilitude, COGAT called its own figures “inaccurate”, saying that Israel had met and even exceeded its humanitarian commitments.)

author: Lindsay McCabe
title: Changes to coronial legislation to broaden next-of-kin determinations
content:
Readers please be advised that this article mentions First Nations people who have passed away, including children.


On Tuesday 22nd September 2026, the Minns Labor Government announced changes to the

Coroners Act 2009

 NSW, specifically, the section of the legislation that instructs coroners to determine and appoint a Senior Next-of-Kin. This followed a statutory review of the Act, and is in response to one of the many recommendations made by the review. 


When a person’s death is reported to the coroner, a Senior Next-of-Kin is appointed. The Senior Next-of-Kin has the exclusive authority to make decisions regarding the person who has died while they are in the care of the coroner. For example, the Senior Next-of-Kin can object to a post-mortem examination being conducted. Being appointed Senior Next-of-Kin also means that the coroner has an obligation to provide mandatory notifications about the progress of a coronial investigation to the Senior Next-of-Kin. When, where and how a person is laid to rest is also under the authority of the Senior Next-of-Kin. 


Who is appointed as Senior Next-of-Kin is decided by a strict legal framework. The

Coroners Act 2009

 (NSW) s 6A states that the Senior Next-of-Kin must be the deceased person’s spouse or de facto partner; if they have no spouse or de facto partner, then any of the adult children of the deceased person can be appointed. If the person has no adult children, then the person’s parent/s may be appointed. 


This appointment-flow hierarchy has been problematic for Mob for many years, across many jurisdictions. It does not take into account our kinship systems, laws, or spiritual beliefs. One of the earliest challenges of the Senior Next-of-Kin hierarchy involved

two Aboriginal parents

 who could not agree on where to bury their deceased adult child. The mother wanted to hold a Catholic ceremony and burial in Darwin; the father however wanted to have a burial on their homelands, Bardi Country, and provided the Court with supporting information outlining the cultural obligations to do so. The Court ruled in favour of the mother. 


In

2016

, the NSW Supreme Court was asked to rule on a matter where the Senior Next-of-Kin appointment had been challenged. In this matter, the coroner had appointed a deceased man’s de facto partner as the Senior Next-of-Kin, as per the legislation. This allowed the partner, a Gumbaynggirr woman, to make arrangements for the deceased man’s burial to take place in Bowraville. The man’s sister however, wanted the man to be taken home to Weilwan Country and to be buried alongside his ancestors. The Court ruled in favour of the man’s de facto partner, citing common law precedent. Further, because the de facto partner of the deceased man established her de facto status to the Court, she held ‘administrative priority’; in other words, she had the highest right as per the legislation. 


More recently, in 2024, the Supreme Court of NSW decided on a dispute between a deceased man’s de facto partner and mother who could not agree on where to bury him. The de facto partner of the man insisted he wanted to be buried in La Parouse; his mother wanted to take him home to his father in Cherbourg, Wakka Wakka Country, where he could be buried on Country. The Court held in favour of the man’s de facto partner, accepting that she was the deceased man’s de facto partner at the time of his death. 


So, who is appointed Senior Next-of-Kin when a person dies has significant ramifications for where, when, and how a person is returned to Country. 


There have however been instances where the appointment of Senior Next-of-Kin has affirmed cultural responsibilities and laws, albeit outside of NSW. In

1999

, the non-Aboriginal spouse of a deceased Aboriginal man sought to bury them in Port Augusta. The deceased man’s father wished to bury him in Oodnadatta, where other members of the family had been buried, and on Yankintatjara Country. Several affidavits were presented to the Court, highlighting that, according to cultural responsibilities and practices, the head of the family should be empowered to make these decisions, not the spouse. The deceased’s spouse, on the other hand, argued that the children of the deceased would not be able to visit their father’s grave if it were located 700kms away in Oodnadatta. Significantly, the Court ruled in favour of the father of the deceased man, allowing him to take his son home, and to be buried according to …

author: Isaac Nellist
title: RAFFWU members locked out of work, rally against ‘union-busting’ Book Grocer
content:
Retail and Fast Food Workers’ Union (RAFFWU) members at the Book Grocer in Naarm/Melbourne rallied outside the Northcote store on November 21 to demand it end its lockout of workers.

The Book Grocer notified workers of the lockout at 8pm on November 20, shutting unionised workers out of their workplaces and stopping their pay at Bourke St, Spencer St, Northcote and its Tullamarine warehouse.

RAFFWU said in a media release that members had been bargaining since May for their first enterprise agreement, demanding a right to a safe workplace, protections from unfair treatment and options for permanent jobs. RAFFWU said the Book Grocer “rejected all their claims”.

RAFFWU members notified their employer on November 16 that they would be taking protected industrial action as part of their bargaining campaign, including handing out information flyers and wearing stickers to promote their campaign.

RAFFWU secretary Loukas Kakogiannis said the Book Grover had “crossed a line no retailer in Australian history has crossed”.

“Book Grocer has locked its own workers out in response to workers notifying that they would take action as small as wearing a sticker on their shirt while at work … “t has cut off their pay, just weeks out from Christmas, to starve them into giving up. That is a cowardly, vindictive attack on booksellers whose only crime is asking for fair treatment.”

Kakogiannis said this made The Book Grocer “the worst union-busting employer in the retail sector”.

“The Book Grocer would rather shut their stores and see their workers struggle to put food on the table than give them secure jobs.”

Book Grocer worker and RAFFWU delegate Fen Strangeways said the lockout would be difficult for workers. “Being locked out just weeks before Christmas is going to put real strain on our ability to pay rent and put food on the table.

“We’ve said from the start that we are open to compromise, we just want a safe workplace and to be treated fairly. Some of us have worked as casuals for ten years and just want to be made permanent.”

But workers are “not going to be intimidated”, Strangeways said. “We are sticking together.”

Retail and Fast Food Workers Union (RAFFWU)

author: Jack Munafo
title: City of Newcastle chooses business bottom line over the climate
content:
The Newcastle City Council has voted to ban Rising Tide, Australia’s largest climate activist group, from hosting events on council-owned land. The motion, put by right-wing independent mayor and former weather reporter Gavin Morris, has sought to rid Newcastle of climate protests.

For many years, Rising Tide has forced the Newcastle City Council to confront the reality of hosting the world’s largest coal port. One hundred and fifty million tonnes of coal left the port in 2025, over 95 percent of which was sold to various Southeast Asian countries. Emissions from its usage, which are approximately 1 percent of Earth’s total CO2 emissions each year, are not counted towards Australia’s CO2 emissions.

The council motion passed 7-6. Voting against were three Greens and three Labor councillors. One Labor councillor, failed mayoral candidate Declan Clausen, voted for the bill. He attended the council meeting over Zoom from the COP31 climate conference in Türkiye. 

The council’s ban is not restricted to Rising Tide. It also applies to “its associates, subsidiaries, affiliated Issue Motivated Groups; and individuals”. Who counts as an “issue motivated group or individual” is at the discretion of the council. When interviewed by ABC Radio the morning after the vote, Morris said he “would be comfortable with” the wide-reaching powers of prohibition granted to the council targeting other groups. He specifically mentioned Palestine-related groups as being potentially affected by this motion.

Morris’ principal bugbear is Rising Tide’s annual People’s Blockade, where protesters take to Newcastle Harbour to prevent coal ships from moving into the port. Morris couched his motion in terms of community safety, but Business Hunter CEO Bob Hawes, in his letter of support for the motion, was willing to say the quiet part out loud:

“[Rising Tide] continues to have adverse impacts on regional businesses and the local visitor economy ... Rising Tide supporters might not like what some of these operators do but they are undertaking legal business activities ... and they have a right to undertake them without disruption.”

The operation of the port alone generated about $107 million in 2025, let alone the profits that come from actually selling the goods that move through it. 

Morris also received letters of support from NSW Premier Chris Minns and police minister Yasmin Catley. Their support tells you everything you need to know about Labor’s stance on climate change. These letters came only weeks after Minns’ approval of the largest coal expansion in NSW history, and months after his announcement that the Great Koala National Park will be funded by pay-to-pollute carbon credits.

Morris was elected in February this year. He has taken his election as a mandate from “the community” to clamp down on Rising Tide. We must show him that the Newcastle community stands with Rising Tide and for real action on climate change, not the profits of the coal industry.

author: @ndy
title: The struggle is real with Jillian Segal.
content:
See also : Jillian Segal and husband funding far-right group “Advance”, Anthony Klan, The Klaxon, July 12, 2025.

Jillian Segal — the South African–born Australian lawyer, business executive, and Australia’s Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism — recently dropped another Report, ASECA Priorities. According to the Special Envoy, a newly-hatched “modern progressive antisemitism” … is taking “the hostility of Islamic extremism and far-left antisemitism, together with traditional antisemitic tropes”.

My first reaction on reading this passage was to recall the unforgettable 2014 framing by the Australian Defence League of the alleged “evil anarcho-pinko-anarchist-islamic cabal of dirt”; the wicked coalition then allegedly intent on turning Penrith into a no-go zone for patriots.

In any case, inre the Report, Jeffrey Loewenstein doesn’t hold back in It’s time to sack Jillian Segal (Deepcut News, November 2, 2026), the Jewish Council of Australia (October 30, 2026) has slammed it, and Jeff Sparrow has characterised it, not unfairly, as a Trumpian plan to curtail free speech (Crikey, November 2, 2026). The Report is also subject to critical scrutiny by Robert Manne, who examines it in On the Rise of Antisemitism in Australia (November 8, 2026), along with the thoughts of Lord Andrew Roberts and Sir Simon Schama on the subject of ‘antisemitism’. Manne concludes that:

Schama believes he can help combat the rise of antisemitism in the Diaspora by defending the indefensible, the war crimes of the IDF under Benjamin Netanyahu. I believe a more likely remedy would be for leading Diaspora thinkers, like Schama, and influential publishers, like Morry Schwartz, and the leaders in Australia of the principal Israel and Jewish lobbies, like Jillian Segal, to speak the truth about what, under Netanyahu and the two Kahanist-fascist members of his Government, Israel has become, and the moral revolution that has to happen in Israel if Jews in the Diaspora are to be spared from the dreadful rise of antisemitism that is spreading around the Western world.

FWIW, for over 20 years I’ve been attempting, inter alia, to monitor and document organised, public expressions of antisemitism and other racisms in Australia — the better to disrupt it. I’m also an anarchist, and one of many people to hold the view that the Israeli state has engaged in a genocidal assault upon Palestine in the three years since October 7 (the latest chapter in a much longer history of deadly state violence). On that basis, I assume that Segal et. al. would categorise myself as an exponent of ‘far-left antisemitism’, the meaning of which is elaborated upon in this passage:

Far-left antisemitism or issue-motivated antisemitism

Far-left ideology and associated activism feature a worldview that casts the world in terms of ‘oppressors’ and ‘oppressed’. Within this binary framework, Israel is portrayed as a colonial project that is inherently racist and Jews who support Israel’s existence are portrayed as representatives of ‘whiteness’ (regardless of their ethnicity), privilege (regardless of their means), imperialism (notwithstanding the absence of an empire), greedy capitalism and the projection of Western power.

This framing allows longstanding antisemitic motifs to be repackaged in the academic language of anti-racism, decolonisation, human rights, social justice and intersectionality, often in service of a traditional Marxist revolutionary agenda.

When a cause is believed – with ideological fervour – to be absolutely just, its ends can come to justify any means and its adherents can feel free to vilify, harass and seek to destroy those who associate with what is framed as evil.

Over time, the language of human rights and its greatest crimes – apartheid, ethnic cleansing, genocide, etc. – has increasingly been appropriated to portray Israel (and, relevantly, members of the Jewish community who support it) as morally evil, often to the point of being equated to Nazis.

In contemporary Australia, elements of Australia’s historically fringe radical left have sought to appeal to well-meaning mainstream progressive Australians who may perceive the Palestinian cause as a matter of social justice. This ‘gateway’ issue, of sorts, has been used by far-left activists to magnify their appeal and prominence and to attempt to introduce traditionally moderate Australians to radical and anti-Jewish propaganda that would previously have been of little interest.

The strange – but …

author: Jim McIlroy
title: Activist Stephen Langford released after week in Silverwater
content:
Stephen Langford, long-time solidarity activist and member of Socialist Alliance, was released from Silverwater Correctional Complex on November 19 following a week-long stint after being arrested at a regular protest outside the former office of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Marrickville.

Rachel Evans, Socialist Alliance candidate for Heffron, told a rally outside Newtown Court on the day of his release that Langford was targeted because he is a committed activist.

“The police came straight up to him at the protest action he takes every week… They said ‘You are under arrest’ but did not clarify what he was charged with,” she said.

“Stephen did not resist arrest, and was taken to Surry Hills police station, and then to Silverwater. He was only offered one phone call … and we were told Stephen would be held for between one to three weeks, and that we could not visit or video link him. They said he could only call us and refused to allow us to leave messages.

“We condemn all levels of police and corrective services for treating him this way. Stephen is a non-violent, peace and anti-war activist, who worked tirelessly to free East Timor, and was later granted an Order of Timor.”

Langford has previously been arrested for breaching bail conditions after pasting an 1816 quote by former NSW Governor Lachlan Macquarie on his statue in Hyde Park. Macquarie said: “All Aborigines from Sydney onwards are to be made prisoners of war and if they resist they are to be shot and their bodies hung from trees in the most conspicuous places near where they fall so as to strike fear into the hearts of surviving natives.”

Macquarie said this before the infamous Appin Massacre on April 17, 1816, in which at least 14 Aboriginal men, women, and children were killed — shot or driven over cliffs — and several others captured, imprisoned and tortured by colonial troops.

Langford's peaceful protest is intended to be an act of truth-telling, revealing the brutality of the colonial government towards First Nations people.

NSW Police imposed strict bail conditions on Langford, including including restricting his movement in a section of Marrickville, where his recent protests have taken place.

“Stephen is kind and generous. He is a retired nurse and feels injustice to others deeply. He would not hurt a fly, and has spent 30 years fighting to win freedom for oppressed peoples all over the world,” Evans said.

“Political graffiti should not be a jailable offence. Stephen should be given an apology and compensation for the way he's been treated.”

Langford is due to appear in court on January 21.

author: Shirley Killen
title: Building the socialist movement in regional Victoria
content:
Victorians from Mildura to Mallacoota will have the chance to vote socialist for the first time in generations at this month’s state election. In a campaign that’s been full of milestones for the Victorian Socialists, one of the biggest is that the party is standing candidates in all 88 lower house seats for the first time. 

Networks of socialist activists have sprung up across the state with the goal of getting these candidates elected, putting on meetings, organising local rallies, door knocking and letterboxing. In some places, like Bendigo and Ballarat, local branches already existed, while in others, coordinators are starting from scratch.

David Suter is one of the local coordinators starting from scratch. He describes turning up to a polling booth after moving to Garfield, in eastern Victoria and part of the electorate of Narracan, looking at his options and thinking “this is bullshit”. The dearth of organised radical politics in regional areas could easily make a person feel disheartened. But David was encouraged by the result the Victorian Socialists achieved in last year’s federal election, so he signed up to attend the party’s state conference later that year. He left with a list of phone numbers and a plan to activate socialists in his region, and established a crew of seven who began sketching out a state election campaign. Now, the party has candidates contesting all eleven lower house seats, and the beginnings of local branches in Narracan, Shepparton, Bairnsdale and the Mornington Peninsula—to name just a few. 

These are “baby steps”, according to David. It’s a big task to rebuild (or just build, sometimes) a socialist tradition in regional Victoria. But the Victorian Socialists’ state election campaign so far has proved it is not impossible, and that with a common goal and some organisational infrastructure, socialists who previously felt isolated in the regions can make a difference.

Renee Nayef, the Victorian Socialists candidate for Mildura in Victoria’s north-west, described a “meet the candidate” event she put on recently. Two men drove into Mildura separately from a nearby town of 97 people, both assuming they were the only socialists for kilometres. They met for the first time at Renee’s event. Without the scaffolding of a statewide socialist campaign, they might have gone on for years not knowing there was another radical a couple of streets over. 

Sometimes these connections are made in unorthodox ways. For socialist campaigners in metropolitan Melbourne, the movement is built by knocking on other people’s doors and starting up conversations about socialism. Socialists in the regions report the opposite experience—locals are instead knocking on 

their 

doors because they’ve seen a yard sign and are thrilled to know there’s another socialist in town. 

In some parts of the state, the campaign is reviving largely forgotten radical traditions. Bass candidate for Victorian Socialists Chris Jobe had to correct the record when the local paper announced his candidacy with the headline “Red flag planted in Bass for the first time”. In fact, the seat of Bass takes in the old mining town Wonthaggi, known for much of the twentieth century as “Red Wonthaggi” because of the militancy of the local communist-led miners’ union. A more accurate headline would have been “Red flag planted in Bass 

again

”. 

The picture in regional Victoria today is clearly very different from the days when the Wonthaggi miners fought bitter industrial battles with coal bosses and the state. With few exceptions, these seats are the preserve of the Liberals and Nationals, with One Nation now poised to make serious gains. Socialists campaigning outside Melbourne don’t sugarcoat the challenges they are facing.

But socialist politics haven’t been seriously tested outside the state’s biggest cities in decades. It’s not surprising that conservative politics dominate when there’s nothing much else on offer. 

And working-class people in rural Victoria face the same stresses as their counterparts in Melbourne. The rising cost of living, the health system stretched to breaking point, the failure of successive governments to invest in transport and education—these issues are coming up all across the state. 

For Hera Sheppard, Victorian Socialists candidate for the South-West Coast, it was growing up in Warrnambool’s public housing that made her a socialist. She witnessed the way Labor neglected its housing stock and failed to …
