author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: After joining protests, Ayta leader faces military harassment
content:
An Ayta community leader in Zambales faced military interrogation and surveillance days after joining protests against the US-backed Pax Silica initiative, raising concerns over the harassment of Indigenous Peoples defending their ancestral lands.

Orlino Lahut, also known as Tiyong Nilo, was visited by a military personnel identifying himself as Jasper Dalit in the afternoon of November 19 at the residence of an Ayta community elder in Iram, Zambales.

According to statements from Indigenous Peoples’ and environmental organizations, Dalit questioned Lahut about the community’s recent trip to Manila, including who organized their participation in the protests, who provided their “Reject Pax Silica” shirts, and how they financed their transportation.

Lahut was also reportedly coerced into completing a form requiring his personal information and organizational affiliations. Dalit threatened to return with additional personnel to question other community members.

The incident followed reports that unidentified men in civilian clothing monitored Ayta delegates during their journey home from Manila.

Katribu Youth Katipunan, Amihan National Federation of Peasant Women, and Kalikasan People’s Network for the Environment condemned the incident, describing it as an attempt to intimidate Indigenous communities exercising their right to protest.

Lahut rejected claims that the Ayta were manipulated by outsiders, asserting that their participation in the demonstrations was based on their own decision and opposition to projects threatening their ancestral domains. “We are not fools,” he said.

For the Ayta communities in Central Luzon, opposition to Pax Silica is premised on the threat to their ancestral lands, livelihoods, and environment.

The initiative, alongside the Marcos Jr. administration’s Luzon Economic Corridor, includes proposed developments such as the Aboitiz solar power project in Olongapo and an artificial intelligence and semiconductor hub in New Clark City, Tarlac.

These developments threaten ancestral and agricultural lands, including areas containing Ayta burial grounds. Amihan also warned that affected communities could face relocation to areas without adequate livelihood opportunities and access to clean water.

The proposed data hub is projected to consume up to 1.8 billion gallons of water annually and operate around the clock, with noise levels potentially reaching 105 decibels, according to Amihan.

Zenaida Soriano, national chairperson of Amihan, said that the initiative would further expose the country’s natural resources to foreign exploitation at the expense of Indigenous communities and farmers. “Pax Silica is a project of wealthy countries that will only destroy our lands, waters, and Indigenous communities.”

She stressed that the developments also threaten national food security, particularly with the planned expansion of the Luzon Economic Corridor across major ports in Luzon.

The harassment of Lahut coincided with another attack against an environmental defender, Lumad youth activist Mawing Pangadas, coordinator of Panalipdan Youth Davao. He was pursued by 10 to 12 suspected state agents wearing black clothing and caps along Upper Madapo Hills in Barangay 8-A, Davao City.

Read: Groups decry abduction attempt on Lumad youth activist in Davao City

Kalikasan condemned both incidents, stressing that these are growing threats against environmental defenders who oppose destructive projects and protect their communities’ land and resources.

For 13 consecutive years, the Philippines has been Asia’s deadliest country for environmental defenders, according to environmental organizations.

Despite this record, the Marcos Jr. administration has proposed a P9.75-billion ($152 million) budget for the National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC) in 2027, nearly P2 billion ($31 million) higher than its previous allocation.

Kalikasan criticized the proposed allocation, saying it results in sustained red-tagging, surveillance, and militarization instead of addressing the needs of communities affected by land grabbing and environmental destruction.

Soriano also condemned the continued military presence in rural communities, saying intimidation would not stop farmers and Indigenous Peoples from defending their rights. “Marcos and the military serve their master Donald Trump rather than the Filipino people. They resort to violence and intimidation to seize land and sell it to …

author: Unknown
title: Women artists: No peace or justice without women's freedom
content:
Actors Lale Mansur, Jülide Kural and Merve Asya Özgür spoke to ANF on the occasion of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on 25 November.


The actors said that male dominance in the arts negatively affects women's creative work and visibility, while also drawing attention to television content that fuels violence. They said that men are emboldened by the failure of the justice system and stressed that there can be no justice, peace or democracy in a society where women are not free.


Lale Mansur: Male perpetrators are emboldened


Lale Mansur stressed that violence against women and femicide should be on the agenda not only on 25 November, but every day, even every moment. She said, "In Turkey, we need to talk about this five times a day. Turkey has become a slaughterhouse for women! We have reached this point because there is impunity. There is no rule of law, the law is not enforced, and there is no justice. Murderers walk among us. They search for the body of one woman and find the bodies of two more women in a well. How much worse can it get?"


Lale Mansur said that murders do not simply result in the loss of one life, but also devastate the lives of mothers, fathers and other relatives. She emphasised that the culture of impunity emboldens perpetrators, adding, "Male murderers are emboldened by impunity."


Lale Mansur also addressed the situation in the media and the shrinking space for opposition, saying that television programmes and series fuel violence: "The absence of any opposition, the disastrous state of television series... Truly disgraceful things are being produced on national television channels, including content that incites violence. They even made a television series about Abdullah Çatlı."


'Male dominance also prevails in television channels'


Lale Mansur said that male-dominated structures also prevail in the arts: "The owners and executives of television channels are mostly men. Male dominance exists there too. As for actors, many people have children to educate and support. With the high cost of living, they are forced to take part in such productions to earn money. Of course, there are very rare cases of people who refuse, saying, 'I'd rather sell lemons.' But when you have children or a family to support, you have little choice."


Lale Mansur said that impunity and the male-dominated mentality lie at the root of violence and femicide. She stressed that the problem cannot be resolved through criminal penalties alone, but requires a fundamental transformation of attitudes across society: "The biggest factor fuelling violence is impunity. They walk among us, and these people are murderers... This language, which targets and objectifies women, confronts us in every aspect of our lives. There is nothing we can tell women. You cannot say something like 'Don't let yourself be killed.' People say, 'Those men were raised by their mothers.' No, they were not raised by their mothers alone; they were raised by society. And society is now morally rotten."


Jülide Kural: There can be no democracy without women's freedom


Jülide Kural said, "25 November is a day of struggle and solidarity for women across the world against all forms of violence, discrimination and inequality. Violence is not directed only at the body. Discrediting a woman's character, disregarding her labour and will, and surrounding her with lies, insinuations and systematic attacks are also forms of violence."


Jülide Kural said that depriving women of their agency over their own lives, defining them through the existence of a man and attempting to confine them to a passive and dependent identity are among the most deeply rooted forms of violence produced by the male-dominated mentality. She emphasised that this violence is not perpetrated exclusively by men, adding, "Anyone who reproduces the male-dominated mentality and its discriminatory language can become part of this violence. Violence does not have a gender; it has a mentality that sustains it."


Jülide Kural stressed that no woman should have to prove her existence, worth or dignity through the judgements of others. She said, "25 November is not merely a day to condemn violence, but a day to confront the social and political order that produces it. In a society where women are not free, there can be no genuine democracy, justice or peace."

author: CMI Argentina
title: Lesbicidios nunca más: Emoción por la sentencia y deuda con Sofía
content:
La condena a Barrientos contempló por primera vez en la Justicia la orientación sexual de las víctimas. La sentencia provocó emoción, es un punto de partida para los derechos de las mujeres lesbianas y deja deudas. La reparación que falta.


Por Maby Sosa. Fotos: Ariel Gutraich. Edición: María Eugenia Ludueña.


Fue un crimen de odio.

Lo confirmó la justicia

 este miércoles 18 de noviembre cuando en la sentencia del juicio contra Justo Fernando Barrientos lo condenó por “homicidio agravado con ensañamiento y alevosía por odio a la orientación sexual de las víctimas”. Barrientos las mató por lesbianas, y la cantidad de pruebas (muchas menos de las que se evaluaron) así lo demostró en los seis meses que duró el proceso judicial.


La noticia, en las afueras de Tribunales, fue recibida bajo una intensa lluvia que se desencadenó casi a la misma hora que se conociera la condena. Lágrimas, gritos, sonrisas, abrazos y cánticos se multiplicaron entre les activistas que esperaban desde primeras horas de la mañana por el ingreso de Tucumán al 1300.


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida por Presentes (@presenteslatam)


“Lo que le hicieron a ellas nos lo hicieron a todes”


La ultima jornada del juicio arrancó con las palabras finales del asesino de las tres mujeres. En la pequeña sala donde se desarrolló el debate oral, la defensa integrada por Ricardo Richiello y Florencia Díaz Cantón -que días antes habían pedido la absolución de Justo Fernando Barrientos por falta de pruebas-, le acercó el micrófono. El acusado habló: “Me siento inocente”.  Sus palabras no fueron más que la confirmación de que existe un contexto de odio hacia las diversidades sexuales. De acuerdo a los últimos informes, las agresiones aumentaron con la llegada del gobierno de Javier Milei. El ataque en el hotel de Barracas, en mayo de 2024, fue diez días después de que Nicolás Márquez, el “biógrafo” del actual presidente,

difundiera un marcado mensaje de odio

 en una entrevista realizada por Ernesto Tenembaun en Radio con Vos.


Ayer al mediodía, luego de que se cortara el segmento entre las calles Talcahuano y Uruguay, se realizaron las diversas actividades planeadas para esperar la resolución del tribunal integrado por los jueces Adrián Pérez Lance, Juan Manuel Grangeat y Cinthia Oberlander. El nerviosismo previo a la lectura de la sentencia se convirtió en una celebración catártica

cuando se leyó el veredicto

 del Tribunal Oral en lo Criminal Correccional N°5 que condenó a Barrientos como autor de los lesbicidios de Pamela Cobbas, Roxana Figueroa y Andrea Amarante, y en grado de tentativa en relación al ataque de Sofía Castro Riglos.


Sin embargo, quedó el sabor amargo del rechazo a las

medidas de reparación para Sofía Riglos Castro

, la única sobreviviente del ataque, que la querella encabezada por Luciana Sánchez había solicitado.


Bajo una incesante lluvia, Samanta Pedrozo quien encabezó la querella colectiva por parte de la Federación Argentina de Lesbianas, Gays, Bisexuales y Trans (FALGBT) salió del edificio de justicia entre aplausos y lágrimas. Frente a la carpa de la Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más donde sobre un papel brillante se leía “Pamela, Roxana, Andrea, ¡presentes!” la abogada abrió una pequeña conferencia de prensa.


“Fue un proceso muy difícil y complejo, hace dos años venimos acompañando este caso”, dijo Pedrozo. Ayer recordó que se enteró del caso por una amiga que le escribió preocupada. “Mataron a tres lesbianas y están tirando todas las cosas de ellas a la calle. ¿Qué podemos hacer?”, recuerda que le dijo. Desde entonces, se acercó a las asambleas que, en ese entonces, se convocaban para pedir justicia. Tiempo después, desde la FALGBT la llamaron para llevar adelante la querella.


“Fueron meses de escuchar testimonios, de poder descubrir ese elemento que era tan difícil de probar: el odio. Fuimos escarbando, interrogando y pudimos demostrar que la muerte de estas chicas no fue un hecho aislado, fue un hecho que ocurrió en un contexto de odio y discriminación”, destacó la abogada querellante. “Lamentablemente está pasando,  sigue pasando y va a seguir pasando porque tenemos un gobierno que nos discrimina. Y cuando los discursos de odio vienen de allá arriba, es muy difícil para las diversidades, para las mujeres y también para las infancias sobrevivir a esta ola de odio.”

author: Julius Gavroche
title: World of Hurt
content:
Abolitionist Reflections on the Root Causes of Harm


from the

CrimethInc.

 collective, 17/11/2026


What causes people to harm others? Reactionaries label certain individuals—or, worse, entire demographics—inherently harmful to justify their own efforts to inflict harm via vigilante attacks, policing, and the court system. Others suggest that experiencing harm can lead some to harm others, as suggested by the common catchphrase “

Hurt people hurt people

.” Here, we examine this popular notion and propose a more useful framework for understanding the root causes of harm.


Today, a ruling class headed by billionaires and aspiring autocrats is making

the celebration of violence

 central to their narratives and policies, openly campaigning against empathy itself. In this context, the question of what causes harm—and how to interrupt it without reinforcing cycles of suffering and oppression—has become increasingly urgent.


World of Hurt


Abolitionists

 who envision a world without

police

 or

prisons

 often face questions about how to address serious forms of interpersonal harm.

Mutual aid

 and resource redistribution may reduce behaviors that arise as a consequence of lack of access to basic needs. But how can we understand those who seem to hurt others out of cruelty or disregard? If we don’t accept the idea that some people are monsters who must be locked up to keep the rest of us safe, how can we make sense of their actions?


Defenders of the criminal legal system frequently cite rape and abuse to justify prisons and imprisonment. In response, abolitionists have devoted considerable energy to developing

alternative approaches

 to addressing sexual violence. Groups such as Generation Five have proposed

principles for responding to child sexual abuse

 through transformative justice frameworks. By focusing on one of the most stigmatized forms of harm, they aim to cut to the root of

carceral thinking

 in order to reimagine safety and justice.


But creative responses beyond the state are not enough. To end sexual violence, we also need to understand its root causes.


Feminist activists coined the term “

rape culture

” to describe how social norms and institutions enable sexual harm. In addition to these structural effects of gender and power, others argue that past experiences of harm shape the behavior of individuals who go on to harm others. One of the most common ways to articulate this principle appears in the phrase “

Hurt people hurt people

.”


Let’s take a closer look to see where this popular saying came from, how it is used, and its implications for an abolitionist understanding of harm.


The Trajectory of a Slogan


From

self-help books

 and

therapist blogs

 to the

writings of abolitionist activists

, “hurt people hurt people” has become an influential account of the psychology of violence. It suggests that some people harm others not because they are pathological monsters, but because they too are victims whose unresolved trauma shapes their hurtful actions.


The precise origins of the phrase are opaque, but it has been in circulation

at least since the 1950s

. It seems to have begun trending in the 1990s in therapeutic and pop psychology circles. A popular 1993 Christian self-help book titled

Hurt People Hurt People

 promised to support readers in healing from painful past relationships “with empathy and biblical insight.” In recent years, this phrase has been repeated by everyone from megachurch pastor Rick Warren to Hollywood actor Andrew Garfield to the stripper con artist character Destiny in the movie

Hustlers

 to

the metal band Mudvayne

. It appears most widely in discourse about therapy, self-help, trauma, and religion.


On the surface, “hurt people hurt people” might seem an odd slogan for radical critics of the

prison industrial complex

. As a maxim of folk wisdom that spans mainstream, religious, feminist, and radical circles, we should consider carefully whether it aligns with our values.


In some ways, it makes sense that abolitionists would find this formulation promising. It humanizes people who cause harm, whereas dehumanizing them paves the way for carceral responses. It attributes the roots of harmful behavior not to inherent depravity, but to contingent circumstances that can be changed. It resonates with the lived experiences of some people who are struggling to heal and to be accountable for hurting others. It seems to offer a hopeful …

author: Brian Hioe
title: Lo Ta-yu Stokes Controversy for Comments Lashing Out at Pan-Green Camp, Misogyny
content:
ICONIC SINGER-SONGWRITER Lo Ta-yu provoked controversy earlier this month after comments in an interview lashing out at the pan-Green camp.

Some of Lo’s comments strayed into misogyny. Specifically, Lo lashed out at former President Tsai Ing-wen and current Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim for being unmarried women who do not have children. Lo claimed that this marked their unsuitability for public office, in that not having children meant that they did not have a stake in the future of Taiwanese society.

Such claims have been used against Tsai and Hsiao in the past, as a form of misogyny directed at female politicians. Indeed, such claims have also occurred from within the pan-Green camp. Veteran independence activist and entrepreneur Koo Kwang-ming, who died in 2023 at age 96, previously made comments suggesting that the ROC military should not be led by a woman who wears a skirt, and suggesting that Tsai not having children made her unsuitable to lead the DPP. Koo suggested, then, that Tsai should step aside to become “mother of the nation” and allow a male leader–his preference being current president Lai Ching-te–to take power. Koo backed Lai in his unsuccessful challenge against Lai in 2020 for the DPP’s presidential nomination.

Nevertheless, one notes that frequent public scrutiny of female politicians has led many female politicians to remain unmarried in the public eye. Despite Taiwan’s prevalence of female politicians in both the pan-Green and pan-Blue camps, gendered biases against female politicians remain strong. Tsai later responded to Lo, criticizing his depiction of her as uninvested in Taiwan’s future.

Other comments by Lo lashed out at music critic Ma Shih-fan, long a champion of Lo’s work, as favoring the pan-Green camp, alleging that Ma was paid off by the pan-Green camp. Ma later responded by quoting Lo’s lyrics in a social media post in what was perceived as a veiled criticism of Lo. Among the online responses to Lo’s attacks on Ma was the view that Lo had unfairly attacked someone who had historically been one of his promoters.

Lo is a figure that is best known as associated with the 1970s campus folk song movement. Among his best-known songs is Lukang, the Little Town, highlighting the stark contrast between his rural hometown of Lukang and the bright lights of Taipei. At the same time, Lo’s pan-Blue-leaning views are well-known, in that while Lo previously criticized both camps, he eventually veered more toward the stances of the KMT. This included participating in commemorations of Ma Ying-jeou’s election victory.

Indeed, one notes that many artistic figures who are strongly associated with Taiwanese identity, such as filmmaker Hou Hsiao-hsien and fellow singer-songwriter Lim Giong, are in fact known for starkly pan-Blue views. This has at times included openly campaigning for KMT politicians, or lending the weight of their cultural prestige to the KMT. At the same time, one notes that in the present, there are fewer and fewer cultural figures who hold such views, which may be why Lo’s comments led to such controversy–as well as through the expression of misogynistic views seen as out of step with the times.

The Anarchist Network of “Vancouver Island” (“Victoria”) remembers our comrade Tasha Diamant fondly.

Tasha was a passionate ecological artist, firebrand sneaky actionist, a loving mother, rageful ecofeminist, and matriarch of the Network.

Tasha was an ardent revolutionary mother who fought against patriarchy, hierarchy, and colonization. She was a prolific organizer and consciousness raiser in “Victoria” (Lekwungen), anchoring major in-city supports and disruptions to bolster direct actions against domination in all its forms.

She also spearheaded The Human Body Project to rouse consciousness; in a misogynistic, dissociative society. She at the time did not have words for what she later understood simply as a violent culture, instead using her naked body to share and create space for vulnerability and a process of bearing witness to self participation in estrangement.

These consciousness raising efforts culminated in hundreds of street actions and performances. This work also extended itself into Humans of Fairy Creek, a theatrical series that focused on humanizing the thousands of arrestees in the struggle ignored by the self-appointed hierarchics in the Fairy Creek leadership.

While Tasha herself did not identify as an anarchist, (preferring the label ‘ecofeminist’) she was most often aligned with anti-patriarchal, anti-capitalist, and anti-hierarchical modes of organizing.

Tasha started FreeSkool Victoria in 2022, was involved in the ‘Victoria’ Anarchist Bookfair Collective in 2023, and supporting the People’s Park Palestine liberation encampment on the University of Victoria quad in 2025 through an “Elders” affinity group she started.

Upon connecting with anarchist youths (note from some youths: we playfully called ourselves “strays”) here, she explained:

“This whole time, in my whole life, no one told me the Anarchists were always there. I wish I’d found you all sooner.” When Tasha learned about the anarchist Mujeres Libres (Free Women) of the Spanish Revolution, she lamented she “would’ve surely joined and stood with them.”

Tasha also understood the privatized Victorian city as a collection of open canvasses that ‘ought to be reclaimed from “fuckers,” painting sanctioned murals and unsanctioned guerrilla artworks around the city. She was also a talented and seamless acquirer and redistributor of various goods to poor folks.

Tasha volunteered with William Head on Stage (WHoS, the only prison theatre company in ‘Canada’) for a number of years. She was blacklisted from volunteering at William Head Institution when the administration decided they did not approve of her friendships with incarcerated artists, as well as conducting The Human Body Project outside the prison, after arbitrary and misogynistic police interventions in street demos. Her shortfilm Handcuffed (2020) documents one of these interactions.

Tasha was an underappreciated …

title: World of Hurt: Abolitionist Reflections on the Root Causes of Harm
content:
What causes people to harm others? Reactionaries label certain individuals—or, worse, entire demographics—inherently harmful to justify their own efforts to inflict harm via vigilante attacks, policing, and the court system. Others suggest that experiencing harm can lead some to harm others, as suggested by the common catchphrase “Hurt people hurt people.” Here, we examine this popular notion and propose a more useful framework for understanding the root causes of harm.


Today, a ruling class headed by billionaires and aspiring autocrats is making

the celebration of violence

 central to their narratives and policies, openly campaigning against empathy itself. In this context, the question of what causes harm—and how to interrupt it without reinforcing cycles of hurt and oppression—has become increasingly urgent.


World of Hurt


Abolitionists

 who envision a world without

police

 or

prisons

 often face questions about how to address serious forms of interpersonal harm.

Mutual aid

 and resource redistribution may reduce behaviors that arise as a consequence of lack of access to basic needs. But how can we understand those who seem to hurt others out of cruelty or disregard? If we don’t accept the idea that some people are monsters who must be locked up to keep the rest of us safe, how can we make sense of their actions?


Defenders of the criminal legal system frequently cite rape and abuse to justify prisons and imprisonment. In response, abolitionists have devoted considerable energy to developing

alternative approaches

 to addressing sexual violence. Groups such as Generation Five have proposed

principles for responding to child sexual abuse

 through transformative justice frameworks. By focusing on one of the most stigmatized forms of harm, they aim to cut to the root of

carceral thinking

 in order to reimagine safety and justice.


But creative responses beyond the state are not enough. To end sexual violence, we also need to understand its root causes.


Feminist activists coined the term “

rape culture

” to describe how social norms and institutions enable sexual harm. In addition to these structural effects of gender and power, others argue that past experiences of harm shape the behavior of individuals who go on to harm others. One of the most common ways to articulate this principle appears in the phrase “

Hurt people hurt people

.”


Let’s take a closer look to see where this popular saying came from, how it is used, and its implications for an abolitionist understanding of harm.


The Trajectory of a Slogan


From

self-help books

 and

therapist blogs

 to the

writings of abolitionist activists

, “hurt people hurt people” has become an influential account of the psychology of violence. It suggests that some people harm others not because they are pathological monsters, but because they too are victims whose unresolved trauma shapes their hurtful actions.


The precise origins of the phrase are opaque, but it has been in circulation

at least since the 1950s

. It seems to have begun trending in the 1990s in therapeutic and pop psychology circles. A popular 1993 Christian self-help book titled

Hurt People Hurt People

 promised to support readers in healing from painful past relationships “with empathy and biblical insight.” In recent years, this phrase has been repeated by everyone from megachurch pastor Rick Warren to Hollywood actor Andrew Garfield to the stripper con artist character Destiny in the movie

Hustlers

 to

the metal band Mudvayne

. It appears most widely in discourse about therapy, self-help, trauma, and religion.


On the surface, “hurt people hurt people” might seem an odd slogan for radical critics of the

prison industrial complex

. As a maxim of folk wisdom that spans mainstream, religious, feminist, and radical circles, we should consider carefully whether it aligns with our values.


In some ways, it makes sense that abolitionists would find this formulation promising. It humanizes people who cause harm, whereas dehumanizing them paves the way for carceral responses. It attributes the roots of harmful behavior not to inherent depravity, but to contingent circumstances that can be changed. It resonates with the lived experiences of some people who are struggling to heal and to be accountable for hurting others. It seems to offer a hopeful pathway towards a world without sexual violence by intervening in support of those who have been harmed in order to …

author: MissyRedaktion
title: Der neue Medienpass
content:
Wir verbünden uns mit GoodImpact, Krautreporter, Übermedien und Surplus und launchen den Medienpass, mit dem du auf alle digitalen Inhalte von allen fünf Publikationen zugreifen. Das haben wir vor:

Gemeinsam mit GoodImpact, Krautreporter, Übermedien und Surplus launchen wir den neuen Medienpass. Dieser erlaubt dir, unbegrenzt auf alle digitalen Inhalte von allen fünf Publikationen zugreifen.

im Probe-Pass: 90 Tage lang als Jahrespass: 365 Tage lang

Und das für nur 15 Euro im Monat!

Fernab großer Verlage gibt es im deutschsprachigen Raum eine vielfältige, unabhängige Medienlandschaft – mit vielen tollen Inhalten.

Das Problem: Bisher bedeutete jedes neue Angebot auch ein weiteres Abo. Mehrere unabhängige Medien zu lesen und zu unterstützen, geht schnell ins Geld. Auf Dauer wird das schlicht zu teuer und zwingt zur Qual der Wahl. Das Ergebnis: Du verpasst spannenden Content bei anderen – und wir viele Leser*innen!

Das ändern wir jetzt: Mit dem Medienpass kannst du für einen günstigen Preis deinen Horizont erweitern und fünf unabhängige Medien supporten. Denn in Zeiten von Desinformation, KI-Slop und aufgeheizten Diskursen braucht es deren kritische Berichterstattung ganz besonders!

Mit dem Medienpass hast du Zugang zu den Themen, Expertisen und Perspektiven von fünf Medien, die sich für kritische Berichterstattung, verlässliche Fakten und eine starke Demokratie engagieren.

Der Medienpass kostet einmalig 180€ für ein Jahr oder 53€ für 90 Tage – das sind nur 15 € im Monat und über 50% preiswerter als die jeweiligen Einzelabos der fünf Medien kombiniert. (Wenn dir das zu viel ist: Wir freuen uns auch sehr, wenn du ein reguläres Missy Online-Abo für 5€/Monat abschließt.)

Uns kennst du ja schon <3 Wir stehen seit 18 Jahren für queeren und intersektionalen Feminismus in Pop, Kultur und Politik. Die Missy erscheint alle zwei Monate in Print und Online. Unser Online-Angebot umfasst zusätzlich mehr als 4000 feministische Texte zu Pop, Kultur und Politik sowie den Pissy Podcast.

Die Plattformen berichten seit 2010 konstruktiv über gute Ideen und Lösungen. Getragen wird ihre Arbeit aktuell von ca. 6.000 Menschen, die uns durch eine Good Membership und freiwillige Beiträge unterstützen.

Das genossenschaftliche Online-Magazin wird von über 15.000 Mitgliedern getragen. Die Redaktion berichtet seit 2014 ohne Drama und tiefgründig über Bildungspolitik, Klima und weitere aktuelle Themen.

Seit zehn Jahren ist das Team die Instanz für Medienkritik. Getragen wird das Online-Magazin von 7.000 Abonnent:innen.

Surplus ist das Wirtschaftsmagazin, das sich um die Interessen der großen Mehrheit und nicht der Reichsten dreht. Täglich veröffentlicht Surplus Texte, wöchentlich Video- und Podcastformate und zweimonatlich ein digitales sowie gedrucktes Magazin.

Bestehende Abos werden angerechnet Wenn du bereits ein Missy Online-Abo hast (oder auch ein Abo bei einer der anderen Medien), wird dir dieses angerechnet. Das System erkennt nämlich deine e-Mail Adresse wieder. Das heißt: Du musst für Abos, die du schon hast, nicht doppelt zahlen!

Der Medienpass ist kein Abo Die Laufzeit vom Medienpass ist ein Jahr. Es gibt keine automatische Verlängerung. Und wenn du dir noch nicht ganz sicher bist: Mit dem Probe-Pass kannst du 90 Tage lang testen, ob dir der Medienpass taugt.

Erstmal nur für jetzt Das Angebot ist zeitlich befristet und endet am 6. Januar 2027

Faire Verteilung Alle Einnahmen werden gerecht zwischen den fünf Medien aufgeteilt. Jedes Medium bleibt absolut eigenständig.

We <3 Community Statt (vermeintlich) gegeneinander zu konkurrieren, bieten wir euch diesen Pass gemeinsam an. Wir wollen miteinander statt gegeneinander gegen den Rechtsruck kämpfen!

Dein Medienpass unterstützt unseren feministischen und unabhängigen Journalismus und hilft dabei, Missy zu erhalten. Danke für deinen Support, wir wissen ihn sehr zu schätzen! <3

Übrigens: Den Medienpass kann man auch als Geschenk-Pass für jemand anderen kaufen. Stichwort Weihnachten. Just saying ;)

Just do it again! Für die Freiheit, für das Leben, für die Revolution!


Militarismus, Kapitalismus und Faschismus müssen wir zusammen denken, denn sie stärken sich gegenseitig und profitieren voneinander. Lasst sie uns gemeinsam bekämpfen!


Wir erleben eine Militarisierung in allen Bereichen der Gesellschaft. Seit langem ist dies ein schleichender Prozess, seit kurzem ein offen ausgerufenes Ziel. Wofür Aufrüsten? Unter anderem, um den deutschen Wirtschaftsstandort und seine global relevante Rolle aufrechtzuerhalten. Das kapitalistische System ist mal wieder in der Krise. Statt alternative Wirtschaftssysteme zu etablieren, die weniger Raubbau an Natur und Menschheit verursachen, wird ein autoritärer Staatsumbau legitimiert, der jegliche erkämpfte Errungenschaften wie Arbeitsrechte und Arbeitslosengeld, freie Bildung, den Klimaschutz,etc. über die Klinge springen lässt.


Gleichzeitig fließen massiv viele Ressourcen in den Ausbau eines Überwachungsapparats, der die Bevölkerung mittels KI ausspioniert, soziale und antifaschistische Proteste kriminalisiert, während eine faschistische Partei auf dem Vormarsch ist.


Junge Menschen haben keinen Bock ihr Leben und ihre Karriere aufs Spiel zu setzen, um Deutschland den Arsch zu retten. Sie wollen keinen Staat und kein Wirtschaftssystem, was ihnen eine positive Zukunftsperspektive verwehrt.


Wir grüßen an dieser Stelle die Gen Z- Proteste!


Faschismus ist die Herrschaftsform des Kapitalismus in der Krise.


In dem was „Zeitenwende“ genannt wird, geht es um die Erneuerung des Kapitalismus in einer Phase wirtschaftlichen Niedergangs. Diese Phase soll einmal mehr durch Aufrüstung, Krieg und die militärische Sicherstellung der Zugänge zu Ressourcen, auf die es vermeintlichen Anspruch gibt, überwunden werden.


Um die Militarisierung voranzubringen, wird vor allem Angst und Unsicherheit in den Köpfen verursacht. Bedrohungsszenarien und teils angestaubte Feindbilder sollen die breite Präsenz und Einflussnahme des Militärs in den zivilen Bereich legitimieren. Schulen und Ausbildungsstätten werden als Rekrutierungszentralen benutzt. Medizinisches Personal für Kriegszeiten mit vielen Verwundeten geschult. Soldat*innen in Uniform in der Öffentlichkeit und großflächige Werbung gewöhnen uns an einen militarisierten Alltag.


Militarisierung und Sozialabbau gehen Hand in Hand mit der zunehmend autoritären Formierung des Staates. Diese wird von bürgerlichen Parteien vorangetrieben und die faschistische Partei AfD als Teil der Neuen Rechten kann die Lorbeeren ernten, wenn es um eine Übernahme des ausufernden Überwachungsstaats, restriktive Aufenthaltsgesetze oder den Umgang mit Protest geht. Rechte und faschistische Kräfte nehmen dann ihre klassische, vom System zugedachte Rolle ein: das Aufbegehren von Teilen der Bevölkerung und den Zusammenhalt untereinander anzugreifen und zu zerschlagen.


Moderner Faschismus und Autoritarismus


Der moderne Faschismus in Deutschland greift natürlich auf Kontinuitäten zurück, die an den Anfang des 20. Jahrhunderts zurückreichen. Die Neue Rechte besteht aus intellektuellen rechtsradikalen Projekten, nationalkonservativen, neoliberalen Ansätzen, gepaart mit völkischen Schlägertrupps und Parteirechten. author: Michael_1973
title: South Africa’s ANC Is Collapsing. The Far Right Is Rising.
content:
The African National Congress is losing its working-class base. The beneficiaries: parties of the Right. South Africa’s local elections expose the fallout of three decades of economic failure — and the need to rebuild working-class power.

In this article, Zwelinzima Vavi, the General Secretary of the South Africa Federation of Trade Unions, reflects on the rout of the ANC in the local government elections on 4 November 2026.

While the global left celebrates the recent successes of the Workers’ Party in Brazil and the Democratic Socialists of America in the United States, the African National Congress (ANC) has suffered a historic collapse in South Africa’s November 4 local government elections. After three decades of mass unemployment, deepening inequality, corruption, and economic policies that have failed the working class, the former liberation movement is losing its political authority. The principal beneficiaries of the ANC’s electoral rout are parties of the Right, including an increasingly powerful far right that has built its project around aggressive and often violent xenophobia.

With more than 70 percent of votes counted, the ANC’s national share of the vote fell to around 32 percent. The ANC is not expected to retain an outright majority in any major city, and the center-right Democratic Alliance (DA), historically the principal party of the white liberal establishment, is making substantial gains and is projected to become the largest party in most of South Africa’s big cities. Former President Jacob Zuma’s Zulu nationalist uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) is on track to be the largest party in Durban. The far-right ActionSA has made a strong showing in Johannesburg and Pretoria and is likely to be the second-largest party in Pretoria, with the ANC in third place.

The central question is not only why the ANC has lost so much support. It is why the suffering and anger of the working class have failed to produce a powerful democratic socialist alternative, and why the Right has been so successful in presenting itself as the answer to a crisis created by the existing economic and political order.

The defeat of apartheid was an extraordinary achievement. We won universal suffrage, democratic institutions, constitutional rights, and legal protections for workers. Those victories were won through generations of sacrifice and collective struggle, and they must be defended. But political apartheid was defeated while the economic structures inherited from apartheid remained largely intact.

The liberation movement historically brought together different classes and social groups united against racial oppression. That unity was indispensable to apartheid’s defeat. But national identity does not abolish class contradictions. Instead of using democracy to transform the ownership and control of the economy in the interests of the majority, the ANC increasingly became an instrument through which a new elite could enter and benefit from the existing economic order.

The ownership and control of the commanding heights of the economy were never fundamentally transformed. Land ownership remained extraordinarily unequal. The former Bantustans, created as reservoirs of cheap African labor, were never provided with the productive economic foundations needed to overcome their inherited poverty.

Over time, the ANC came to treat the advancement of an emerging black capitalist class as evidence of economic transformation. A narrow layer of businesspeople accumulated wealth, in some cases extraordinary wealth, through access to political power, state contracts, and opportunities created by the Black Economic Empowerment policy, while the overwhelming majority remained excluded from meaningful economic power.

The ANC’s adoption of neoliberal economic policies in the 1990s deepened this problem. The language of economic liberation gave way to investor confidence, competitiveness, and market reform. Brutal austerity, liberalization, and dependence on private investment displaced the redistributive ambitions of the liberation struggle.

We were repeatedly told that economic growth would eventually deliver employment and redistribution. We were also told that redistribution must wait for economic growth and the development of the productive forces. But if redistribution had to wait while productive capacity developed, why did South Africa simultaneously deindustrialize?

We have become what I have described as a “warehouse economy …

author: Zane McNeill
title: The “Blue Tsunami” Can’t Leave Trans People Behind
content:
On this Trans Day of Remembrance, Democrats must recommit to rolling back the anti-trans assault of the past two years.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Many are interpreting the “blue tsunami” that swept the nation earlier this month as a resounding rebuke of the MAGA movement’s fearmongering around transgender rights. But this Trans Day of Remembrance (TDOR), we owe it to ourselves and those we have lost to anti-trans violence to sit with the complicated, nuanced truth and not just comfort ourselves with a convenient, feel-good narrative.

It is true that many candidates who campaigned on explicitly anti-trans messaging and policies lost their elections, in spite of the hundreds of millions of dollars they spent on anti-trans ads. In fact, despite the deluge of anti-transgender messaging, many Democrats who refused to throw trans people under the bus, no matter what anti-trans rhetoric was thrown at them from their opponents, won their races across the country. Ten transgender people were elected into office — in Alabama, Georgia, Delaware, Montana, Florida, Washington, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan. Vermont voters approved a constitutional amendment adding explicit equal protection guarantees for sexual orientation, gender identity, and gender expression.

Polling suggests that voters have grown weary of the weaponization of trans issues by the far right, which they view as an attempt to distract them from the issues that matter most in their lives: inflation and the cost of living; jobs and the economy; and skyrocketing health care bills. Voters who were disenchanted with Donald Trump and the Republicans’ failure to deliver a better life for them mostly ignored the anti-trans messaging and voted blue.

But voting blue doesn’t automatically equate to being pro-trans. Some Democrats who did run on anti-trans policies still won their elections. Further, anti-trans ballot initiatives targeting transgender youth in schools passed in Washington, Arizona, Colorado, and Nebraska, and NBC exit polling showed that 52 percent of people in the U.S. feel that support for transgender rights has “gone too far.”

This sentiment persists despite the fact that at least 25 transgender people have died as a result of violence in the United States over the past year. The actual number of transgender people who have been murdered is certainly higher because the rampant misgendering and deadnaming in news reports and the lack of formal data collection makes accurate tracking and reporting difficult.

The United States has become increasingly untenable for trans people, who now must struggle greatly to survive, let alone thrive. More than half the country has banned medically necessary medication and surgical care for transgender youth and restricted their ability to participate in sports consistent with their gender identity. Across the country, 10 states prohibit people from correcting the gender marker on their birth certificates, eight states ban updates to gender markers on driver’s licenses, and nine states prohibit transgender people from using bathrooms and facilities that align with their gender identity in government-owned buildings and spaces, including K–12 schools and colleges.

Such policies have prompted 9 percent of trans people polled to relocate since 2024, fleeing states with anti-trans laws for supposedly safer havens like Washington and Colorado. But those states, too, have now passed similar anti-trans measures through ballot initiatives (though trans rights advocates have said they will fight to repeal them via legislation and litigation).

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has made attacks on transgender rights a central policy priority, making it increasingly difficult for trans youth to feel safe anywhere in the country. The Trump administration is especially fixated on undermining medical research and standards of care for transgender youth and has challenged states’ sovereign authority to regulate the practice of medicine within their borders. The Trump administration has also issued civil and grand jury subpoenas to hospitals in attempts to obtain transgender youths’ private medical records, targeted the medical associations responsible for researching and developing standards of care for transgender youth through civil investigative subpoenas and litigation, and stopped reimbursing …

author: Freedom Editor
title: Trans remembrance & everyday resistance
content:
The transphobes may have won their draconian legislation, but they have lost the culture war

In July 2017, the Tory Government announced a public consultation on legal gender recognition in the United Kingdom. It aimed to bring in a system based on statutory declaration, and like many European countries, allow trans persons to obtain a Gender Recognition Certificate on the basis of a statutory declaration. This proposed change was supported by the Labour opposition and was not seen as significantly controversial.

Almost immediately, we witnessed a systematic attack on trans children, starting with claims about protecting them from untested medical inteventions and the outright lie that children under 18 were undergoing surgery. In an important case funded by American anti-abortionists, it was argued that young people aged 15 were too young to fully appreciate the consequence of taking puberty blockers. When the lower court ruled that children under 18 should not be able to receive any medical intervention, The Guardian celebrated this in its editorial as a return to common sense.

The Appeals Court judges ruled it was legal nonsense, undermined Gillick competency, and if it upheld could undermine access to contraception for women under 16 (which is why the anti-abortion brigade funded it in the first place). But by now, rebranded ‘gender criticals’ were up in arms and the damage was done to our community. The transphobes were given new life and more foundations to persecute the Tavistock Clinic for Young People and attacking youth services and schools.

Then came the billionaire author J.K Rowldemort, who got involved and began tweeting transphobia to her millions of followers and funding transphobic hate groups. Then came legal intervention by the now Labour (Blue State) government. For Women Scotland, Sex Matters and the LGB Alliance worked as a mesh to split Trans people off from LGB. Freed from the ideological shackles of Sheila Jeffries radical feminist talking points, these new transphobes could move on to fear mongering and hate not seen since the heady days of the persecution of Martina Navratilova in tennis (herself sadly now a terf)

But these culture-war attacks would have gone nowhere without the State. From Boris Johnson to Rishi Sunak to Keir Starmer, a series of deeply transphobic prime ministers have followed complete with transphobic health secretaries, education ministers and home secretaries. One minister made it illegal for teachers to refer to children in school by their preferred name. An employment tribunal agreed that gender critical employees could legally misgender their colleagues at work. Two health secretaries, one from each party, banned all prescription of hormone replacement therapy and puberty blockers for under 18s. One of them (Wes Streeting) had previously worked for leading LGBTIA campaign group Stonewall and appeared on television to defend trans women as women.

So here we are, today on this Trans Day of Remembrance: a new ‘left wing’ Labour prime minister with a gay defence secretary, a Muslim woman home secretary, a Jewish foreign secretary—honestly it sounds like an American Democrat’s fantasy—yet this government will continue to enable and apply a draconian set of transphobic policies that amount to wholesale segregation and apartheid.

Adult trans people cannot use the toilets or changing rooms of their gender identity. They will be housed in prison wards, youth offender wings, immigration hostels and hospital wards of their birth sex. They will be searched by police officers, prison officers and immigration officer on their birth sex/ In Wales, all sex replacement surgery has been cancelled despite people waiting for a decade on waiting lists.

Yet resistance persists. I don’t know a single trans person who uses the toilets of their birth sex. And there has yet to be a single reported incident of a venue or organisation forcing someone to leave. The transphobes may won their legislation, but they have lost the culture war they started. Most people see us as just women, men and nonbinary people who are surviving, just like them, in a toxic authoritarian country ruled by death eaters and bigots.

Personally, I’ve not had one woman in the toilets offer me anything other than acceptance. In those small moments when a woman tells me my dress looks nice in a public toilet, I feel a sense of recognition and solidarity. That gives me hope that out of our remembrance of past …

Το σκάνδαλο μεγατόνων της Pizza Fan δεν αποτελεί απλώς υπόθεση ακραίας φορο – κλοπής. Είναι το πιο κραυγαλέο, έως τώρα, μνημείο της κυβερνητικής απάτης περί «πάταξης της φοροδιαφυγής», περί θαύματος της ελληνικής εστίασης και «προστασίας» των εργαζομένων από την «εθνική κοινωνική συμφωνία» για τις συλλογικές συμβάσεις…


Την ώρα που η κυβέρνηση τσακίζει τα φτωχά νοικοκυριά με ΦΠΑ στο 24% (ενώ καλπάζει ο πληθωρισμός που γεννά το σύστημα και οι πόλεμοι που συμμετέχει το Μητσοτακέικο), εξοντώνει τα μικρομάγαζα της γειτονιάς με τη σύνδεση Ταμειακών Μηχανών – POS και τα ψηφιακά τιμολόγια, έκανε πλάτες και άφηνε στο απυρόβλητο ένα επιχειρηματικό θηρίο να στήνει «πάρτι» εκατομμυρίων προπαντός σε βάρος των εργαζομένων του και των ίδιων των εσόδων του δημοσίου.


Αλλά ακόμα και τώρα που το κράτος αποκάλυψε το σκάνδαλο (προφανώς για να αρπάξουν άλλα επιχειρηματικά μεγα – θήρια το άθαφτο πλέον πτώμα της Pizza Fan), δεν δίνει δεκάρα για τους εργαζομένους – θύματα της εταιρείας.


Πριν το λουκέτο, πίσω από τις βιτρίνες βασίλευε η μαύρη εργασία, οι εικονικές 6ωρες συμβάσεις, «μαύρες» πληρωμές στο χέρι και η πλήρης γελοιοποίηση της ψηφιακής κάρτας εργασίας. Μετά το λουκέτο, βασιλεύει η απειλή της ανεργίας, της μη αποζημίωσης και της ανυπαρξίας κρατικής στήριξης!


Οι συνδικαλιστές «εκπρόσωποι» των εργαζομένων της Pizza Fan, δεν κάνουν τίποτα ουσιαστικά άλλο εκτός από να παρακαλούν την κυβέρνηση και τους εργοδότες να κάνουν το «νομίμως» δυνατό, την ώρα που αυτή μετράει και το παραμικρό σεντς (αν πρόκειται για τους εργαζομένους), ενώ σκάει δις για πολεμικές δαπάνες.


Και γιατί να τηρήσουν το νόμο οι ιδιοκτήτες της Pizza Fan τώρα που έχουν βαρέσει «κανόνι», αφού δεν το έκαναν όταν θησαύριζαν;


Μάς λένε ψέμματα για άλλη μια φορά! Αλλά να μην τους αφήσουμε ξανά να μας τα επιβάλλουν. Παλεύουμε για:


– Καμιά απόλυση στην Pizza Fan! Διασφάλιση όλων των θέσεων εργασίας!


– Άμεση πληρωμή δεδουλευμένων και ενσήμων με ταυτόχρονη κατάσχεση και ρευστοποίηση της κινητής και ακίνητης περιουσίας του απατεώνα ιδιοκτήτη!


– Τοπικές επιτροπές στήριξης των εργαζομένων της Pizza Fan. Στάσεις εργασίας από τοπικά σωματεία.


– Mετατροπή όλων των συμβάσεων σε 8ώρες συμβάσεις με βάση την Κλαδική Συλλογική Σύμβαση στην εστίαση. Αναδρομικές αυξήσεις από την ημέρα πρόσληψης για την αποκατάσταση των χαμένων μισθών από την αδήλωτη εργασία!

author: TGEU
title: Joint Statement: Why Portugal’s Self-Determination Act Must Stay
content:
TGEU, IGLYO, OII Europe and ILGA-Europe have submitted joint comments to the Portuguese Parliament on two Bills that would repeal Law 38/2018, the Self-Determination Act, and reinstate the medicalised regime of Law 7/2011: Bill 391/XVII/1, tabled by Chega, and Bill 486/XVII/1, tabled by the PSD. Both parties sit in the ruling government, so together they command the majority needed to pass these Bills into law. We ask Parliament to withdraw both Bills or vote against them in their entirety.


There is no problem to solve.

 The Self-Determination Act works. Between 2018 and 2022, 1,595 people changed their gender marker, more than triple the previous period, and the competent authority, the CIG, reported in 2022 and again in 2026 that it knows of no refusals, no fraud and no misuse. Twelve European countries have self-determination models, some for over a decade; none has repealed them. Where rare problems arose, courts solved them. Legal initiatives that strip people of acquired rights need a demonstrated need, and none exists.


What these Bills would do


Bring back pathologisation and clinical gatekeeping.

 Trans adults would once again have to prove their identity to two multidisciplinary medical teams, undergo years of psychological monitoring and, as drafted, in practice show proof of surgery before the State recognises who they are. The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that no one should have to accept surgery or sterilising treatment to be recognised, and the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe has called for procedures based on self-determination. Worse still, Portugal already struggles with a shortage of professionals in trans-specific healthcare: a procedure requiring two teams, years of monitoring and a surgical pathway would make legal gender recognition effectively inaccessible in practice, squandering scarce medical resources on certifying instead of treating or meeting actual health needs. These Bills would put doctors, not trans people, in charge of trans people’s identities.


Exclude 16 and 17 year olds from legal gender recognition

, despite the existing safeguards (legal representatives, a personal hearing and a capacity report) and no recorded refusals, fraud or abuse. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child requires capacity-based assessment, not fixed age limits. The reality for those affected: every exam, train ride, job application or school registration becomes a forced outing, in a country where nearly three in four LGBTQI students report bullying or insults at school.


Weaken protection of intersex children.

 Portugal made history in 2018 as the second European country to ban non-consensual medical interventions on intersex children. Bill 391 repeals that ban without an adequate replacement; Bill 486’s weakly defined “health exception” could still permit medically unnecessary “normalising” surgeries. Both Bills regress on Recommendation CM/Rec(2025)7, which Portugal helped adopt only very recently in October 2025.


Roll back healthcare and education rights.

 Bill 391 would ban all gender-affirming care for under-18s by statute, overriding the judgment of doctors, parents and the young people themselves, and restrict teaching on gender diversity in schools, an approach the EU Court of Justice has already rejected in its judgment against Hungary. Bill 486 removes the protected ground of gender expression, restricts sports participation by “biological sex”, risks excluding trans and intersex children from youth and school sport, and deletes the right to a social name, which migrants, minors and non-binary people rely on to live as themselves in schools, workplaces and public services.


Rely on outdated, pathologising and stigmatising terminology

 (“gender identity disorder”, “transsexuality”, “hermaphrodites”) that contradicts ICD-11, which Portugal supported, and the human-rights based language that all 46 Council of Europe member States have adopted with CM/Rec(2025)7. Words matter: law that frames people as disorders invites treating them as such.


Not in line with international human rights law


Restricting fundamental rights requires a pressing social need under Article 8(2) ECHR and the Portuguese Constitution. These Bills offer conceptual or hypothetical worries, thinly sourced on Portuguese practice, not demonstrated problems. Rolling back rights people already hold requires full justification and consideration of all alternatives; these Bills …

author: anred
title: 19N: un grito colectivo contra la violencia sexual hacia las niñeces y adolescencias
content:
En el marco del Día Internacional contra las Violencias Sexuales hacia Niñeces y Adolescencias, organizaciones feministas, transfeministas, sobrevivientes y madres protectoras se movilizarán este jueves 19 de noviembre frente al Congreso de la Nación. Bajo la consigna «Yo sí te creo», denunciarán la impunidad judicial, las revinculaciones forzadas con agresores y el desmantelamiento de las políticas públicas de protección. La jornada combinará denuncia, memoria, organización colectiva y un festival para recuperar el espacio público desde el encuentro y la celebración

. Por ANRed


Este 19 de noviembre, el Congreso de la Nación será escenario de una nueva edición del

Grito Global contra las Violencias Sexuales hacia Niñeces y Adolescencias.

 La convocatoria, impulsada por el Colectivo Yo Sí Te Creo junto a organizaciones sociales, feministas y transfeministas, reunirá a sobrevivientes, madres y familiares protectores, profesionales de la salud, docentes y activistas que desde hace años se organizan para denunciar una de las formas más silenciadas de violencia.


La jornada se inscribe en una trayectoria de trece años de lucha y visibilización, que desde 2020 se articula en distintos territorios del país bajo la iniciativa del Grito Global. Su objetivo es romper el silencio, denunciar las responsabilidades institucionales y construir redes colectivas de acompañamiento y protección.


Según los datos citados por las organizaciones convocantes,

una de cada cinco niñas y uno de cada siete niños atraviesan situaciones de violencia sexual

. En Argentina, señalan que cerca del 80 % de estos hechos ocurren en el ámbito intrafamiliar o en entornos de confianza. Estas cifras, advierten, no alcanzan a reflejar la verdadera magnitud del problema, debido a la enorme cantidad de situaciones que nunca llegan a denunciarse.


La violencia sexual contra las infancias no constituye un problema exclusivamente privado o familiar. Las organizaciones denuncian que se encuentra atravesada por relaciones desiguales de poder, condiciones económicas, estructuras patriarcales y prácticas institucionales que muchas veces terminan garantizando la impunidad de los agresores.


Una justicia que revictimiza y desprotege


Uno de los principales ejes de la convocatoria será la denuncia del funcionamiento del Poder Judicial frente a las situaciones de abuso sexual infantil.


El documento cuestiona la utilización del denominado Síndrome de Alienación Parental (SAP) y de argumentos derivados, como las supuestas falsas memorias o los relatos inducidos, para desacreditar las denuncias de niños, niñas, adolescentes y sus entornos protectores.


Las organizaciones advierten que estas prácticas pueden convertirse en herramientas de revictimización y derivar en decisiones judiciales que obligan a las infancias a mantener contacto con personas denunciadas por abuso sexual.


En ese sentido, rechazan las revinculaciones forzadas y exigen el apartamiento de funcionarios judiciales responsables de vulnerar los derechos de las niñeces. También reclaman el regreso de las niñas Arociris, de La Rioja, y Cielo, de Chaco, a sus respectivos entornos protectores.


La criminalización de las madres que denuncian constituye otro de los puntos centrales. Bajo la consigna «No somos obstructoras, somos protectoras», las organizaciones denuncian la persecución judicial de mujeres que intentan proteger a sus hijos e hijas y reclaman la libertad de Flavia Saganías.


A estas situaciones se suman las dificultades materiales para acceder a la justicia: falta de patrocinio jurídico gratuito, investigaciones que se prolongan durante años, ausencia de acompañamiento especializado y desigualdades económicas que condicionan las posibilidades de sostener una denuncia.


Las organizaciones reclaman presupuesto, equipos interdisciplinarios, atención psicológica especializada, acompañamiento a sobrevivientes y condiciones laborales dignas para quienes trabajan en los dispositivos de protección.


En particular, reivindican la implementación efectiva de la Ley Nacional de Educación Sexual Integral, con formación docente y contenidos científicos en todos los niveles educativos, como una herramienta fundamental para que las infancias puedan reconocer situaciones de violencia, identificar sus derechos y acceder a redes de cuidado.


Asimismo, defienden el acceso a la interrupción legal y voluntaria del embarazo y recuperan la consigna «Son niñas, no madres», frente a las maternidades …

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Administration’s Bid to Restrict Gender Affirming Care for Incarcerated People
content:
On October 21, 2026, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s request to restrict medical treatment and accommodations for transgender people in federal prisons. The decision allows a lower court order blocking the policy to remain in place while the legal challenge proceeds. The ruling is an important development in the ongoing debate over transgender rights, access to healthcare, and the federal government’s authority over incarcerated people.

The dispute began after President Donald Trump issued an executive order restricting federal funding for certain medical treatments for transgender people in government custody. In response, the Bureau of Prisons introduced a policy that would end hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries for incarcerated people with gender dysphoria. The policy also sought to restrict certain accommodations for transgender prisoners.

Gender dysphoria is the distress some people experience when their gender identity does not align with their sex assigned at birth. The administration argued that these gender-affirming treatments were not necessary and that restricting them was justified by security and administrative concerns within federal prisons.

However, the policy faced legal challenges from three transgender people incarcerated in federal prisons, including one transgender woman and two transgender men. Their attorneys argued that the new restrictions would force the end of treatments that the Bureau of Prisons had provided to people with gender dysphoria since 1992.

The policy could affect nearly 1,000 incarcerated people in federal custody. The lawsuit raises questions about whether the government can discontinue established medical treatments for incarcerated people and what constitutional protections apply to people in its custody.

A lower federal court blocked the administration from enforcing the policy. The Justice Department then appealed to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to pause that ruling and allow the restrictions to take effect while the case continued. On October 21, the Supreme Court rejected the emergency request in an unsigned order. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas stated that they would have granted the request. The decision leaves the lower court’s order in place, preventing the administration from immediately enforcing the restrictions.

However, the Supreme Court’s decision does not resolve the underlying lawsuit or determine whether the administration’s policy is constitutional. The legal challenge will continue in the lower courts.

The case highlights the challenges transgender people face when seeking health care in settings where the government controls their medical decisions. Incarcerated people depend on prison authorities for access to doctors, medication, and other necessary services so when a policy restricts particular treatment, people in custody may have limited options for obtaining care independently.

Although the ruling does not end the case, it prevents the Trump administration from immediately implementing the restrictions while the legal proceedings continue. The outcome of the lawsuit will have important consequences for transgender people in federal prisons if the restrictions are placed and as the case moves forward, it shows the importance of questioning how government policies affect vulnerable populations and how government decisions apply to people whose freedom and access to healthcare are already limited.

author: Unknown
title: Toujours pas d'héro·ines, d'égo(trip) !
content:
Communiqué unitaire de

collectifs français pratiquant la street medic

 comme moyen de lutte face aux oppressions


Depuis plusieurs semaines, des manifestant·es s'organisent pour apporter les premiers soins sur les lieux de mobilisation. On ne peut que se réjouir de toutes ces initiatives, et les encourager

 

! Cependant, dans ces élans de solidarité, et accompagnant la création de nouveaux groupes en ligne qui se réclament de la street medic, certain·es se disent ouvertement apolitiques et neutres. Nous entendons même souvent : Nous, on soigne tout le monde. Policiers ou manifestants, peu importe. Certain·es refusent même la prise en charge de ce qu'iels considèrent comme de mauvais·es manifestant·es ou des casseur·euses. La street medic est pourtant bel et bien une pratique politique, avec tout ce qui en découle de valeurs et d'engagement

 

!


Aucun grand mouvement social depuis celui des gilets jaunes n'avait cherché à autant mettre le projecteur sur la pratique de la street médic comme nous l'observons aujourd'hui. Depuis le mois de septembre et la vague de mobilisation impulsée par les lycéennes, nous sommes de nouveau exposé·es. Nos pratiques se voient encore une fois instrumentalisées, par des personnes se revendiquant de la street medic, par les médias ou même par les forces de l'ordre (

FDO

), et risquent de se voir affaiblies et détournées de leur but.


C'est pourquoi, 7 ans plus tard, nous [les signataires] avons décidé de prendre à nouveau la parole pour ré-affirmer l'essentiel de ce que nous sommes et redéfinir les pratiques auxquelles fait référence le terme de Street Medic et autour desquelles nous nous organisons depuis plusieurs années maintenant. Ce communiqué est un écho et une mise à jour de celui de 2019, duquel nous nous sommes profondément inspiré.es.


D'où vient ce terme

 

?


La street medic est une pratique de lutte, née dans les années 1960 lors du mouvement des Civils Rights aux États-Unis, qui fut développée par le Black Panthers Party et l'American Indian Movement. Au-delà du simple cadre des manifestations auxquelles sont associé·es les Street Medics aujourd'hui, il s'agissait alors de mettre en place un véritable système d'accès au soin communautaire, autogéré et indépendant à destination des personnes noir·es aux États-Unis, avec notamment l'instauration de street clinics ( hôpitaux de campagne ). Si notre action la plus visible et courante se situe effectivement dans le cadre des manifestations aujourd'hui, elle ne saurait s'y limiter obligatoirement.


Ainsi, au même titre que les legal teams (soutien juridique) et les trauma teams (soutien psy), le terme street medic n'est pas neutre. Il induit un caractère fortement et indéniablement politique. De même que le black bloc ne saurait être considéré comme un ensemble de groupuscules organisés mais est bien une pratique tactique adoptée lors des manifestations, la Street Medic est une pratique militante, et non un statut. Il ne s'agit pas simplement d'adapter le secourisme au cadre des manifestations, mais de lutter contre la répression policière et étatique, pour la réappropriation des connaissances en premiers secours et pour l'accès aux soins à toustes.


Force est de constater qu'aujourd'hui les secouristes présent·es en manifestation ne pratiquent pas toustes la street medic.


Il nous paraît donc nécessaire de marquer clairement notre opposition à certaines méthodes qui rentrent en totale contradiction avec les valeurs de la street medic, mais cependant utilisées par des secouristes s'en réclamant.


Ce que nous dénonçons


Aujourd'hui, comme il y a 7 ans, nous observons et nous opposons à des pratiques et des postures incompatibles avec notre histoire et notre philosophie :


La délation de camarades de lutte

 La posture de sauveur·euse

 La sélection des personnes légitimes à pratiquer les premiers soins

 L'instrumentalisation par les médias

 Les pratiques virilistes, validistes, classistes et racistes

1. La délation de camarades de lutte


Avant même la délation, nous constatons continuellement des pratiques dangereuses et des prises de risques numériques graves pouvant entrainer des ruptures de confidentialité et d'anonymat, à la fois des camarades en luttes, mais également des militant·es et manifestant·es auprès desquels nous réalisons des premiers soins : photos non floutées publiées sur les réseaux et partage public d'informations spécifiques susceptibles de permettre la localisation des personnes prises …

author: Marianne Dhenin
title: Authors Sue LA Library Over Anti-Palestinian Discrimination After Talk Cancelled
content:
Even institutions meant to be dedicated to free speech and inclusion are censoring Palestinian writers.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Two authors have filed a lawsuit against the City of Los Angeles, alleging that the Los Angeles Public Library engaged in anti-Palestinian discrimination and violated their free speech rights after the library’s leadership canceled an online event last December where the two were slated to speak to teens about their books, which feature Palestinian characters. This lawsuit against one of the largest public library systems in the nation comes at a time when anti-Palestinian racism and censorship are growing more entrenched across the country, now more than three years into the U.S.-backed genocide in Gaza.

“The stakes are really high, and it’s about so much more than the rights of the authors or even the rights of the readers,” Nora Lester Murad, one of the authors and plaintiffs in the case, told Truthout. “If kids and adults can’t be exposed to representation of Palestinians that’s diverse and nuanced and human and complex and multifaceted, [that erasure] converges with the anti-Palestinian and anti-Muslim narratives that are being used to justify genocide.”

Murad and Palestinian American author Jenan Matari filed the lawsuit in the Superior Court of Los Angeles in late September to demand accountability for the Los Angeles Public Library’s cancellation of their event and to draw attention to anti-Palestinian censorship in the arts.

Matari is the author of the picture book Everything Grows in Jiddo’s Garden, about a young Palestinian girl and her grandfather. Murad was slated to discuss Ida in the Middle, her young adult novel about a 13-year-old Palestinian American girl. The two were scheduled to speak at an online event on December 6, 2025, as part of Read Palestine Week, a global weeklong program highlighting Palestinian authors and stories celebrated in late November and early December each year.

The Los Angeles Public Library’s teen council, a youth volunteer group, voted to host a Read Palestine Week event, and the library’s Middle Eastern North African Affinity Group invited Murad and Matari and acted as liaisons between the authors and library administration in the lead-up to the scheduled event, according to the legal complaint.

But just three days before the event was scheduled to take place, the group notified Murad and Matari that the library administration had canceled it. The notice provided no further explanation for the cancellation, according to the legal complaint.

Records obtained by Los Angeles Public Press in a public records request and cited in the legal complaint later revealed that a staff librarian had emailed library leadership in mid-November 2025, accusing Murad and Matari of having “strong terrorist ties and virulently antisemitic views.” The email said it was sent on behalf of a group of Jewish library staffers and referenced an article from the right-wing Washington Free Beacon and profiles of the authors on Canary Mission, a pro-Israel doxxing platform. It also accused the Middle Eastern North African Affinity Group of having “deeply antisemitic views” and showing “racist behavior to me and others in our Heritage group.”

“This attack was not from outside but from inside the library.”

Later in December 2025, City Librarian John Szabo sent an internal email to staff claiming Murad and Matari’s event had been canceled because the library “has a responsibility to remain nonpartisan and apolitical” and that doing so was “necessary to uphold the Library’s commitment to an inclusive environment free of hate, discrimination, and harassment,” according to a copy of that email obtained by The LA Reporter in a public records request.

Szabo did not respond to Truthout’s request for comment before deadline. A member of the library’s public relations team told Truthout that the library cannot comment on pending litigation.

Murad told Truthout the accusations and cancellation follow a familiar pattern in which criticism of Israel is conflated with antisemitism in order to silence Palestinian speakers like Matari, anti-Zionist Jewish speakers like Murad, or others who speak out to criticize Israel or in support of Palestinian liberation. But, she added, the Los Angeles Public Library case is also unique because the pressure to censor Palestine-related speech came not from …

author: Rizomatica
title: Juana Paillalef denuncia discriminación racial hacia su familia y la infancia Mapuche en Lavkenmapu
content:
Luego de que la machi Millaray Garrido Paillalef, del territorio Lawen Mapu, Lanalhue, realizara un video denunciando violencia institucional y discriminación en el hospital de Arauco, su madre, Juana Paillalef, quien fue directora del Museo Mapuche de Cañete durante 20 años, junto a Mario Cayupi hacen una reflexión sobre diversas situaciones de discriminación racial hacia su familia.


Juana Paillalef a través de su relato explica cómo han vivido vulneraciones, violencia institucional y discriminación, a través de todas las generaciones de su familia. Ella, su hija y ahora su nieta, ven como se vulneran los derechos de niños, no solo mapuches. Comenta cómo han sido vulnerados en su mogen, en su vida como Mapuche, luego de haber levantado a su hija Machi, quien desde estudiante vivió vulneraciones, en el liceo se le discriminó por el uso de sus chaway y su tukuluwün y en la universidad también existieron educadores que la discriminaron por ser Mapuche. En su primer embarazo también vivió vulneraciones en centros de salud, y ahora en la actualidad denuncian haber vivido discriminación y maltratos por un profesional de la salud del hospital de Arauco en contra de su nieta.


“

Se habla de interculturalidad, cambiando por el racismo, ¿pero qué hemos visto de interculturalida hasta este momento? Seguimos en lo mismo. La colonización ha triturado nuestro pensamiento, nuestras formas de vida, nuestras formas de comportamiento, nuestra forma de exigir nuestros derechos, nos han apagado en vez de abrirnos. Llamo a la población a no dormirse, estar atentos y no dejar de caminar al lado de nuestros niños. Hay muchos niños y jóvenes en colegios que se están levantando como machi, y no hay como atender esas situaciones.”


*Video enviado  a la radio


Esta información se publicó en

Radio Kurruf
