author: Rachel Evans
title: Anti-racists counter protest far-right ‘Australia Marches’ rally
content:
About 300 people joined the “No to Racism: Migrants and Refugees Are Welcome” rally at Sydney Town Hall on November 8. It was organised by the Refugee Action Collective Sydney (RAC) to counter the far-right Australian Marches rally against migration.

The far-right rally, which featured speakers from One Nation, Libertarian MP John Ruddick and other right-wing influencers, rallied at the Royal Botanic Garden and drew about 500 people.

Speakers at the counter-protest included Lynda-June Coe, Wiradjuri and Badu Island woman and NSW Greens upper house candidate; Nour Salman from Australia Palestine Advocacy Network; Ishita Chakrabarty from Hindus for Human Rights; Bidjigal/Gweagal activist Jordan Ryan-Hennessy; Ann El Khoury, from University of Sydney Staff for Palestine; Beau Lyon from Action for Public Housing’ and Anisa, a Somali refugee who was held in the Naoero detention centre.

Chakrabarty spoke about the racism faced by Indian migrants and linked One Nation and the Australia Marches rally to the far-right Narendra Modi government in India.

Ian Rintoul from RAC, who chaired the rally, said the United States midterm elections were a huge blow to the racist politics of US President Donald Trump, but said anti-racist campaigners still need to get organised.

“The tragedy is that the racist policies of Australia Marches and One Nation are being fueled by anti-migration and anti-refugee policies of the Labor government,” Rintoul said.

“Labor is linking migration with the housing crisis; cutting the numbers of international students; has introduced fees that will make it harder for refugees to seek asylum in Australia and is implementing an ICE-like compliance force to round up people on temporary visas.”

Lyon said those in power are pushing racism to distract from the real cause of the housing crisis, the for-profit housing system.

“Migrants are not responsible for the housing or cost of living crisis,” Rintoul said.

author: Reisegruppe
title: Reisebericht Paris Herbst 2026
content:
Die Bilder einer „Klasse, die den Kopf wieder hochhebt“


Gespannt saßen wir vor unseren Geräten. „The Revolution will not be televised“, aber scheinbar „live on tiktok“. Ohne große, sichtbare Event-Mobilisierung blockieren die französischen Schüler*innen ihre Oberschulen. Auf dem fruchtbaren Boden einer langjährigen Tradition in Frankreich und einer ersten Blockade in den französischen Koloniegebieten dieses Jahr, beginnt ein Gymnasium einer Pariser Vorstadt aus Wut über die Bedingungen, die sie jeden Tag vorfinden, ihre Schule zu verbarrikadieren. Über die Verbreitung von Videos von der Aktion entsteht schnell eine landesweite Bewegung mit hunderten Nachahmer*innen, die auch die reichen Teile Frankreichs erfasst und nicht lange fackelt, den Protest mit Feuer und Militanz zu untermauern. Die Schüler*innen Frankreichs gehen in Teilen seit 2 Monaten nicht mehr zur Schule und haben sich zu einer Staatsgefährdenden Kraft entwickelt, die selbst mit 5 Milliarden des tief verschuldeten Macron-Regime nicht einzufangen ist. Das ganze steht nicht im Kontext einer Reformbestrebung oder ähnlichem sondern ist die Fortsetzung der Nahel-Revolte von 2023.


Währendessen bekommen wir von Überall aus Europa Nachrichten, wie sich junge Leute dem Aufstand der Schüler*innen anschließen und „wie in Frankreich“ protestieren, blockieren, plündern und angreifen. Wir fragen uns wann es in Deutschland los geht, ob wir als Erwachsene etwas tun können und kommen erstmal nur in Passivität. Uns erreichen die ersten Aufrufe eines Gelbwesten Revivals was mit der aktuellen GenZ-Revolte verknüpft werden soll. Die Lebenserhaltungskosten in Frankreich sind wie in Deutschland enorm gestiegen. Die Polizei hat die Schüler*innen mit allem bekämpft was wir von ihnen kennen, inklusive amputierten Händen, ausgeschossenen Augen und tausenden herabwürdigenden Festnahmen bei Minderjährigen. Dies ruft, verständlicherwise, Empörung bei allen Eltern und empathischen Menschen hervor. Das Land scheint also zu brodeln und meine Güte ist der Vulkan ausgebrochen. Hunderte Verletzte Polizt*innen, Tausende geplünderte Geschäfte und hunderttausende Beteiligte beschreiben nur im Ansatz das was dort am 17.10. an aufständiger Freude, Gemeinschaft und Power stattgefunden hat und was alle die wir getroffen haben nur als „historisch“ beschreiben konnten.


Im Kontext der letzten Geschehnisse war für uns klar, wir müssen dahin um uns selbst ein Bild von der Lage vor Ort zu verschaffen.


Als Deutsche auf einem Protest in Frankreich


An einem regnerischen Herbstag ging es früh los. Ausgerüstet mit Atemmasken, Schutzbrillen und ordentlich Proviant zog es uns in Richtung Innenstadt. Angekommen in der Nähe vom Place de la Republique suchten wir vergebens nach den viel beschriebenen aufständigen Personen. Nach einiger Zeit erfolglosem Suchen breitet sich die erste Enttäuschung in unseren Köpfe aus. Ist der Funke einer neuen Protestbewegung erloschen?


Nicht wirklich. Zum Glück konnten uns vorortig wohnende Genoss*innen Bescheid geben, dass die heutige Demo am Stadtrand noch stattfinden wird. Anscheinend hatten die heftigen Krawalle vom 17.10 dem französischen Innenminesterium so einen Schrecken eingejagt, dass sie aus Angst die Pariser Innenstadt vor jeglicher Demonstrationen schützen wollten.


Also ging es mit der U-Bahn Richtung Osten der franz. Hauptstadt. Schon am Gleis bemerkten wir, dass es um uns herum voller geworden ist. Es schien als ob ganz Paris zur Demonstrationen fahren will. Und BAM! Der Auftaktkundebungsort ist eine riesige Blase an Menschen. Man kann das Ende nur erahnen und wir kriegen Gänsehaut beim Anblick der Jugendlichen auf den Haltestelldächern und den tausenden Leute die ACAB grölen (obwohl das hier eher ACAB singen ist). Die Vorfreude steigt auf das Kommende. Nach kurzer Pinkelpause setzte sich der Protestzug in Bewegung. Es gibt keinen Punkt von dem man aus, das Ende sowie den Anfang der Demo sehen kann. Er ist schlicht zu lang. Sowas haben wir in der Form in Deutschland noch nicht erlebt. Das hier ist kein FFF-Protest, kein inhaltsloses Unteilbar-Bündnis sondern eine über 100.000 Personen-Versammlung, die eine eigene Bewegung darstellt. Zwar folgte die Mehrheit einem Aufruf der nicht-revolutionären Gewerkschaften, trotzdem ist es bewundernswert, wie sich die Aufständigen von den massiven Repressionen der letzten Wochen nicht einschüchtern lassen. Zudem stehen die heutigen Proteste als Nachfolge und in Solidarität mit den landesweiten subversiven …

author: Ezra
title: OG FFM: Aufenthaltsverbote nach den GenZ-Protesten in Frankfurt am Main
content:
OG FFM: Aufenthaltsverbote nach den GenZ-Protesten in Frankfurt am Main


Das Resümee auf Seiten der Teilnehmer*innen an den Protesten gegen soziale Ungleichheit, steigende Lebenshaltungskosten, Kürzungen im Bildungsbereich und die Wehrpflicht ist erschütternd. Viele, gerade junge Menschen, erlebten während und nach der Demonstration brutale Polizeigewalt. 

„Im Nachgang der Demonstration meldeten sich viele Betroffene bei uns und anderen Organisationen und berichteten von Verletzungen, die durch den Polizeieinsatz entstanden sind. Neben zahlreichen Augenverletzungen durch den massiven Einsatz von Pfefferspray gab es auch schwere Gehirnerschütterungen, Rippenbrüche und Knochenbrüchen“, so Anna Kaiser von der Roten Hilfe Ortsgruppe Frankfurt. 

Auch in Sozialen Medien ist einerseits das rücksichtslose Vorgehen der Polizei gegen alle Teilnehmenden der Proteste dokumentiert. Andererseits zeugen Berichte von den unbeholfenen und widersprüchlichen Polizeitaktiken vor Ort. Teilnehmende, welche den Protestzug verlassen wollten, wurden von der Polizei teilweise gewaltsam daran verhindert und kollektiv in der Frankfurter Innenstadt eingekesselt.

Einige der Protestierende erhielten in den letzten Tagen Post durch das Polizeipräsidium Frankfurt, genauer die

SOKO

 3110. Ihnen wurde ein Aufenthaltsverbot für die Frankfurter Innenstadt angedroht. 

„Nach wochenlanger medialer wie stadtpolitischer Hetze gegen die Proteste schien es Aufgabe der Polizei zu sein, Bilder der Eskalation mindestens hinzunehmen, oder sogar mit zu produzieren“, so Anna Kaiser. „Die nun folgenden Grundrechtseinschränkungen dienen dazu, die rassistische und autoritäre Hetze zu untermauern.“ Viele der Verbote sollen willkürlich bis Januar 2027 ausgesprochen werden.

Die Gewalt und die jetzigen Versuche, die geplanten Proteste gegen die Wehrpflicht am 20. November zu kriminalisieren, zeugen davon, dass die Polizei kein neutraler Akteur ist. Die Rote Hilfe empfiehlt, nicht mit der Polizei zu kooperieren, gegen Auflagen und Aufenthaltsverbote Widerspruch einzulegen und sich juristisch und politisch dagegen zu wehren.

Rote Hilfe – Ortsgruppe Frankfurt am Main


Ezra


21.11.2026 - 00:46


Pressemitteilung


Während der GenZ-Regelt-Proteste in Frankfurt am Main am 31.10.2026 erlitten dutzende, meist junge Menschen durch den brutalen Einsatz der Polizei schwere Verletzungen – vom Rippenbrüchen bis zur schweren Gehirnerschütterungen. Darüber hinaus erhielten einige Protestierende in den letzten Tagen eine schriftliche Androhung eines Aufenthaltsverbots für die Frankfurter Innenstadt. Teilweise bis Januar 2027. Die medialen Szenen, welche die Polizei mitzutragen hat, dienen nun für weitreichende repressive Grundrechtseinschränkungen.

author: Sofia Little
title: Protests Across the Pond: Gen-Z and the Fight for Affordability in Europe
content:
Across Europe, rising living costs, unaffordable housing, low wages and underfunded public services have fueled a growing wave of protests. Since mid-September, more than 1,700 cost-of-living demonstrations have taken place in 31 European countries. The protests have brought students, workers, and community members into the streets, with young people playing a visible role in organizing and demanding change.

In France, a country with a centuries-long history of protest, the demonstrations began with students demanding more resources for underfunded schools. Students raised concerns about overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, and crumbling infrastructure. The demonstrations grew into a broader movement, drawing in labor unions and other activists who called out the rising cost of living and declining public services. On October 17th, an estimated 550,000 to 800,00 people protested nationwide.

Other countries began following suit. Since mid-September, demonstrations over high living costs, low wages, and lack of public services have broken out all across Europe. From Spain and Portugal to Germany and Albania, these protests have largely been led by Gen Z. In Spain and Portugal, protesters established encampments in public squares across major cities, demanding stronger laws to protect renters following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid.

In Italy, the “Italia in Piazza”, or Italy in the Streets movement, brought thousands of protesters to the streets. Demonstrators called for better employment, healthcare, education, access to housing, and better wages. Major demonstrations have also taken place in Albania, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Germany, and Serbia.

While the majority of demonstrations have been peaceful, some have escalated into riots involving looting, fires, and property destruction. Only 20% of the recorded events involved riots. However, the police response has been overwhelmingly severe, regardless of whether these protests have been peaceful or violent. French authorities have deployed military-style tactics to antagonize peaceful demonstrations, tactics that have long since drawn condemnation from international human rights monitors.

It is clear that all over the continent—all over the world— Gen Z is tired of waiting for promises to be delivered. They are demanding more than promises from political leaders. They want a future in which they can build secure lives. Young people are confronting economic and social challenges while remaining underrepresented in many of the institutions responsible for addressing them. Their participation in these movements shows that they are not willing to remain on the sidelines while decisions about their futures are made without them.

Across the world, communities are struggling to make rent, afford groceries, and childcare. We must demand more for ourselves, our communities and our future. And so, the fight for affordability continues.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Lawyers condemn human rights violations vs protesters
content:
The National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) condemned the arrest, restricted legal access, and prolonged detention of more than 300 protesters apprehended during demonstrations at Liwasang Bonifacio and Sucat People’s Park ahead of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.

During a press conference at the Liwasang Bonifacio on November 17, the lawyers’ group stressed that human rights violations were committed against the detained protesters.

Legal counsels assisting the detainees criticized law enforcement authorities for allegedly delaying their access to clients, filing sweeping criminal complaints, and leaving them in detention over a long non-working holiday period.

Ephraim Cortez, president of NUPL, denounced police authorities for requiring clearance from higher authorities before allowing legal counsels to confer with their detained clients.

He said, “A lawyer’s access to their clients cannot rely upon clearance from higher-ranking officials, as this is our clients’ right to counsel.”

Cortez added that the detention already exceeded the 18 hours allowed by the law. “Those arrested are innocent. They were just protesting. They should be released.”

The protesters were taken into custody during standoffs at the Liwasang Bonifacio and Sucat People’s Park.

Lawyer Mary Jane Real said that arresting demonstrators inside Liwasang Bonifacio violates the law on public assemblies. She stressed that Liwasang Bonifacio is a freedom park. “You cannot be arrested for protesting here, because we have the freedom to protest in this place.”

According to Real, the nine individuals arrested in Manila are facing multiple charges including illegal assemblies, direct assault, resistance and disobedience to a person in authority, tumults and other disturbances of public order, and violations of the Public Assembly Act.

Real also raised alarm over procedural delays caused by the ASEAN Summit work suspension in Metro Manila, noting that even if bail is recommended, detainees remain behind bars since there will be no court personnel to process release orders.

“The inquest concluded yesterday… We are currently awaiting the prosecutor’s decision, but since today is a holiday, no action can be taken until everyone returns to the office on Thursday,” Real said. “Consequently, even posting bail is not possible, as there is no one available to sign the necessary documents.”

On the other hand, lawyer Zoe Caballero of Sentro Para Sa Tunay Na Repormang Agraryo

denounced the reported P9-million cumulative bail required for the detained protesters, most of whom are farmers, workers, and students from the Southern Tagalog region.

“They themselves have nothing to eat, so where are they supposed to get the P9 million? If they actually had P9 million, they wouldn’t have marched all the way to Manila just to make their voices heard,” Caballero said. “Now, we’re being told: ‘Yes, you have the right to speak, but this is the price you must pay to say what needs to be said.’ It turns out you have to be wealthy just to be heard.”

Real urged the public to stand in solidarity with the detained demonstrators, stressing that their protests against Pax Silica are meant to protect ordinary Filipinos from worsening poverty and hunger. “If we don’t oppose this, all we’ll get here in this ‘Pax Silica’ is hunger and poverty. These people, they are the ones making sacrifices so that we may uphold our rights.”

“We have a responsibility toward them; we must help them gain their freedom, because they risked their own lives and peace so that we could be free,” Real said. (AMU, DAA)

author: By  Jo Kimmy, Contributor
title: From Hospitals to Palantir HQ: Protests Across England Over Controversial Healthcare Data Deal
content:
London, England — “We need to take our power back! Our UK government needs to represent the interests of the British public, who elected them into power, not the Zionist entity,” said Taby Khan, a health research scientist protesting outside The Royal London Hospital.


On October 1, doctors, nurses, health care workers and members of the public took to the streets at more than 40 locations across England, demanding an end to the controversial £330 million ($442 million) contract between the National Health Service (NHS) and U.S. technology company Palantir.


The mobilization was organized by the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Health Workers for a Free Palestine, Amnesty International, Medact, Keep Our NHS Public, and other groups. They argue that a company known for its work with military and immigration agencies, including the development of AI and surveillance technologies, should not have access to the sensitive health data of

60 million people

 in England.


The protests began outside hospitals across the country, including four locations in London, before culminating in a demonstration outside Palantir’s London headquarters.


Located in central London, Palantir’s London office is the company’s

largest globally

, employing more people than its Silicon Valley headquarters. In front of the building, with its dark, heavily tinted windows and no visible signs identifying it as Palantir’s offices, hundreds of people chanted, held signs and displayed a giant symbolic notice calling for the contract to be terminated.


The demo was largely peaceful, although verbal tensions arose between anti-Palantir protesters and Zionist agitators who were trying to disrupt the demonstration and provoke tensions. Some protesters accused the police of allowing these tensions to develop.


The protest brought together concerns that might otherwise remain separate: the privatization of public services, the security of patient information, the expansion of surveillance technology and Palantir’s involvement in war crimes.


Palantir and the NHS: Who Owns Britain’s Health Data?


The NHS was officially

established

 on July 5, 1948, marking the first time a Western country provided free medical care to its entire population, regardless of status.


The relationship between the NHS and the U.S. tech company

began with an “emergency” contract

 under which Palantir offered to support the vaccination program and data management projects. In 2023, with little consideration for alternative solutions, Palantir was awarded the

contract

 to deliver the

NHS Federated Data Platform (FDP)

.


As the

NHS Data Professionals

 explain: “duplications and local variations prevent smooth linkage across datasets and regions.” The FDP is intended to help NHS organizations connect information held across different systems, making it easier to coordinate services, plan capacity and support operational decisions.


The underlying challenge is real: information can be fragmented across hospitals, general practices and regional services, making it difficult to build a joined-up picture of patient care.


Data analysts have raised concerns about the FDP’s highly centralized structure. Palantir supplies data engineers and manages the underlying infrastructure, which provides limited transparency and leaves NHS organizations with less ability to independently adapt the software to their needs.


From Military Intelligence to Public Healthcare


“Palantir is here to disrupt…and, when it’s necessary, to scare our enemies and, on

occasion, kill them.” –

Alex Karp, Palantir CEO


During the protest in front of Palantir’s London headquarters, a letter written by an anonymous NHS data analyst was read aloud. In it, the analyst described how she had begun to hate her job, working with software developed by a company responsible for the deaths of hundreds of her healthcare colleagues.


Palantir initially focused on government, military and intelligence agencies before expanding into the commercial and wider public sectors. The NHS FDP operates on the Foundry software, which is marketed as a system for the “modern enterprise.” Its other products include Gotham, used for “defense and resilience,” and Apollo, which manages software deployment.


The company’s military business is central to why many healthcare workers oppose its role in the NHS. Its

author: Mehran Khalili
title: What’s next for Europe’s autumn of protests?
content:
This article

What’s next for Europe’s autumn of protests? 

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


It was a Wednesday afternoon in late October, and several marches were converging on Syntagma Square in Athens, the epicenter of Greek protest. There were teachers on strike, university students who’d camped in the square overnight, and high schoolers holding painted banners that read “From Greece to France, we’re fighting for modern schools.” Parents pushed strollers through the growing crowd, their toddlers looking on in wonder.


But not everyone was there for the same reason. Groups of black-clad young men ducking in and out of the march, faces covered, were play-fighting each other in a way that looked like a rehearsal. Riot police were lining the side streets, watching over it all with the bored expression of men waiting for their shift to end. And photojournalists were circling, hoping for the youths and the police to meet in a burst of violence that would pay for their day.


The violence didn’t happen this time. According to the

police count

, 10,000 people marched peacefully through central Athens. Afterwards, people hung around, arguing about politics and passing water bottles in the autumn sun. 


I keep thinking about those bored riot police, though, because they seemed to understand what organizers sometimes don’t: A government that has seen a lot of marches knows how to wait one out. The question for the teachers and students in Athens — and in Paris, Milan, Brussels, Lisbon, Madrid, Berlin, Vienna, Tirana and every other city caught up in Europe’s autumn of protest — is how to make saying no cost their governments more than saying yes.


An autumn of anger


The energy in Europe’s streets is bigger than many realize.  Young people have been protesting in at least nine European countries this autumn, most of them since mid-September. 


In France, a walkout over the lack of teachers at one high school in Créteil in September

spread to hundreds of schools

 within weeks. By mid-October, about 550,000 people (by the

government’s own count

) were marching in cities and towns across the country. In Spain and Portugal, the anger is about housing. Protesters set up camps in

Madrid’s Puerta del Sol

 and

Lisbon’s Rossio,

 and on Nov. 11, Spain’s tenants’ unions, backed by the big trade unions, held the country’s

first general strike in 14 years.

 It came after Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old widow in fragile health, was forcibly removed from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for most of her life. She

died in hospital

 two weeks later.


Demonstrators march for the right to housing  after the eviction of  an 87-year-old woman from the home where she had lived for around seventy years in Madrid, Spain. (Wikimedia Commons)


The grievances overlap without being the same. It’s about schools in France and Greece, university tuition in

Belgium

 and

Albania

, university budgets in

Austria

, military conscription in

Germany

, and rent in Portugal and Spain, where the average rent is now

98.7 percent

 of what a young person earns in a month. But running beneath most of them is a familiar story: governments that say there’s no money for schools, or for people who are struggling, always, somehow, manage to find it for something else, often weapons.


In France, Germany and

Italy

, protesters have made that link. France’s

2027 budget

 adds $7 billion for defense and just $1.2 billion for schools, while

cutting 1,588 teaching posts

. In Germany, young people marched in more than 30 cities on Oct. 31, angry, as

Al Jazeera reported

, that military spending is rising while education funding is cut. 


The protests have achieved some modest wins. On Oct. 26, France’s government promised to

replace Parcoursup

, the hated university admissions system, cap first-year high school classes at 28, and add 500 teaching posts. And in Serbia, a student movement that began after a railway station canopy

collapsed in Novi Sad two years ago

 turned itself into an electoral list and, on Oct. 25,

beat Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s strongman of 14 years

. 


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Facts like these are why, in my organizing circles, there’s a lot of talk of a “European wave.” I think we should be careful with that phrase, though, because it suggests a level of coordination and a plan that doesn’t — yet — exist. The reporting I …

author: Ariadna Wdowiak
title: El Servicio Penitenciario Federal es responsable directo de las condiciones inhumanas
content:
11 de febrero de 2026: El hombre que ríe acaba de arrastrar más de cincuenta metros a un fotoperiodista enceguecido por el gas pimienta en spray a quemarropas que le echó Gendarmería desde el otro lado de las vallas sobre la cara


Milton Tolomeo y Eneas Gallo no son protagonistas de una zaga de aventuras ni de una serie policial. No son héroes mitológicos. Son dos trabajadores precarizados que militaron y participaron de la cosa pública siempre que pudieron y lo sintieron de esa manera. Pero hoy siguen en prisión preventiva en el penal federal de Marcos Paz por su participación en las protestas del 11 de febrero contra la reforma laboral, frente al Congreso. Tolomeo fue detenido el 15 de febrero. Y Gallo, el 18 de marzo. El Ministerio de Seguridad denunció de terrorismo a los responsables de los incidentes, y el fiscal Carlos Stornelli pidió aplicar el artículo 41 quinquies, que duplica las penas, pero el juez Gonzalo Rúa rechazó ese agravante al dictar la preventiva. Hoy, ambos esperan un juicio oral sin fecha. Desde el 8 de noviembre, Tolomeo hace huelga de hambre en reclamo de su libertad, de agua potable y alimentos, y de mejoras en las condiciones de detención. CORREPI y la Gremial de Abogadas y Abogados piden el cierre de la causa, mientras el Gobierno sostiene que hubo una acción organizada para desestabilizar el orden institucional.


Texto y fotos Andrés Manrique (

ANRed).


 


23 de septiembre de 2026: un Carlston.


El miércoles 11 de febrero, mientras el Senado aprobaba la reforma laboral, una multitud se movilizó frente al Congreso en una marcha convocada por la CGT y distintos sectores sociales y políticos.

El operativo de seguridad, según el Gobierno, terminó con 71 detenidos

. 51 detenciones estuvieron a cargo de fuerzas federales, y 20 las ejecutó la Policía de la Ciudad. La fiscalía fue liberando a la mayoría de los y las detenidas los días siguientes. Entre otros, se detuvieron a personas en situación de calle, a kilómetros de los hechos, sin la más mínima prueba y a más  de un mes de la movilización. Pero quedaron algunos casos por definir. Milton Tolomeo y Eneas Gallo, no fueron apresados ese día, ni cerca del Congreso.


11 de febrero de 2026: reforma laboral


El 11 de febrero, mientras Senadores aprobaba una flexibilización nueva para el trabajo y una forma más radicalizada de precarizarlo, afuera del Congreso

 las fuerzas represivas estuvieron durante más de tres horas

 disparándole a manifestantes, a familias, a vecinos y a fotorreporteros con postas de goma, escopetas Byrna a gas comprimido, dos hidrantes, gas pimienta y granadas de gas lacrimógeno. En ese escenario bélico sostenido por

decisión unilateral del ejecutivo

, unos manifestantes arrojaron unas molotovs del otro lado de las vallas.


Los derechos no se consiguieron pidiendo por favor


La causa


Milton Tolomeo


Milton fue detenido el 15 de febrero en su trabajo

, donde era operario de maestranza. Además, es masajista deportivo, oficio que ejercía por las tardes. Dicho en sus propias palabras, es una «persona que no soporta las injusticias y que siempre creyó que es posible cambiarlas, que siempre hay que involucrarse cuando éstas suceden y no resignarse ni mirar para otro lado», lo que lo llevó a movilizarse contra la reforma laboral el 11 de febrero de 2026.


Entre el 12 y el 13 de febrero, Alejandra Monteoliva -Ministra de Seguridad-, anunció que su cartera denunciaría por terrorismo a los responsables de los incidentes. Dijo que habían realizado una acción organizada para desestabilizar el orden institucional. En esa campaña, el Ministerio difundió un video con cuatro sospechosos y una lista de 17 implicados: Milton Tolomeo no figuraba en el video nu en la lista.

A Monteoliva se la denunció penalmente junto a jefes del operativo por incumplimiento de deberes

. Tolomeo fue detenido a mediados de febrero y el Gobierno lo estigmatizó, difundiendo su cara, con el rótulo de “anarquista de la Molotov”. El domingo 15 de febrero, la ministra salió a celebrar por redes: “Dijimos que lo íbamos a encontrar y lo encontramos” No tenía pruebas suficientes.


9 de septiembre de 2026


La Coordinadora Contra la Represión Policial e Institucional (CORREPI), quienes asumieron su defensa, explican que se lo acusa por los delitos de resistencia a la autoridad, intimidación pública y tenencia de material incendiario. content:
Fotoğraf: DHA / Kolaj: Evrensel

İstanbul Gaziosmanpaşa'ya bağlı Barbaros Hayrettinpaşa Mahallesi’nde 19 Kasım Perşembe günü saat 23.15 sıralarında 5 katlı binanın 1’inci katındaki dairede yangın çıktı. Kısa sürede binayı saran duman nedeniyle en üst kattaki dairede bulunan Ömer Ege Özyurt (12), D.Ö. (6) ve E.Ö. (13) ile birlikte toplam 6 kişi dumandan etkilendi.

Dumandan etkilenerek hastaneye kaldırılan 12 yaşındaki Ömer Ege Özyurt, hayatını kaybetti. Özyurt’un futbola Kemerburgaz Spor Kulübü’nde başladığı ve bu sezon Yıldırım Bosna Spor Kulübü’nde forma giydiği öğrenildi.

title: Hatimoğulları: Treatment of sick prisoners amounts to torture
content:
The vigil demanding the release of seriously ill prisoners outside the Turkish Ministry of Justice in Ankara continues. On the fifth day, Tülay Hatimoğulları, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), described the state’s treatment of sick prisoners as torture. She stated that prisoners were being denied timely medical treatment and prevented from being released despite suffering from life-threatening illnesses. The government must put an end to this practice, she said, referring to the ongoing peace and democratization process.


Relatives of prisoners Ömer Güneri, Yakup Akman, Mehmet Ali Taşkın, and Selim Çiftçi were among those taking part in the vigil organized by the Federation of Legal and Solidarity Associations of Prisoners’ Families (TUHAD-FED). The Co-Chairs of MED TUHAD-FED, Pınar Sakık Tekin and Kerem Canpolat, as well as representatives of various civil society organizations, also attended the vigil. Carrying banners and chanting slogans, the demonstrators demanded the release of sick prisoners, including Newroz Bozkurt and Evin Zapsu.


Criticism of forensic medical reports


Hatimoğulları accused the Turkish Forensic Medicine Institute of refusing to issue the medical reports needed by seriously ill prisoners, thereby preventing their release. “Everyone in Turkey now knows that the institute is incapable of issuing the necessary reports for sick prisoners. It remains an institution that fails to uphold the obligations of the Hippocratic Oath.”


The DEM Party politician addressed the medical professionals responsible directly: “You are doctors! Your duty is to keep people alive.” Even when prisoners obtained a medical report stating that they could no longer remain in detention, prison administrations often failed to act on it. This is another injustice that we cannot accept,” she said.


As an example of the consequences of delayed medical care, Hatimoğulları recalled political prisoner Tuncer Sağlam, who died recently after a long denial of treatment. “If families are holding a vigil outside the Ministry of Justice today, it is because they want to prevent another coffin from being carried out of prison. Correctional facilities have become places where prisoners are left to perish. From here, the families are calling out: Do not let prisons become morgues.”


https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/fc17a848_20261121134205_2026-11-21-ankara-tulay-hatimogullari-dem-parti-es-genel-baskani-adalet-bakanligi-eylem-1.mp4


“Can you take responsibility for this?”


Hatimoğulları gave a particularly harrowing account of the situation of Evin Zapsu, who has been imprisoned for nine years. Zapsu, who is being held in Kayseri Women’s Prison, was diagnosed with stage-four cancer, yet the necessary treatment has not been initiated, she said. “Everyone has heard her daughter’s desperate cry. Evin Zapsu has been in prison for nearly ten years. Her daughters chose to study at Istanbul University so they could visit their mother. The burden falls not only on prisoners but also on their families. Transfers to prisons far from home make family visits even more difficult. Many families are already living in severe poverty.” Addressing the Turkish Minister of Justice, Hatimoğulları asked: “What conscience, what religion, what faith can justify knowingly leaving sick prisoners to die? Can you take responsibility for this?”


Delayed medical treatment of Newroz Bozkurt


Hatimoğulları also addressed the situation of seriously ill prisoner Newroz Bozkurt. During a visit to Sincan Women’s Prison, the women incarcerated there had given her detailed accounts of prison conditions and mistreatment. “We have repeatedly spoken with the Ministry of Justice to ensure that Newroz Bozkurt receives medical treatment. Our lawyers have worked day and night on this. Nevertheless, she has not received adequate treatment. It has been postponed again and again, repeatedly. The families’ desperation has now reached an unbearable level. When mothers say they will set themselves on fire if necessary unless their children are released, it shows just how hopeless they feel their situation has become. Our mothers are holding this vigil in tears. Enough is enough.”


“How do they intend to make peace under these conditions?”


Hatimoğulları directly linked the situation in prisons to the Peace and Democratic Society Process. She stated that the DEM Party was repeatedly confronted with the same question at public gatherings …

title: İHD, tutuklanan ÇHD'li avukatlar için serbest bırakma çağrısı yaptı
content:
İnsan Hakları Derneği (İHD), İzmir merkezli yürütülen bir soruşturma kapsamında 17 Kasım 2026 tarihinde ev baskınlarıyla gözaltına alınan ve 19 Kasım’da tutuklanan Çağdaş Hukukçular Derneği (ÇHD) üyesi dört avukata ilişkin yazılı bir açıklama yayımladı.


İzmir'de gözaltına alınan 4 avukat tutuklandı


20 Kasım 2026


Açıklamada, dört avukatın derhal serbest bırakılması ve savunmaya yönelik baskıların sona erdirilmesi istendi.


SAVUNMA MAKAMINA YÖNELİK BASKILARA SON VERİLSİN, TUTUKLU AVUKATLAR DERHAL SERBEST BIRAKILSIN! İzmir merkezli soruşturma kapsamında 17 Kasım 2026 tarihinde ev baskınlarıyla gözaltına alınan Çağdaş Hukukçular Derneği üyesi Av. Veysi Çetin, Av. Yemen Cankan, Av. Erdoğan Akdoğdu ve Av. Bahattin Özdemir, 19 Kasım’da tutuklanmıştır. Aralarında derneğimiz üyelerinin de bulunduğu avukatların 24 saati aşkın süre müdafileriyle görüştürülmemesi ve mesleki faaliyetlerinde kullandıkları dijital materyallere el konulması, savunma hakkı ve avukatlık mesleğinin bağımsızlığı açısından ağır hukuki ihlal oluşturmaktadır. Ceza hukukunun temel ilkesi, kişilerin kimlikleri, düşünceleri veya mesleki faaliyetleri üzerinden değil, somut fiilleri ve hukuka uygun deliller temelinde yargılanmasıdır. Günther Jakobs’un kavramsallaştırdığı düşman ceza hukuku anlayışı, bireyin işlediği fiilden ziyade devlet tarafından tehlikeli olarak tanımlanmasını esas alarak hukuki güvencelerin daraltılmasını ifade eder. Avukatların mesleki faaliyetlerinin kriminalize edilmesi, bu anlayışın savunma makamına yönelmesi tehlikesini ortaya koymaktadır. Savunma faaliyetlerinin suçla ilişkilendirilmesi, ceza muhakemesini adaletin gerçekleştirilmesi amacından uzaklaştırarak bir baskı mekanizmasına dönüştürür. İnsan Hakları Derneği olarak, yargı makamlarını Anayasa’nın 19. maddesi ve tutuklamanın istisnailiği ilkesi doğrultusunda dört avukatın derhal serbest bırakılmasını sağlamaya çağırıyoruz. Savunma makamının bağımsızlığını hedef alan her türlü müdahalenin karşısında duracağımızı, Çağdaş Hukukçular Derneği ile tutuklanan avukatlarla ve savunma hakkını koruyan bütün hukukçularla dayanışma içinde olacağımızı kamuoyuna duyuruyoruz. Adalet, yalnızca bugün hakları ihlal edilenlerin değil, herkesin bir gün ihtiyaç duyacağı evrensel bir güvencedir. https://t.co/HDOfHtVibs


— İHD Genel Merkezi (@ihdgenelmerkez)

November 21, 2026


Çalışma materyallerine el konuldu


Açıklamada, avukatların mesleki çalışmalarında kullandıkları dijital materyallere de el konulduğu belirtildi. İHD, bu durumun avukatlık mesleğinin bağımsızlığını zedelediğini belirtti.


İHD, avukatların mesleki faaliyetlerinin suç konusu yapılmasının savunma makamını hedef alan bir baskı anlayışını gösterdiğini söyledi.


Serbest bırakma çağrısı


İHD, tutuklanan avukatlar Veysi Çetin, Yemen Cankan, Erdoğan Akdoğdu ve Bahattin Özdemir'in derhal serbest bırakılmasını istedi. Dernek, bu talebini Anayasa'nın 19. maddesindeki kişi özgürlüğü güvencesine ve tutuklamanın istisnai bir tedbir olduğu ilkesine dayandırdı. Ayrıca Çağdaş Hukukçular Derneği (ÇHD) ve tutuklu avukatlarla dayanışma içinde olacaklarını açıkladı.


Ne olmuştu?


17 Kasım'da İzmir merkezli soruşturma kapsamında ev baskınlarıyla gözaltına alınan avukatlar, 19 Kasım'da tutuklandı. Dört avukat da ÇHD üyesi. İHD, açıklamasında avukatların serbest bırakılmasını istedi.


(FY)

content:
Oggi dalle piazze italiane è passato un messaggio chiaro: lo sciopero è del popolo. L’accordo “sindacati-imprese” sigilla un tradimento non nuovo di chi dovrebbe rappresentare gli interessi dei lavoratori e lavoratrici – perlomeno quelli che hanno un contratto, un salario, delle condizioni minimamente garantite – e invece tutela quelli del padrone. E oggi le piazze in Italia hanno sottolineato questa realtà delle cose con la serenità di chi sa che non ha più niente da perdere ma tutto da prendere. 


foto di Marioluca Barona


L’inimicizia, per usare un eufemismo, nei confronti di un sindacato come la Cgil non ha però dissuaso dal fare sciopero, anzi. Ha fatto sì che il popolo scendesse in piazza, sfruttando l’ultima delle garanzie che sopravvivono a stento in questo Paese, ossia sottrarsi dall’espropriazione del proprio lavoro, per continuare a manifestare con forza la propria contrarietà al riarmo e, quindi, al carovita. Le piazze di oggi non sono state della Cgil, sono state del popolo che dice basta. 


Oltre la metà degli italiani è contrario, secondo un

sondaggio

, all’invio di armi all’Ucraina e al sostegno della guerra. Questo è quanto emerge dai sondaggi ma ad avere occhi per guardare è ciò che viene di fatto richiesto dalle mobilitazioni di questi mesi. In fondo ciò che sta accadendo in Francia, in Italia, in Albania, in Serbia, è la riappropriazione dell’ultimo baluardo di ciò che ci rimane, ossia la possibilità di aggregarsi intorno a un’idea-forza quale il proprio territorio “nazionale” – e le bandiere italiane, la marsigliese cantata dagli studenti di periferia, la bandiera albanese ne sono il simbolo – come elemento di potere per difendere i propri interessi collettivi, di popolo. Un’identificazione che non è da leggersi nei termini “reazionari” del becero sovranismo che i Vannacci di casa nostra vorrebbero rappresentare pur facendosi finanziare dagli Stati Uniti, ma nei termini di una sorta di nuovo patriottismo, o meglio, di nuovo sentimento collettivo che respira aria internazionalista. Questo è possibile oggi grazie alla Palestina, come orizzonte dal quale apprendere il significato di emancipazione. Diventa quindi evidente, anche in queste piazze, ulteriore passaggio di mobilitazione che si iscrive in un ciclo mobilitazione diffusa, che l’unica via per difendere un interesse comune non passa dall’alimentare una guerra come quella Ucraina, tritacarne per giovani ucraini e russi, in funzione degli interessi degli Stati Uniti. Non c’è da difendersi dalla fantomatica guerra della Russia, ma c’è da difendersi da una cricca di mentecatti pronti a tutto solo per salvaguardare la poltrona. C’è da difendersi da una élite europea pronta a tutto pur di far mangiare le proprie lobby di armi e di speculazione e garantirsi il proprio pezzo della torta. Questi sono stati i messaggi di questa giornata di sciopero. 


Lo si vede a partire dal fatto che in tutte le città si sono sviluppati cortei che, o hanno preso le distanze dal principio dalla chiamata della Cgil, o hanno pensato di occupare quello spazio perché era naturale essere in piazza con i temi all’ordine del giorno per il Paese. Così è stato a Torino, dove lo spezzone sociale ha raccolto 20 mila persone che, dopo una prima parte di corteo, hanno deciso di deviare raggiungendo l’ingresso dell’autostrada per poi riconvocarsi la sera stessa per un corteo giovane e vivace che ha tentato di attraversare il centro a più riprese senza arrestarsi a fronte di cariche, lacrimogeni e idranti. Così a Roma, dove 50 mila persone sono scese in piazza e gli studenti universitari hanno sanzionato il Ministero dell’Istruzione e del Merito. Così a Modena, dove un determinato spezzone di giovani (ma non solo) è riuscito a deviare dal corteo sindacale e per poi prendere il palco della Cgil, arrivando prima della testa. Così a Cosenza, dove lo spezzone studentesco e sociale non ha concluso il corteo con la Cgil ma ha proseguito fino all’ufficio scolastico regionale. Così a Bologna, dove un corteo partecipato da decine di migliaia di persone ha raggiunto la sede di Confindustria, difesa dalla polizia che ha risposto al tentativo di avvicinarsi con cariche. Così a Padova, dove il corteo studentesco ha occupato la tangenziale, ma anche a Venezia, Trento e Vicenza dove migliaia di persone sono scese in piazza per contestare le scelte vigliacche del sindacato e contestare i responsabili del carovita. title: Helau! Kontoerhalt der Roten Hilfe bei der Sparkasse Göttingen!
content:
Helau! Kontoerhalt der Roten Hilfe bei der Sparkasse Göttingen!


Elf Monate hat es gedauert bis nun im Hauptsacheverfahren das Konto der Roten Hilfe bei der Sparkasse Göttingen erhalten werden konnte. Heute am 11.11.26 ist die Entscheidung des Landgerichts Göttingen nun rechtskräftig. Wir hatten gegen die Kündigung durch die Sparkasse Göttingen Klage eingelegt und konnte diese in zwei Instanzen im Eilverfahren vor Gericht gewinnen. Dabei konnte das

OLG

 Braunschweig keine Begründung für eine Kontokündigung feststellt.

Die Göttinger Sparkasse ließ es dennoch auf ein

Hauptsacheverfahren ankommen und kassierte vor Gericht eine Niederlage

. In dem Urteil wird festgestellt, dass der erhöhte Aufwand zur Prüfung aufgrund einer Beobachtung der Roten Hilfe durch den Verfassungsschutz sowie die mutmaßliche Unterstützung einer von der

US

-Regierung auf eine Terrorliste gesetzten und konstruierten »Antifa Ost« nicht ausreicht, um das Konto zu kündigen.

Der

Hinweisbeschluss des

OLG

 Braunschweig vom 15.07.2026 findet sich

u. a.

 auf der Seite der Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte

Für uns bedeutet das:

Die Konten der Roten Hilfe sind gesichert und eine existenzgefährdende Bedrohung für den Verein wurde abgewendet.

Doch Druck gibt es weiterhin, auf Linke und linke Bewegungen und damit auch auf die Rote Hilfe. Dagegen braucht es solidarische Gegenwehr.

Wir stehen weiter solidarisch an eurer Seite und leisten Antirepressionsarbeit.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Freed Southern Tagalog activists to file counter charges vs police
content:
Photo by Kyle Justin Macabalitao/Bulatlat

This is the spirit of the released delegates of the Lakabayan Southern Tagalog who were violently arrested and detained by the police last November 15 in barangay Sucat, Muntinlupa City. In a press conference on November 19, they announced that they will file counter charges against the officers of the Southern Police District (SPD).

National Union of People’s Lawyers (NUPL) President Ephraim Cortez said the arrest of more than 200 activists and 18 journalists can be considered illegal. Cortez maintained that the police violated the provisions of the Batasang Pambansa Blg. 880 for obstructing or disrupting a peaceful assembly, Article 124 of the Revised Penal Code for arbitrary detention, and Republic Act No. 7438 for the right to counsel.

“The police have already violated their own guidelines and the rights of their arrestees on how they should have been treated during the arrest, not to mention the injuries that they sustained,” said Cortez.

Niezelle Visaya, spokesperson of the Lakbayan Timog Katagalugan, recalled how hundreds of police personnel from the SPD intimidated and harassed the delegates of Lakbayan, from morning until 2 p.m. of November 15 while they were holding a program at Sucat People’s Park.

Visaya said that at around 2:00 a.m. of November 15, hundreds of police from the SPD went to the Sucat People’s Park, intimidating the delegates who were there to rest. The police also started to block the entry and exit points of the delegates.

“They began violently arresting the organizers. Some of us were brought up to the Barangay Police Headquarters, where we were placed in small rooms that don’t have proper ventilation. They continued to bring mothers, Indigenous People, and even children into these rooms,” Viasaya said.

Community journalist Marky Casquite from the Southern Tagalog Exposure also recalled how he was arrested by the police despite his assertion that he is a member of the media.

“I was suddenly picked up and arrested by the police despite showing my media ID,” Casquite said.

“They handcuffed me. They were not even content with that, they also dragged me to the barangay hall leaving me with injuries to my arm from the tightly fastened handcuffs and to my knee from being dragged,” Casquite said, adding that he did not receive first aid even though he was already bleeding.

Lucky Oraller of the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan – Timog Katagalugan (BAYAN-TK) demanded that charges against them and others who were arrested should be junked.

“While Marcos welcomed Trump through the red carpet, his forces dragged, caught, and arrested the ordinary Filipino just to welcome Trump for the ASEAN Summit,” said Oraller.

Oraller also decried how their cellphones and other protest paraphernalia were confiscated, including the vehicle and effigy.

While it was confirmed that the phones were returned to the delegates, the placards, streamer, effigy, and the vehicle along with the bags inside have not been returned, Oraller said.

“We’re not sure what the police could do to our vehicles and bags that are still in Camp Bagong Diwa. [W]e call to the people to monitor the case, as there are threats that they would plant evidence to frame us up,” said Oraller.

title: Agent Who Recorded Activist’s Arrest That Turned Into Racist White House Meme Identified
content:
St. Paul, MN — Homeland Security Investigations Special Agents Charles Engle and John Zappone sat parked outside the Aloft Hotel in downtown Minneapolis on Jan. 22. Their boss, Tonya Price — promoted to assistant special agent in charge six months earlier — instructed them to record the arrest of civil rights attorney and activist Nekima Levy Armstrong.


The testimony emerged during a recent federal court hearing detailing how Homeland Security Investigations, or HSI, carried out arrests against the federally charged Cities Church protesters, known as the

Righteous 39

. Not long after ICE agents fatally shot

Renee Good

 and

Alex Pretti

, activists learned that St. Paul ICE Field Director David Easterwood also served as a pastor at Cities Church in St. Paul.


Following a peaceful protest that interrupted a church service on Jan. 18, President Donald Trump suggested on Truth Social that the demonstrators and a journalists “should be thrown in jail, or thrown out of the Country.” Attorney General Pam Bondi announced an active investigation after speaking with lead pastor Jonathan Parnell.


Trump Admin Targets Press and Activists in Minnesota, Indicts ‘The Righteous 39’


On the hotel’s third floor, FBI agents tackled Satara Strong-Allen, a Black woman who stepped out of Levy Armstrong’s room to walk next door.


Levy Armstrong had a hunch that she would be targeted. “My suspicions at the time were correct because they thought she was me, even though I am several inches taller than my friend,” she said. “We saw a man run out of the hotel room across the hall from mine and start chasing her. These goons were willing to tackle and attack me in the hallway, not saying freeze, not saying you’re under arrest, but acting like they were on a football field with regard to the brutality that they exhibited towards another Black woman, again, thinking that it was me. That’s absurd and it’s unconscionable.”


Levy Armstrong fired off text messages to an organizer at 2 a.m. saying she wanted to turn herself in. Diagnosed with a brain tumor in 2022, she did not want to risk getting tackled in the hallway. Her attorney Jordan Kushner said he

called

 U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen to arrange a peaceful surrender.


Nekima Levy Armstrong speaks outside the federal courthouse in St. Paul on Feb. 27, 2026.


Chauntyll Allen speaks with her wife Satara Strong-Allen on the left of the image in the gray jacket.


“So I gave him my proposal, which is, we can take her down to the federal courthouse in Minneapolis,” Kushner said. “She can go the Marshals office and turn herself in there, and we don’t have to have any incident, no circus, no nothing. He agreed.”


Charles Engle, one of the HSI agents tasked with filming Levy Armstrong’s arrest, recently testified that his supervisor told him that she “couldn’t turn herself in.”


“Ms. Price notified me that she had heard that [Nekima] was going to try to turn herself in,” Engle said. “I was not told that she couldn’t turn herself in at the courthouse. We had heard that she was going to try to turn herself in at the courthouse.”


Also recently testifying was Special Agent

Zachary Kliniske

, who tasked with arresting St. Paul School Board Member Chauntyll Allen. He was questioned by Allen’s attorney Jill Brisbois.


“There was talk that they were going to self-surrender, but I never got any specifics on that,” Kliniske said. “I don’t know about why the arrest was supposed to be made. It’s just, I was the supervisor put in charge of arresting this person because they have an active arrest warrant.”


Kushner said Rosen later backed out of the courthouse plan.


“So [Rosen] calls me back and says, ‘Oh, no, we can’t do it that way. We have to arrest her at the hotel’ … because they wanted the photo op. It had nothing to do with justice, nothing to do with public safety,” Kushner said.


Rosen declined to say whether an agreement existed.


“The answer is any deal for her peaceful surrender was that she walk out of the hotel room she was hiding in and she says ‘I surrender to the federal law enforcement officers that were in the hallway’ and that’s exactly what occurred,” Rosen said.


Engle and Kliniske testified they were not issued body cameras, so Zappone recorded Levy Armstrong’s arrest on his cellphone.


“Why are you recording this?” Levy Armstrong said. “I don’t want to be a trophy for MAGA.”

A Brief History of Anarchism in Indonesia

Punk and the Re-birth of Anarchism in Indonesia

Repression of Punk and Anarchism

Resistance to Neoliberalism (and Neoliberal Policing)

Anarchism in contemporary Indonesia shares numerous connections with punk counter-culture. Repression against punks and anarchists has long been a problem for the movement there, but the motivations behind that repression have changed in recent years, as has the response of punk and anarchist communities to this repressive context.

This article will provide a quick overview of the historical trajectory of anarchism in Indonesia over the last century, before focusing on the re-emergence of anarchism alongside punk in the very late 1980s and 1990s. Some of the forms of repression faced by punks and anarchists will be detailed, especially the religious dimension of that repression, before charting a partial shift in the authorities’ understanding of anarchism and how that has altered the form and scope of repression.

To set some historical context then, it is well-known that Marxism was the dominant ideology of the revolutionary Left in Indonesia throughout the first half of the twentieth century and into the 1960s, especially as manifested in the mass-movement Partai Komunis Indonesia (PKI, Communist Party of Indonesia)—this was at one point the largest Communist Party in the world that hadn’t yet seized power, with several million members. However, anarchism was also a significant political strand, not least within the wider movement opposing the Dutch colonial government. Anarchism even had some influence within the explicitly Marxist PKI. In 1926, the Party’s newspaper, Api, featured quotes from the anarchist political philosopher Bakunin on its front page, and this was such a strong influence that a leading PKI figure named Darsono insisted that members should remember that ‘the Communism of Marx and not the anarchism of Bakunin must govern the party’ (Benda & McVey 1960). According to Bima Satria Putra’s (2018) book about anarcho-syndicalism in Indonesia in the early twentieth century, anarchist ideas have coloured Marxist and social-democratic organisations throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and, in fact, differences in political ideology within the Indonesian Left were not a significant problem, because they had a common enemy in the ‘invaders’ of the Dutch East Indies.

It appears that this anarchist current in the PKI was successfully suppressed by the orthodox Marxists, and, indeed, anarchist-minded activists would have been able to organise independently within specifically anarchist organisations and unions. Despite the increased dominance of the PKI and Marxism over the Left towards the mid twentieth century, anarchism persisted to at least some extent within the political lexicon of Indonesia into the 1960s. It is notable that the prominent …

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Russian Indigenous Activist Daria Egereva Remains Jailed; Arrested After 2025 U.N. Climate Talks
content:
Human rights and climate groups are calling on Russia to release two prominent activists, Daria Egereva and Natalia Leongardt, who have been held in pretrial detention in Moscow for nearly a year, since December 2025. Egereva, a leading Indigenous rights activist in Russia, was arrested shortly after attending the COP30 United Nations climate summit in Belém, Brazil, where she served as co-chair of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change. Leongardt has worked for decades to support Indigenous rights.


“Right now all we are demanding is the release of Daria and Natalia, because they shouldn’t be in prison. You shouldn’t be arrested for activism,” says Viktor Suliandziga-Bagat, an Indigenous rights activist and representative of the Udege people from the Russian Far East. He is living in exile due to the risk against activists. “I don’t think I can come back to Russia,” he says.

author: Matthew Guariglia
title: EFF to Congress: Mass Surveillance Is Too Important to Shove into Must-Pass Bill
content:
In June 2026, the surveillance authority

Section 702

 of FISA

expired

 absent a consensus among lawmakers over the

terms of its reauthorization

. Now, with the program set to truly turn off within the next few months, surveillance hawks and national security maximalists are rushing to renew this secretive power

by shoving it into a must-pass bill, like a continuing resolution to fund the government or the National Defense Authorization Act

 (NDAA) or an end of year, rushed, funding bill to prevent a shutdown. This would be both undemocratic and suppress any real chance at reform. In an effort to prevent that, EFF has singed into a

letter

 with over 25 civil liberties organizations, including the ACLU, Color of Change, and the Brennan Center, to urge Congress not to allow such a significant and dangerous program to be tacked onto a must-pass bill.

 


The letter says: “The NDAA is among the most important bills Congress considers each year. It should not be used as a vehicle to circumvent or to cut short this long-running bipartisan debate over Americans’ civil liberties and constitutional rights, nor to force lawmakers to choose between supporting our national defense and ending warrantless spying on Americans. Adding language in the NDAA conference to reauthorize Section 702 that has not been fully debated and voted on would be a serious procedural and substantive failure, and a betrayal of the democratic process.”

 


You can read the entire letter

here

. 

 


Section 702 grants the government authority to compel a telecommunications company to hand over data to the National Security Agency (NSA) in an attempt to protect national security by monitoring communications overseas—but this is only a piece of what the law does. Because we live in a globalized world, communications between people in other countries and in the United States often gets hoovered up. Once it does, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and several other agencies give themselves permission to search through U.S. persons’ data without a warrant. This is unconstitutional, undermines our right to private communications, and creates a dangerous and potent tool for would-be despots who might use that communication to discriminate, marginalize, or punish people based on their identities and political beliefs. 

 


This is

not

 the kind of policy Congress should be considering without necessary reforms, open debate, and the ability for lawmakers to vote against without forcing them to vote “no” on all defense policy.

 


We once again urge Congress not to put Section 702’s future in a must-pass bill like the NDAA.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Israel Uploaded 3.5M Photos of Palestinians to Amazon Facial Recognition Tech
content:
For years, Israel has used facial recognition technology to enforce its occupation and restrict Palestinian movement.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A new report reveals that Israel uploaded 3.5 million photos of Palestinians to Amazon’s facial recognition platform shortly after it launched its genocide in Gaza — shining yet more light on the tech industry’s complicity in repression and human rights abuses around the world.

The report, written by Harry Davies and Yuval Abraham and published in The Guardian this week, documents how the Israeli military uploaded the images to Amazon’s cloud soon after the start of Israel’s invasion and bombardment of Gaza in 2023. The military told Amazon that they uploaded the images specifically for the purpose of using Amazon’s Rekognition platform for facial recognition, according to documents leaked to the Guardian.

For years, the Israeli military has used facial recognition technology to enforce its occupation and enact harsh restrictions on Palestinians’ freedom of movement. Soldiers use a smartphone app called Blue Wolf, for example, to scan and catalog the faces of Palestinians passing through Israeli checkpoints in the occupied West Bank.

In Gaza, Israel has increased its use of facial recognition technology since the start of its 2023 assault. In early 2024, The New York Times called Israel’s facial recognition program in Gaza an “experimental effort” — acknowledging that the mass surveillance at times “wrongly flagged civilians as wanted Hamas militants.”

Davies and Abraham’s latest report builds on Abraham’s prior reporting for The Guardian and +972 Magazine, as well as the findings discussed in NAZA, a 2026 documentary co-directed by Abraham. The film highlights how Israel has used AI-based surveillance systems to facilitate Israel’s remote killings of thousands of civilians in Gaza since 2023.

The report also demonstrates how Israel has deepened its relationship with Amazon over the course of its genocide in Gaza. As noted by Who Profits, Israel awarded Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS) a large-scale tender in 2021, known as Project Nimbus, allowing Israel to transfer large quantities of data onto its services. Israel’s use of AWS has only expanded since then.

Last December, Mohammed Mhawish, a Palestinian journalist from Gaza, wrote about how Israel has intensified its use of surveillance since the start of the genocide.

The Israeli military has used “artificial intelligence to generate kill lists, monitoring our social-media accounts, and storing in bulk the audio of our phone calls,” he wrote.

Israel used these technologies to target journalists specifically — both within their own homes and while they were reporting, Mhawish said. Microsoft, Google, and Amazon, as well as other companies like Palantir Technologies, provide the infrastructure for the Israeli military to store Palestinians’ phone calls, analyze their communication, and decide who to target with a drone strike and when.

Last year, an investigative report by Abraham revealed the extensive use of Microsoft’s Azure platform by the Israeli military in order to surveil Palestinians’ phone calls before identifying targets for aerial bombardment. The revelations prompted tech workers to organize to force Microsoft to end Azure cloud storage and AI services in a partial withdrawal of contracts with Israel, though activists say that the company still retains contracts with the country.

Activists, including tech workers in No Tech for Apartheid, continue to organize against Google and Amazon’s Project Nimbus, and campaigns have grown internationally against Palantir.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

Our fundraiser ended last night, but there’s still time for us to meet those basic operating expenses — we need only $10,000. If you can support Truthout …

author: EDRi
title: EDRi-gram, 19 November 2026
content:
What has the EDRi network been up to over the past few weeks? Find out the latest digital rights news in our regular newsletter. In this edition: Making sense of the Digital Fairness Act, a very unmerry birthday to the Digital Omnibus, and more!

Last week, the European Commission put digital fairness on the menu with a proposal for its long-awaited Digital Fairness Act (DFA) – and we have some food for thought.

This law will strengthen consumer protection against manipulative and exploitative commercial practices, such as fake notifications designed to keep bringing us back to an app, endless scrolling that keeps us online way longer than you intended, and other personalised techniques used by online services that exploit our vulnerabilities. First things first, proposal actually takes some important steps forward by introducing new prohibitions on deceptive design, extending specific protections beyond the biggest online platforms, and recognising the harms associated with addictive digital features. However, we were left wondering – why promise digital fairness yet leave the users to do all the work instead of holding manipulative online services responsible? Read our analysis on Tech Policy Press.

Despite it all, the DFA proposal – something that actually might protect our rights online – is a welcome respite in the current wave of deregulation in the EU. This week, we’re also reckoning with the fact that November 19, 2026 marks one year since the Commission published the proposals for the Digital Omnibus. We, along with many other civil society organisations, had warned that this would be a massive reopening of EU’s core digital protections that would risk dismantling the very foundation of human rights and tech policy in the EU. One year on, it seems like we were granted Apollo’s gift of prophecy. On this unfortunate occasion, we’re standing strong with 100 organisations, experts, academics and more to urge EU lawmakers to not simplify away our rights.

In this edition, you can also explore our extremely thorough guide to the European Parliament’s 1840 amendments to the Digital Omnibus on Data, focusing on what they would mean for privacy, data protection and, ultimately, people’s rights. Yes, 1840, you read that right. Hungry for more? Also read our thoughts on the EU governments’ position on the Digital Omnibus.

1,840 amendments, one basic question: will the Data Omnibus simplify EU digital rules or weaken people’s rights? author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: The death of the word?
content:
Michelangelo,

Cumaean Sibyl

 (c. 1511), Sistine Chapel, Vatican City


This short article was originally published under the title “Morte della parola?” in the Italian newspaper

Paese Sera

 on 8 February 1968. It has been republished in the latest issue of the French magazine

Entétement

, although the original version can be found on the

La Voce di Fiore

 archive website. A Spanish translation of the same can be found at th magazine

Ficción de la razón

.


A book has recently been published in Paris,

Of Grammatology

 (1967), a work destined to cause a stir not only in the field of linguistic studies. Jacques Derrida, one of the most original figures in the new wave of French philosophical criticism, begins with the observation that, today, “through a movement whose necessity we can barely glimpse, everything that, for at least twenty centuries, has tended to be defined under the name of language, is beginning to be summarised under the name of writing”. It does indeed seem that writing—which, according to Rousseau, was nothing more than a complement to speech—is gradually freeing itself from its subordination to the phonetic medium, to the point of reversing its traditional relationship with language: writing would therefore not be a technique in the service of language, but rather, on the contrary, it is language that can be considered a specific case, an aspect, of writing.


To better understand the phenomenon to which Derrida refers when he speaks of writing dissociated from the phonetic element, one need only consider the example of mathematics, whose symbolic notation does not refer to any spoken language. If we consider that today we are witnessing a process of mathematisation across all the sciences, the “liberation” of writing described by Derrida becomes an extremely concrete phenomenon (readers who have followed recent news regarding the

in vitro

 synthesis of living matter, carried out by certain American scientists, will recall having heard talk of writing and “programmes” even in relation to the most elementary processes of the living cell). The “liberation” of writing described by Derrida becomes an extremely concrete phenomenon.


On the basis of these premises, Derrida deduces the need for a pure science of writing, which considers writing prior to speech and independently of it: this science is, precisely, “grammatology”; and, to define its aims, it suffices to substitute this term for “semiology”, the term Saussure uses to outline the programme of his famous

Course in General Linguistics

: “We shall call it grammatology… and, as it does not yet exist, we cannot say what it will be; but it has a right to exist, and its place is determined in advance”. The age of speech, which began under the creative power of the verb, is drawing to a close before our very eyes; the character of this new age might be summed up in the following formula: “In the beginning was the written word’’.


Whilst it is true that, from this perspective, linguistics must become a mere branch of grammatology, Derrida seems, however, to overlook the fact that a science already exists which considers language not as speech, but as code and writing; consequently, grammatology itself should necessarily be understood as a sub-branch or a section of that science. This is cybernetics, which, from its beginnings in Wiener’s theories, defined its world as a universe of writing and coding. The very idea of grammatology is already fully contained within the notion of “programme”, one of the key concepts of cybernetics. Etymologically, “programme” —pro-grammer— means “to put the letter (that is,

writing

) first”, whilst “prophecy” means, by contrast, “to put the word first”. Indeed, in the programme assigned to an electronic brain, everything that constitutes the living, phonetic element of language is erased to make way for a system of absolute writing that can be deciphered but not pronounced. It is fair to say that, up to now, our civilisation has known two types of language that have gradually diverged: the language of science is, essentially, written language —code, writing—, whilst the language of poetry and philosophical thought is spoken language —breath, word—. Nevertheless, these two domains—which, for convenience’s sake, we might call the “sphere of the programme” and the “sphere of prophecy”—are drawing ever closer together today thanks to cybernetics; through the mathematisation of human phenomena, cybernetics …

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Harassment won’t stop a son’s search for his missing father
content:
Marklen Lariosa, son of missing Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) labor organizer William Lariosa, speaks during a rally in Davao City on the first anniversary of his father’s disappearance on April 10, 2025. Photo by Kath Cortez/Davao Today

“Family members searching for their disappeared loved ones have to endure threats and harassment from state forces on top of the terrible uncertainty and emotional turmoil they are already going through.”

Is it a mistake for a son to demand justice and accountability?

Marklen, son of disappeared labor organizer William Lariosa, raised this question following the recent incident of harassment and surveillance he experienced. Members of his family were alarmed after two unidentified individuals were looking for his residence on the night of October 25.

He told Bulatlat that this was the first time such an event had happened since his father, a labor organizer under Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) Southern Mindanao, was abducted in Quezon, Bukidnon, on April 10, 2024.

Marklen could not think of other possible reasons, suspecting that the incident may have something to do with his continuing involvement in campaigns and mobilizations that demand the surfacing of Lariosa. “Is it a mistake for a son to search for his missing father?” he further asked.

Read: After 2 years, son laments continuing disappearance of Mindanao labor organizer

Neighbors of the Lariosa family in their hometown in Davao de Oro province were the ones who encountered the two individuals. They reportedly wore helmets and were on board a black motorcycle, introducing themselves as “collectors” when they were asked.

For Marklen, the response and presence of the two raised suspicions. Aside from the fact that they visited the community around 7 p.m., which is outside the regular working hours, Marklen said that he did not apply for any financial loan.

After the incident, he was concerned for the safety of his family, prompting them to lodge a blotter report with the barangay. However, he stood firm that it won’t stop him from continuing his cause.

Desaparecidos, an organization of families and friends of enforced disappearance victims, denounced the incident, urging the government to put an end to this kind of harassment.

“Family members searching for their disappeared loved ones have to endure threats and harassment from state forces on top of the terrible uncertainty and emotional turmoil they are already going through,” JL Burgos, Desaparecidos chairperson, said in a statement.

Rights groups Karapatan and the Center for Trade Union and Human Rights (CTUHR) also expressed strong condemnations about what happened.

Marklen, a member of the National Board of Desaparecidos, has raised a possibility that the two individuals who recently visited their neighborhood might be connected to those who visited their house several times prior to the disappearance of his father.

He said they were visited by individuals who allegedly introduced themselves as state agents once in 2022 and three times in 2023, accusing Lariosa of being involved in communist insurgency. There were warnings, he added, that they would get dragged into it if they would not cooperate.

The series of visits was reportedly the primary reason why Lariosa was forced to take refuge in Bukidnon. Marklen affirmed that his father, who remains missing, had been a labor organizer.

On July 8, the Supreme Court required certain commanders and elements of Philippine Army units to comment on the petition for review on certiorari filed by the family.

Read: Military ordered to reply to missing Mindanao labor organizer’s case

Since 2024, KMU Southern Mindanao has documented 57 cases of human rights violations against its members and organizers.

The labor group released a statement on October 24, presenting the faces of some individuals, including former high-ranking New People’s Army (NPA) member Roberto Rosete Jr., who allegedly harassed KMU’s leaders and members.

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Peasant organizer persists despite surveillance
content:
Jesus Monasterial. (Photo from Photo from Tanggol Magsasaka-TK)

Repeated surveillance restricted his movements and caused anxiety over his family’s safety.

When he was a university student, he questioned the purpose of agricultural education. Now he is organizing landless farmers and fisherfolk.

Jesus Monasterial has spent more than two years working with rural communities in Southern Tagalog. However, his work resulted in repeated surveillance by state forces, peasant groups said.

On October 31, Tanggol Magsasaka–Timog Katagalugan reported that a police intelligence operative identified as “Bruno” had been asking about Monasterial’s whereabouts in Lian, Batangas. The operative was reportedly previously assigned in Nasugbu.

At the time, Monasterial was assisting a protest camp in Barangay San Diego, where farmers, fisherfolk, and residents opposed the possible demolition of several houses.

“I was on my way back to the people’s protest camp in San Diego when news reached us that someone had been asking about my personal information,” he said.

The camp was established by Samahang Mangangawil 1979 and the San Diego Homeowners’ Association, with support from the Katipunan ng mga Samahang Magbubukid sa Timog Katagalugan (KASAMA-TK) and Pambansang Lakas ng Kilusang Mamamalakaya ng Pilipinas–Timog Katagalugan (PAMALAKAYA-TK).

The incident prompted fellow organizers to discuss security measures. They also plan to file a complaint before the Commission on Human Rights (CHR).

Monasterial’s involvement in peasant organizing began at the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) where he was enrolled in BS Agricultural Biotechnology.

Coming from a family of farmers in Bicol, where his grandparents worked as agricultural tenants, he became increasingly critical of an agricultural education system that he said served the interests of transnational corporations rather than addressing farmers’ lack of land and government support.

Through the League of Filipino Students–UPLB, he became involved in social issues action and joined community immersions with farmers in Tartaria, Silang, Cavite, as well as Mangyan communities in Mindoro and Dumagat communities in Rizal.

These experiences led him to leave his studies and become a full-time organizer. He now serves as deputy secretary-general of KASAMA-TK.

His work involves staying in communities, conducting consultations and political education, and helping establish local farmers and fisherfolk associations.

“Being a full-time organizer means devoting my entire time to the communities and being far from my loved ones,” he said, adding that he had to set aside his plan to finish college.

The October 31 incident was not the first reported surveillance involving Monasterial.

On July 19, 2026, soldiers from the 16th Infantry Battalion of the Philippine Army reportedly sought to identify the organizers of KASAMA-TK’s Regional Peasant Consultation in Barangay Malinis, Lemery, Batangas.

On September 21, a man introducing himself as “Del” Dela Cruz reportedly approached a member of Sugarfolks’ Unity for Genuine Agricultural Reform (SUGAR-Batangas), attempting to persuade the member to leave the organization and provide information about its activities.

According to Tanggol Magsasaka–Timog Katagalugan, the man showed footage of a protest outside the Department of Agriculture regional office led by the Alyansa ng Magsasaka para sa Kumpensasyon (AMK), SUGAR-Batangas, KAISAHAN, and KASAMA-TK. He allegedly warned the member against working with Monasterial, claiming that the organizer was “already drawing attention.”

The protest resulted in a dialogue with government representatives to demand agricultural inputs and implements for farmers and farmworkers affected by successive calamities.

The groups also cited previous incidents in Barangay Casile, Laguna; Lupang Ramos and Tartaria, Cavite; and Coron, Palawan.

Monasterial said that the repeated surveillance restricted his movements and caused anxiety over his family’s safety. “Repeated surveillance limits my movements as an organizer and makes me fear returning home to my family because they might also be targeted by the state due to my advocacy.”

Despite the threats, Monasterial said that his work remains rooted in the struggles of farmers and farmworkers.
