author: Kristopher Drummond
title: Therapy as Rite of Passage Pt. 2: Cultivating Secure Attachment to the Earth
content:
Photo courtesy of the author.


Therapy, in its crazy way, by emphasizing the inner soul and

ignoring the outer soul, supports the decline of the actual world

. Yet therapy goes on blindly believing that it’s curing the outer world by making better people. We’ve had that for years and years: “If everybody went into therapy, we’d have better buildings, we’d have better people, we’d have more consciousness.”

It’s not the case

.


—James Hillman


W

e know—

we know—

that the future our imaginations were promised is not the future that awaits us. This summer, more than any previous, is our evidence. As I write, fires rage across the American west, bombs drop on children, surveillance architecture is daily being constructed outside rural convenience stores. In our hearts, if we look, the knowing of where we really are is clear.


For many in the West, the future has long been a source of secure attachment. It has been our god, a shining destination justifying the sacrifices of generations. All the brutality of history has supposedly made sense through the lens of progress.

We’re going somewhere amazing.

Utopia has been just around the corner with every technological advance, asking for just a bit more patience, a bit more sacrifice, a bit more relinquishment of our humanity—just enough so that when the robots take our jobs, the foretold dawning of endless leisure will arrive as prophecy fulfilled.


For many, this enculturated fantasy of the future has been the bedrock of busy lives, unconsciously justifying cycles of overwork, burnout, and addiction. For a brief window in time, for some, it seemed true that children could build better lives than their parents and that technological advances did indeed improve the quality of life for a majority of the populace. However, here at the logical conclusion of an infinite growth paradigm, driven by technological development that has greatly outpaced our moral or spiritual development, we are left to contend with the starkness of reality.


Anytime you’re gonna grow, you’re gonna lose something. You’re losing what you’re hanging onto to keep safe. You’re losing habits that you’re comfortable with, you’re losing familiarity. That’s a big one, when you begin to move into the unfamiliar. You know, in the organic world when anything begins to grow it’s moving constantly into unfamiliar movements and unfamiliar things.


—James Hillman


As I discussed in

part one of this essay

, we are at a collective threshold that in another cultural context would imply the need for a “rite of passage.” As Peter Kingsley describes in his book

Catafalque: Carl Jung and the End of Humanity,

the mythic energy fueling our collective stories has withdrawn—our society is like a ship at sea, moving forward without propulsion, carried only by its remaining inertia. Soon, the density of the water will have its way.


Rites of passage are about growing up. They are designed to activate our latent soul capacities, allowing us to rise to moments of change and loss, ultimately pointing back to the fundamental uncertainty of existence. These ceremonies intentionally confront us with the facts of life—birth, transformation, and death—with the aim of engendering our surrender to a larger order. True adulthood is marked by the capacity to live in ever deepening levels of complexity, holding nuance, paradox and change with open hands, neither resisting nor clinging to easy answers.


As eco-depth psychologist Bill Plotkin has expressed through his eco-centric developmental model (presented in his book

Nature and the Human Soul

), mainstream western culture is an expression of arrested development at the adolescent level. Look around—the values of ego strength, material accumulation, competition, hubristic certainty, and tribalistic social organization dominate the discourse. It’s all about speed, growth, victory, dominance, knowledge, vitality. The developmental values of healthy adulthood—humility, community, cooperation, surrender, service, death literacy and wisdom—have not yet been embodied on a collective level. As a result, we cling to a future that only exists in the illusory linearity of our underdeveloped psyches. As the promised future and our capacity to attach to it falls away, we face the daunting task of discovering what remains, and where our security actually comes from.


Stubbornly insisting on life can result in its opposite. The frantic desire to ward off death can actually invite …

Sommaire


Les conséquences pour les auteurices et lecteurices des sites

Pour conclure


Le réseau Mutu (qui héberge notamment Paris Luttes Info) ressort d'une longue tempête de plusieurs semaines et d'une opération de maintenance qui aura duré une dizaine de jours. Comme vous avez peut-être pu le lire

ailleurs chez Indymedia Nantes

, nous avons été victime d'une double attaque particulièrement importante, qui a atteint la «

 

machine hôte

précédent piratage

, nous ont plongé·x·es dans l'urgence de la réinstallation de cette dite machine hôte ainsi que de la «

 

refonte

 

» de toute notre infrastructure. Cela nous a contraint·x·es à une longue période de maintenance, fort heureusement raccourcie grâce à l'aide précieuse de nos camarades trop fortiches de Riseup, d'Infokiosques.net et d'Indymedia Nantes ❤️🖤


Les portes dérobées que nous avons découvertes étaient installées avec les privilèges les plus élevés sur la machine hôte en question. Par conséquent, toutes nos données ont potentiellement été compromises, voire corrompues. Nous avons donc procédé à une remise au propre de nos serveurs (web et mail), ce qui nous a permis de regagner un niveau de confiance suffisant dans nos services pour pouvoir les relancer. Cependant, pour toute information qui vous paraîtrait compromettante ou risquée à nous communiquer, nous vous recommandons toujours l'utilisation d'emails chiffrés. Notez aussi que nous avons à nouveau

changé les adresses

.onion

 des sites

.


La remise en ligne des sites du réseau s'est faite progressivement car nous avons rencontré des difficultés importantes de surcharge de nos serveurs. Peu de temps avant la découverte de ces piratages, vous étiez nombreuxses à faire remonter des ralentissements importants dans l'utilisation de nos sites, chose que nous avions tenté de limiter en ajoutant une page de chargement pour bloquer les robots

IA

 qui aspirent et sur-sollicitent nos sites en permanence, mais avec une efficacité somme toute assez limitée. En fin de compte, ce sont des camarades administrateurices système d'autres sites qui nous ont éclairé·x·es de leurs lumières et nous ont aidé·x·es à résoudre ce fâcheux problème. (Merci encore, plein de cœurs et de paillettes sur vous, les copaines

 

!)


Enfin, ces attaques et la tempête dans laquelle nous avons été pris·x·es ne sont que l'illustration de l'hostilité grandissante qui règne actuellement sur les infrastructures numériques alternatives, autogérées ou militantes. Les failles et les mises à jour de sécurité critiques s'enchaînent les unes après les autres quotidiennement. L'importance de l'autonomie technique pour diffuser nos informations et nos luttes n'a probablement jamais été autant mise sous pression et s'avère d'autant plus cruciale à maintenir.

author: Unknown
title: Vigil for ill prisoners: The right to life is not negotiable
content:
The protest, launched outside the Ministry of Justice following a call by the Federation of Associations for Legal Solidarity with the Families of Prisoners and Convicts (TUHAD-FED), the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) and the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD), will enter its fifth day. 


The indefinite protest will continue every day at 14:00 outside the Ministry of Justice.


On Friday, the relatives of ill prisoners Ömer Güneri, Yakup Akman, Mehmet Ali Taşkın and Selim Çiftçi, Tuncer Sağlam, who died on 7 November in the hospital where he was receiving treatment, attended the protest.


During the demonstration, which was supported by representatives of organisations and members of the public, a banner bearing the names of seriously ill prisoners was unfurled. It read: “We are at the gates of justice; we will open the prison gates through resistance. Freedom for ill prisoners.”


‘Don't stay silent’


Deniz Topkan, a member of the Central Executive Board of the Health and Social Service Workers' Union (SES), called for support for the protest, saying that the vigil outside the Ministry of Justice must not be ignored.


Pointing out that numerous ill prisoners had lost their lives in prison after being denied access to healthcare, Topkan stressed that restricting someone's freedom does not mean their right to health and life can be taken away.


Stating that prisons had become places where illnesses deteriorate and deaths occur, Topkan said that isolation practices in Type S and other high-security prisons negatively affect prisoners' mental health.


Deniz Topkan noted that practices such as delays in hospital transfers, examinations conducted while prisoners are handcuffed, strip searches and intrusive oral cavity searches obstruct prisoners' right to treatment. She called for the release of seriously ill prisoners and guaranteed access to medical care to prevent further deaths.


Ercan Sağlam, a relative of Tuncer Sağlam, who died in the hospital where he was receiving treatment, said that delays in diagnosis and treatment had led to Sağlam's death. Explaining that Sağlam had been transferred from Wan to Ankara Etlik City Hospital and that, despite being unable to meet his own basic needs, there had been attempts to send him back to prison, Ercan Sağlam said:


“We have been experiencing this pain for years. But from now on, we will never accept another one of our comrades dying in prison.”


Noting that while deaths resulting from armed conflict had ceased during the Peace and Democratic Society Process, ill prisoners continued to lose their lives in prisons, Sağlam called for the immediate release of seriously ill prisoners.


‘Responsibility lies with the state’


Nurten Karagöz, co-chair of the Marmara Association for Solidarity and Mutual Assistance with the Families of Prisoners and Convicts (MA-TUHAYDER), emphasised that the right to health and the right to life are fundamental human rights.


Stating that the state is responsible for the lives and healthcare guarantees of all prisoners, Karagöz said: “The deaths of people held in the state's custody should not be this easy. From now on, no ill prisoner should lose their life in prison. The right to life is a sacred right. It cannot be negotiated. Prisoners' lives cannot be used as bargaining chips.”


Karagöz said that while people were speaking about the democratisation of society, it was unacceptable to remain silent as people continued to die in prison. She called for the right to life of ill prisoners to be protected.


‘Prisons must not be turned into places of execution’


Mahfuz Güleryüz, Deputy Co-Chair of the DEM Party, also condemned human rights violations taking place in prisons.


Güleryüz said: “Prisons must not be turned into places of ‘execution’. The state and the Ministry of Justice must immediately abandon these practices. We will continue to oppose this lawlessness, to resist it and to demand justice.”


Families of ill prisoners call for action outside Ministry of Justice

title: Alfred de Zayas: Why should Kurds be denied the right to self-determination? - Part One
content:
The right of peoples to self-determination is one of the fundamental principles of international law. However, its implementation remains contested because of the political and economic interests of states. The international representation of the Kurdish people, who are divided among four countries and have no state of their own, and the protection of their political, cultural and linguistic rights remain among the unresolved issues of international law.


Alfred de Zayas, an expert in international law and human rights who served as the United Nations (UN) Independent Expert on the Promotion of a Democratic and Equitable International Order from 2012 to 2018, spoke to ANF about the Kurdish people's right to self-determination and autonomy, the possibilities of obtaining status within the UN, the treatment of stateless peoples and double standards in international law.


De Zayas said that the Kurdish people's right to self-determination has a strong foundation in international law, emphasising that the main obstacle to exercising this right is political rather than legal. He stressed that the UN has failed to fulfil its responsibilities towards the Kurdish people and said that Kurds should bring human rights violations before international mechanisms, explore interstate complaint procedures and build stronger networks of solidarity within the international community.


De Zayas also strongly criticised the European Union's approach to the Kurdish question, arguing that international law must be applied equally to all peoples. He asked, "If the right to self-determination has been granted to other peoples, why should it not be granted to the Kurdish people?"


ANF spoke to international law expert Alfred de Zayas.


Mr. de Zayas, you have worked for many years within the United Nations on international law, human rights and the right of peoples to self-determination. I would like to begin with a fundamental question. What does the right of a people to self-determination mean under international law? Does this right refer only to establishing an independent state, or can it also be exercised in other forms?


Of course, the right to self-determination can also be exercised internally. If there is a federal state and a people enjoys extensive autonomy, that system can work. But what happens when a state oppresses a people who have lived on their own land for thousands of years? The Kurds are not immigrants who recently arrived in the territories of Turkey, Syria, Iran or Iraq.


If we genuinely took the right to self-determination seriously, we would ask which people have the clearest claim to this right. I would say the Kurds. There are between 40 and 45 million Kurds, divided among four states. Yet they have no state of their own.


After the First World War, they could have had their own state if the Treaty of Sèvres had been implemented. However, Mustafa Kemal fought against the French and British forces at that time. Those forces were expelled from the territory of the new Turkey. The Treaty of Sèvres was subsequently replaced by the Treaty of Lausanne, which made no mention of the Kurdish or Armenian peoples.


What, then, are the legal foundations of the right to self-determination?


You can find them in Articles 1 and 55 of the United Nations Charter, as well as Chapters XI and XII. This right is also enshrined in the common Article 1 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. There is extensive literature on this subject, including my report A/69/272, which I submitted to the UN General Assembly in 2014. In that report, I examine the criteria determining which peoples may claim autonomy or independence.


Before continuing, I would like to mention a book that you may not know about because it has only recently been published. I supervised the doctoral thesis of a young Norwegian researcher, Blerim Mustafa, whose family originates from North Macedonia. He devoted his doctoral research to the right of secession, particularly the concept known in international law as "remedial secession".


His book is entitled Remedial Secession After the Cold War: Self-Determination and the Question of Secession. A substantial part of this work is devoted to the Kurds. The author examines three examples. The first is the people of East Timor, who were previously occupied, colonised and oppressed by Indonesia. The second is Kosovo, which …

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: ‘Predators-in-chief’ attack ICC
content:
Former United Nations (UN) Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial killing Agnès Callamard visited the Philippines after almost a decade of being barred from entering the country.

“It begins with Duterte, in a few weeks. But it doesn’t end there,” said Callamard, also Amnesty International’s secretary-general in a press conference on November 20. “This is bigger than him. It is about the Philippines. It’s about humanity.”

When she was UN Special Rapporteur, she called for investigations into the thousands of killings under Duterte’s anti-illegal drugs campaign. The immigration ban started in 2017 and Duterte ordered that she and any representatives of the International Criminal Court (ICC) be arrested and deported.

Callamard’s immigration ban was lifted in September 2026 after years of petitioning the Philippine authorities, with the support of Amnesty International Philippines and support from several lawmakers.

“The supposed war on drugs was a slaughter that destroyed lives and families. They have carried their grief with little hope for justice and nowhere else to turn for almost a decade,” Callamard said.

Duterte is charged with three counts of crimes against humanity by the ICC for extrajudicial killings during his term as Davao City mayor and President of the Philippines. His trial is set to begin on November 30.

Human rights organizations reported more than 30,000 extrajudicial killing victims from Duterte’s anti-illegal drugs campaign, significantly higher than the official government records of just over 6,000 victims. Only five cases resulted in conviction and some of them remain on appeal.

“We had conversations with the victims, survivors, and families in the past 48 hours [with Callamard]. It is still depressing. The families have accepted that there will be no justice at home and that they are depending on what will happen in The Hague. It is very ironic,” said Ritz Lee Santos III, section director of Amnesty International Philippines. “We have a justice system here at home. The government is claiming that they are working, but the victims’ families are saying that there is no hope. There is still a culture of impunity and a climate of fear.”

These structures, both of them said, are evident in the continuing drug-related extrajudicial killings, Duterte’s children remaining in power, and the widespread vilification of the victims and their families.

Read: Women human rights defenders face rising tech-assisted violence

The United States has imposed sanctions against the ICC, banning transactions with the court to paralyze its resources and ability to operate. The administration of US President Donald Trump previously sanctioned 13 prosecutors and judges of the ICC, three Palestinian human rights organizations, and the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory Francesca Albanese.

Read: US intensifies sanctions vs. ICC

The United States, China, and Russia issued a so-called “peace declaration” in their first trilateral summit on November 29, after Trump’s visit in Manila, Philippines. Particularly, the ICC garnered special attention in their declaration.

“The three heads of state recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction,” the declaration read.

Part of the declaration is to “reform” the United Nations (UN) as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC).

“They are the ‘predators-in-chief’ in our current system. This so-called peace treaty is about as worthless as who they are– predators,” said Callamard, highlighting their aggression in Venezuela, Iran, and Palestine. “They are attacking the ICC because international justice for them is a battle ground.”

“We are calling on the rest of the world to stand up to these predatory actions and threats. There are far more governments that ratified the Rome Statute. So in terms of the numbers, we are far more powerful than they are,” Callamard said.

In her international human rights work, Callamard said that there are less powerful governments living in fear of what the US, Russia, and China could do in their economy. “It is about economic characters being fearful of being kept out of the American market, Russian market, or the China market. And for those reasons, humanity is being thrown out. We’re …

title: Şadiye Dalkıran: Women should never remain where they are subjected to violence
content:
Dilan Aslan was murdered by a firearm in March last year by Abdulvahap Aslan, the husband she was in the process of divorcing. Following the murder, it emerged that the man had attempted to stage the killing as a suicide and had driven around the city for approximately two hours in an attempt to destroy evidence.


During her marriage in Istanbul, Dilan (nicknamed Tuba) was subjected to systematic violence and repeatedly received death threats. After witnessing her children being subjected to violence as well, Dilan decided to divorce and moved from Istanbul to Amed (Diyarbakır), where her family lived.


After staying with her family for a while, Dilan tried to rebuild her life despite threats from the violent husband, Abdulvahap Aslan. However, following his request for reconciliation and pressure from both families, she agreed to reunite with him.


On the night of 31 March, Abdulvahap Aslan and Dilan arrived in the centre of the Xana Axpar (Çınar) district of Amed and went to the house where they were staying in the Bağlar district. There, Aslan first subjected Dilan to violence and then murdered her using a firearm.


After the murder, the perpetrator attempted to destroy evidence at the scene before leaving the house. Calling a relative, Abdulvahap Aslan claimed, “My wife shot herself in the head,” attempting to make the murder look like a suicide. He then drove around the city, remaining unaccounted for approximately two hours.


Approximately two hours later, Abdulvahap Aslan went to the police station and surrendered. Following police procedures that same day, he was arrested and sent to prison.


Killer sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment


Throughout the trial, the perpetrator, Abdulvahap Aslan, maintained that the incident had been a suicide. However, neither the report prepared by the Council of Forensic Medicine (ATK) nor the indictment supported his claim. Evidence and witness testimonies also disproved his defence of suicide, while statements given by Dilan Aslan’s children during the trial revealed the extent of the violence they had suffered and the circumstances surrounding the murder.


The lawyer representing the family in the case had previously made a statement about the incident, noting that Dilan Aslan still bore signs of physical violence when she arrived in Amed. The lawyer said: “Even when she arrived here, there were marks of physical assault on her face and body. Shortly after she arrived, the defendant followed Dilan to Diyarbakır. With family members intervening, attempts were made to reconcile the two. Following these meetings, Dilan did not return to Istanbul. During conversations that took place from time to time, the same threats continued. All family members witnessed the death threats in question. On the day of the incident, the defendant also sent his three children to different homes, leaving only his five-year-old child at home.”


The case, which was launched following the preparation of the indictment, concluded last month with the final hearing at Diyarbakır's 1st High Criminal Court. The court sentenced Abdulvahap Aslan to aggravated life imprisonment for the crime of “intentional killing of a spouse and a woman”, without granting him any sentence reductions.


She lived under violence and threats for years


Since her daughter's murder, Şadiye Dalkıran has regularly visited her grave. She refused to allow the perpetrator's surname to be inscribed on the gravestone. Instead, she had her daughter's family nickname, Tuba, and her own family surname written on it, and decorated the grave with mint and flowers.


 


Praying at her daughter's grave and commemorating other women who had been murdered alongside her, Şadiye Dalkıran spoke about the violence her daughter endured throughout her marriage, the death threats she received and her struggle to build a new life.


Şadiye Dalkıran said that her daughter had married of her own free will and had four children from the marriage. Despite this, she explained, her daughter had lived under violence and abuse for years.


Şadiye Dalkıran added that her daughter had hidden what she was going through because she did not want to upset her family. She continued: “After my daughter got married, I never once saw her smile. She suffered terribly, endured so much pain and was subjected to torture. She did not tell us what she was going through because she did not want us to worry; she constantly kept it hidden.

title: Kara para aklama suçundan aranan Serdar Altınbaş Çekya’da yakalandı
content:
"Sermaye Piyasası Kanununa Muhalefet" ve "Suçtan Kaynaklanan Mal Varlığı Değerlerini Aklama" suçlarından aranan Serdar Altınbaş, Çekya’da yakalandı. İçişleri Bakanlığı, şüphelinin Türkiye’ye iadesine yönelik işlemlerin başlatıldığını duyurdu.


İade süreci


Emniyet Genel Müdürlüğü Interpol-Europol Daire Başkanlığı, İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı ve Adalet Bakanlığı koordinesinde yürütülen ortak çalışmalar sonucunda, hakkında yakalama kararı bulunan Serdar Altınbaş’ın izine Çekya’da ulaşıldı. Çekya INTERPOL birimleriyle kurulan temaslar neticesinde, şüphelinin Prag Vaclav Havel Havalimanı’nın transit bölgesinde bulunduğu tespit edildi.


Bunun üzerine Adalet Bakanlığı ile koordineli biçimde harekete geçilerek 20 Kasım 2026 tarihinde şüpheli hakkında difüzyon mesajı (acil yakalama bildirimi) yayımlandı. Mesajın Çekya makamlarına iletilmesinin ardından Altınbaş havalimanında yakalanarak gözaltına alındı.


Bakanlıktan açıklama


İçişleri Bakanlığı tarafından konuya ilişkin yapılan resmi açıklamada, hukuki sürece ve operasyona dair şu bilgiler paylaşıldı:


"Yapılan incelemelerde, Serdar Altınbaş hakkında İstanbul 8. Sulh Ceza Hâkimliğince 'Sermaye Piyasası Kanununa Muhalefet ve Suçtan Kaynaklanan Mal Varlığı Değerlerini Aklama' suçlarından aranma kaydı bulunduğu, İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığınca da hakkında yurt dışı çıkış yasağı kararı verildiği belirlendi.


ANKA'nın haberine göre, Difüzyon mesajının Çekya makamlarına iletilmesinin ardından Serdar Altınbaş’ın Çekya’da yakalanması sağlandı ve Türkiye’ye iadesine yönelik işlemler başlatıldı. Kahraman Polislerimizi, Interpol Daire Başkanlığımızı, İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığımızı ve emeği geçenleri tebrik ediyoruz. Adalet Bakanlığı görevlilerine teşekkür ediyoruz."


Serdar Altınbaş hakkında bilinenler


Resmi kayıtlara ve yargı kararlarına yansıyan bilgilere göre Serdar Altınbaş; sermaye piyasası mevzuatına aykırı işlemler ve suç gelirlerinin aklanması iddiaları kapsamında İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı tarafından yürütülen soruşturmanın şüphelisi olarak aranıyordu.


Hakkında İstanbul 8. Sulh Ceza Hâkimliği tarafından çıkarılmış yakalama kararı ve başsavcılıkça konulmuş yurt dışı çıkış yasağı bulunuyordu.


(EMK)

title: Yeni Partili Aşkın Genç'ten Bakan Işıkhan’a: "Emeklinin ihtiyacı hikaye değil, geçinebileceği bir aylık"
content:
Yeni Parti Kayseri Milletvekili Aşkın Genç, Çalışma ve Sosyal Güvenlik Bakanı Vedat Işıkhan’ın emekli aylıklarına ilişkin yanıtına, açıklamayla tepki gösterdi. Emeklilerin asgari ücret karşısındaki kaybına dikkat çeken Genç, “2002’deki oran korunsaydı bugün emekli 39 bin 150 lira alacaktı” dedi. Bakanlığın 2027 yılı için somut bir aylık tutarı açıklamamasını eleştiren Genç, “Milyonlarca emeklinin hakkı, Sayın Cumhurbaşkanının gönlünden kopacak rakama mı kaldı” diye sordu.

Bakan Işıkhan’ın 2027 bütçesinin görüşüldüğü Plan ve Bütçe Komisyonunda yaptığı açıklamaları hatırlatan Genç, verilen sözlerin karşılığını yazılı cevapta bulamadıklarını ifade ederek, şunları söyledi:

“Sayın Bakan, 3 Kasım’da Plan ve Bütçe Komisyonuna geldiniz. ‘Emeklilerimizin yaşadığı ekonomik koşulların farkındayız’ dediniz. ‘İyileştirme yapacağız’ dediniz. ‘Adalet ve hakkaniyeti sağlayacağız’ dediniz. Dediniz de dediniz… Biz de size çok basit iki soru sorduk. 2027’de en düşük emekli aylığı kaç lira olacak? Milyonlarca emeklimizin aylıkları arasındaki farkları nasıl gidereceksiniz? Yazılı cevabınız geldi. 2019’u anlatmışsınız, 2023’ü anlatmışsınız, dönmüş dolaşmış yine 2002’ye gitmişsiniz. Yüzde 77’den yüzde 663’e varan artışlardan söz etmişsiniz. Sayın Bakan, biz size 2027’yi sorduk, siz 2002’yi anlatmışsınız. Ama emeklinin ihtiyacı hikaye değil, geçinebileceği bir aylık. Takvimi geriye sarınca marketteki fiyatlar geriye doğru gitmiyor.”

Bakanlığın yazılı cevabında 2002 yılından bu yana emekli aylıklarına yapılan artışların öne çıkarılmasına tepki gösteren Genç, Cumhurbaşkanlığı Strateji ve Bütçe Başkanlığının verilerini gündeme taşıdı.

2002 ve 2026 yıllarındaki en düşük SSK emekli aylığının net asgari ücret karşısındaki durumunu karşılaştıran Genç, emeklilerin yıllar içinde uğradığı gelir kaybına dikkat çekerek, şöyle konuştu:

“Madem 2002’yi bu kadar seviyorsunuz, gelin bir de o tarihe sizin rakamlarınızla bakalım. Cumhurbaşkanlığı Strateji ve Bütçe Başkanlığının tablosuna göre; 2002’de en düşük SSK emekli aylığı 257 lira, net asgari ücret 184 liraydı. Yani emekli, asgari ücretlinin yüzde 39 üzerinde aylık alıyordu. 2026’da emekli aylığı 24 bin 326 lira, asgari ücret 28 bin 76 lira. Emekli, asgari ücretin yüzde 39 üzerindeyken yüzde 13 geriye düşmüş.”

Emekli aylıklarının asgari ücret karşısındaki eski düzeyini koruması durumunda ortaya çıkacak tutarı da hesaplayan Genç, Cumhurbaşkanlığının kendi verilerinin emeklilerin yaşadığı kaybı gösterdiğini vurgulayarak, “Peki, 2002’deki oran korunsaydı bugün emekli ne kadar alacaktı? Tam 39 bin 150 lira. Aradaki fark yaklaşık 14 bin 825 lira. Bunlar Cumhurbaşkanlığının kendi rakamları. Siz yüzdelerle refah masalı anlatırken emekli her ay, ay sonunu nasıl getireceğinin hesabını yapıyor” dedi.

Emeklilerin yaşadığı geçim sıkıntısını TÜRK-İŞ’in gıda harcamalarına ilişkin verileriyle de ortaya koyan Genç, en düşük emekli aylığının dört kişilik bir ailenin yalnızca mutfak ihtiyacını karşılamaya dahi yetmediğini belirtti.

Genç, “TÜRK-İŞ’e göre dört kişilik bir ailenin yalnızca aylık gıda harcaması 38 bin lirayı aşmış. Sizin en düşük emekli aylığı diye açıkladığınız rakam 23 bin 552 lira. Tek emekli aylığıyla geçinen dört kişilik bir aile, daha mutfak masrafını bile karşılayamıyor” ifadelerini kullandı.

2027 yılı bütçesinde faiz giderleri için ayrılan kaynağı hatırlatan Genç, emekli aylıklarının artırılması konusunda bütçe imkanlarının gerekçe gösterilmesini eleştirdi. Genç, iktidarın bütçe tercihlerine ilişkin şu değerlendirmeyi yaptı:

“2027 bütçesinde faize ayırdığınız para belli, 3 trilyon 975 milyar lira. Faize gelince milyarına kadar hesap yapıyorsunuz. Emekliye gelince ‘bütçe imkanları doğrultusunda’ diyorsunuz.”

Bakan Işıkhan’ın komisyon görüşmeleri sırasında emeklilere yönelik iyileştirmeler için Cumhurbaşkanının talimatını işaret etmesine de tepki gösteren Genç, emekli aylıklarının siyasi tercihlere veya talimatlara bağlı olmaması gerektiğini vurguladı.

Genç, açıklamasını şu sözlerle tamamladı:

“Sayın Bakan komisyonda ‘Cumhurbaşkanımızın talimatıyla’ dediniz. Milyonlarca emeklinin hakkı, Sayın Cumhurbaşkanının gönlünden kopacak rakama mı kaldı? Emekli sadaka istemiyor. Yıllarca çalışmış, primini ödemiş… Emekli bunun karşılığını istiyor. Sizden cevap olarak 2027’de emeklimizin aylığı ne olacak, onun cevabını bekliyoruz.”

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Sultangazi'de inşaatın bodrum katında erkek cesedi bulundu
content:
İstanbul'un Sultangazi ilçesinde 4 katlı bir inşaatın bodrum katında kimliği henüz tespit edilemeyen bir erkeğin cansız bedeni bulundu. İlk incelemelerde cinayet ihtimali üzerinde durulurken, otopsi sonucunda kişinin yüksekten düşmeye bağlı boyun kırığı nedeniyle hayatını kaybettiği belirlendi.

Olay, 17 Kasım'da Yunus Emre Mahallesi'nde meydana geldi. İnşaatta çalışan bir işçi, bodrum katta yarı çıplak halde hareketsiz yatan bir kişiyi fark ederek durumu firma sahibine bildirdi. İhbar üzerine olay yerine gelen sağlık ekipleri, kişinin hayatını kaybettiğini tespit etti.

Polis ekiplerinin ilk incelemesinde ölümün yaklaşık 3-4 gün önce gerçekleşmiş olabileceği, kişinin başında ise darp izleri bulunduğu değerlendirildi. Bu nedenle başlangıçta cinayet şüphesi üzerinde duruldu. Ancak Adli Tıp Kurumunda yapılan otopside ölümün düşmeye bağlı boyun kırığından kaynaklandığı belirlendi.

Hayatını kaybeden kişinin kimliği henüz tespit edilemezken, olayla ilgili soruşturma sürüyor.

Olay sırasında sokakta bulunduğunu belirten Rüveyda D., "Saat 23.00 sıralarında polis ekipleri geldi. Sorduğumuzda, ceset bulunduğunu ve büyük ihtimalle cinayet olduğunu söyledi. Erkek ve 50 yaşlarında olduğunu da dedi. Başına vurulmuş ve yarı çıplak halde bulunmuş. Sonrasında savcılık ve olay yeri inceleme ekipleri geldi. Saat 01.30 sıralarında nakil aracı cenazeyi alıp götürdü" dedi.

title: Campagne de soutien à Ali du 22 au 30 novembre
content:
Du 22 au 30 novembre 2024, la campagne pour la libération d'Ali appelle à se mobiliser ne soutien à Ali, refuser son expulsion et exiger sa libération immédiate. Le 30 novembre devait avoir lieu l'audience pour savoir s'il serait expulsé ou non mais elle est reportée.


L'audience du 30 novembre est reportée, à la demande du préfet.


Non à l'expulsion d'Ali


Nous avons été informé-es par M

e

 Kempf, avocat d'Ali, que l'audience devant la commission d'expulsion, prévue le 30 novembre au tribunal judiciaire de Pontoise, a été reportée à la demande du préfet. Aucune nouvelle date n'a été fixée et le motifs de ce report ne nous ont pas été communiqués.


Si ce renvoi retarde la possibilité pour le préfet de prendre une mesure d'expulsion,

Ali reste incarcéré depuis mai 2024 et demeure sous la menace d'une expulsion.


Ce report ne met donc fin ni à la procédure engagée contre lui, ni à l'urgence de la situation.


Notre mobilisation continue jusqu'à la libération d'Ali

 

!


Le report de l'audience ne doit pas affaiblir la mobilisation. Il reste essentiel de faire connaître la situation d'Ali, de renforcer le rapport de force et de maintenir la pression pour obtenir sa libération immédiate, le rétablissement de son statut de réfigué et l'abondon de toutes les charges retenues contre lui.


Nous appelons donc à maintenir et multiplier les initiatives de solidarité tout au long de la semaine du 22 au 30 novembre.

 ___________________________________________________________________________________


Ali est un réfugié palestinien, né dans un camp de réfugié-es en Cisjordanie occupée. À 14 ans, il voit son petit frère de 8 ans être tué par un soldat israélien.

 Deux ans plus tard, Ali est incercéré pour la première fois. Au total, il passera 8 ans de sa vie dans les prisons israéliennes avant d'être contraint à l'exil. Arrivé en France en 2016, Ali obtient le statut de réfugié en 2020 : l'État français reconnaît donc la persécution à laquelle il est exposée de la part des autorités israéliennes. Il reconstruit sa vie en France et y fonde une famille.


Pourtant, en mai 2024, Ali est arrêté lors d'une perquisition violente au domicile familial devant sa femme et ses enfants. Depuis plus de 2 ans et demi, il est incarcéré en France, en détention provisoire, sans jugement ni procès, dans le cadre d'une procédure pénale basée sur des accusations transmises par les services israéliens et son statut de réfugié lui a été retiré

. Depuis son arrestation, quatre demandes de libération ont été refusées, malgré les irrégularités flagrantes présentes dans la procédure, empêchant Ali de retourner auprès de ses enfants et de sa compagne, encore marqué-es par la violence de son arrestation.


Le 28 août 2026,

quatre rapporteur-es spéciaux-les des Nations Unies ont interpellé officiellement la France sur la situation d'Ali, exprimant de graves préoccupations sur les procédures pénales et administratives engagées contre lui et sur son maintien en détention.

 Cette lettre signifie que l'

ONU

 reconnaît officiellement l'injustice subie par Ali.


Le 30 novembre prochain,

 Ali comparaîtra devant une commission d'expulsion au tribunal judiciaire de Pontoise.

Cette commission sera chargée d'émettre un avis

 favorable ou défavorable

quant à une procédure d'expulsion engagée par la préfecture. Mais le préfet gardera la décision finale : même en cas d'avis négatif, Ali peut donc être expulsé

 

!


Du 22 au 30 novembre 2024, la campagne pour la libération d'Ali appelle à se mobiliser ne soutien à Ali, refuser son expulsion et exiger sa libération immédiate. Le 30 novembre, un rassemblement de soutien sera organisé devant le tribunal de Pontoise (3 rue Victor Hugo, 95300 Pontoise). Plus d'infos à venir

 

!

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: ‘They don’t see us as humans’: Indigenous youth call for national day of action
content:
For Ramon Kataquapit of Attawapiskat First Nation, the experience inside a special House of Commons committee reviewing Bill C-39 was troubling.


As lawmakers debated the proposed

Building Canada Strong Act

, Kataquapit said he watched Indigenous consultation become a subject of parliamentary discussion, while Indigenous voices were largely absent from the proceedings.


He said he and fellow youth leader Jeronimo Kataquapit were invited by Gazan to observe the committee’s clause-by-clause deliberations.


“I want to speak about our experience we had yesterday. We were invited in to the committee with Leah (NDP MP Leah Gazan) to watch Bill C-39 be debated clause by clause and within this debate they were talking about Indigenous consultation but yet they had Indigenous people sitting on the sidelines; meanwhile, our only Indigenous representation in that room Leah Gazan was constantly being interrupted,”  Ramon Kataquapit said. 


“When she was fighting for us in there, watching the smirks on the Liberals’ faces, it really dawned on me that they don’t see us as humans, especially when it comes to debating Bill C-39.” 


His account came Friday as First Nation youth leaders announced plans for a national day of action against the proposed legislation on Dec. 8, in Ottawa, coinciding with the Assembly of First Nations’ winter gathering. 


Ramon Kataquapit said the demonstration is intended to bring First Nations people together to challenge what he described as the federal government’s attempt to advance legislation affecting Indigenous rights without adequate consultation.


Ramon Kataquapit speaking during a press conference with MP Leah Gazan on Parliament Hill (November 20, 2026). Photo: Keelan Jacobs/APTN


“I want to continue to fully express our opposition to Bill C-39 and how it’s being pushed through, without due consultation with First Nations,” he said.


The proposed legislation, known as the Building Canada Strong Act, is a sweeping “omnibus” bill that would change how major infrastructure, energy and resource projects are assessed and approved.


Introduced in September 2026, Bill C-39 proposes amendments to several federal laws, including the environmental statutes including Impact Assessment Act, Fisheries Act, and the Species at Risk Act, and the Labour Act. 


Among its measures are provisions intended to accelerate federal project reviews, coordinate regulatory approvals and Indigenous consultations, and establish pathways for certain projects in designated regions of national interest.


Jeronimo Kataquapit echoed those concerns, describing the committee experience as deeply troubling and questioning the federal government’s commitment to reconciliation.


“I stand here today to not only reaffirm our opposition to Bill C-39 but to talk about what myself and Ramon witnessed in the clause-by-clause committee on Bill C-39. It’s so inhumane,” he said. “They’re trying their hardest and fastest to rush this through into law. As we were sitting there, as Ramon was saying, we never saw Indigenous people so objectified as we have seen in that room.”


He said the experience was especially difficult to reconcile with the federal government’s repeated commitments to reconciliation and economic reconciliation.


“It’s disappointing to see that from the federal government that always talks about reconciliation, in this case economic reconciliation.”


Gazan said the government is moving quickly to advance the legislation, despite growing opposition.


“As you know, this government is attempting to fast-track Bill C-39 in committee; we have been sitting long days, in fact, 15 hours a day. We know that there is a lot of pushback that is emerging rapidly from around the country,” she said.


The committee will also sit all day Saturday and Sunday. 


The government has framed the legislation as a way to improve regulatory efficiency, reduce duplication and accelerate projects considered important to Canada’s economic interests.


However, the legislation raises fundamental questions about the relationship between economic development, Indigenous jurisdiction and the Crown’s constitutional obligations to First Nations.


The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, passed in 2021, further commits the federal government to aligning Canadian laws with the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.


For First Nations, the central concern is not necessarily whether …

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: « Nous prenons soin les uns des autres. » : témoignages du square Cabot
content:
Au square Cabot de Montréal, où des Autochtones en situation d’itinérance se rassemblent depuis des décennies, la nouvelle selon laquelle un membre du Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) avait été suspendu pour avoir uriné sur des personnes en situation d’itinérance a été accueillie avec peu de surprise.


Selon des habitués du secteur et des intervenants de rue œuvrant auprès des personnes en situation d’itinérance dans l’ouest du centre-ville, les rapports entre la police et les personnes itinérantes au square Cabot et dans les environs sont marqués par la méfiance et la peur.


Au cours d’une période de deux semaines, les personnes interrogées par APTN Nouvelles au square Cabot ont affirmé avoir reçu de nombreuses contraventions, représentant des centaines de dollars d’amende, pour non-paiement du titre de transport ou pour avoir traversé la rue Sainte-Catherine hors des intersections autorisées. Des personnes buvant de l’alcool dans le square ont aussi rapporté avoir reçu des amendes pour possession de contenants ouverts. Bien peu cherchent à payer leurs contraventions. Pour eux, en recevoir une nouvelle fait tout simplement partie de la réalité au square Cabot, bien que cela puisse éventuellement fournir à la police un prétexte pour les arrêter.


Square Cabot


Mesurant un coin de rue par un coin de rue, le square Cabot constitue le seul grand espace vert dans le secteur ouest du centre-ville de Montréal. Situé rue Sainte-Catherine, à l’angle de l’avenue Atwater, le square fait directement face à l’ancien Forum de Montréal.


Depuis des décennies, le lieu rassemble des personnes autochtones en situation d’itinérance, phénomène attribuable en partie à une politique provinciale de longue date visant à loger au YMCA à proximité les Inuit du Nunavik transférés par voie aérienne vers le sud pour des traitements médicaux.


Bien que les patients du Nunavik soient dirigés vers la résidence Ullivik, dans la banlieue ouest de Montréal, depuis 2016, le square Cabot conserve une communauté de personnes en situation d’itinérance marquée par une forte présence autochtone.


Durant les années glorieuses du hockey à Montréal, la foule se massait au square Cabot avant les multiples défilés de la coupe Stanley des Canadiens de Montréal. C’est là qu’a débuté l’émeute du Forum en 1955, alors que des partisans francophones en colère du grand Maurice « Rocket » Richard s’étaient réunis pour dénoncer sa suspension imposée par le président anglophone de la LNH, qu’ils jugeaient motivée par des préjugés ethniques.


Vue vers le nord-est du square Cabot à partir de l’angle des rues Sainte- Catherine et Lambert-Closse. L’ancien Forum de Montréal se trouve à droite, juste hors champ. Photo : Jesse Staniforth/APTN


Depuis que le Forum a fermé ses portes en 1996, un

rapport municipal sur la revitalisation du secteur

 note que « la disparition de cette importante source d’achalandage a causé une dégradation importante de la rue Sainte-Catherine Ouest ».


En pratique, cela veut dire que le square Cabot est principalement fréquenté par des personnes sans abri.


En 2013, la Ville a réaménagé le square, mais à ce moment-là, la population en situation d’itinérance y était si bien établie que les promoteurs s’attendaient à ce qu’elle revienne. Les concepteurs ont conservé les bancs et les murets sur lesquels les habitués du square dorment régulièrement, et la Ville a rénové le petit bâtiment connu sous le nom de « Maison Ronde », qui est devenu un café ainsi qu’un bureau pour les travailleurs de rue œuvrant auprès des personnes en situation d’itinérance qui fréquentent le square.


Une configuration modeste


Selon un médiateur du Projet du square Cabot, mis sur pied en 2014 par le Foyer pour femmes autochtones de Montréal en partenariat avec l’arrondissement et le programme d’aide aux personnes en situation d’itinérance du YMCA, les personnes qui fréquentent le square ont tendance à se regrouper selon leur langue et leur origine ethnique. Dans la partie est du parc, on trouve davantage de personnes blanches et de francophones.


À l’ouest du square, à proximité de la Maison Ronde, se rassemblent principalement des personnes autochtones et des personnes noires, qui communiquent toutes en anglais. Les bancs entourant la statue de Giovanni Caboto (Jean Cabot), au centre du parc, sont partagés par tous, alors que la ruelle directement à l’est du square est l’endroit où les consommateurs se rendent pour fumer du crack.


Par temps …

title: BM Genel Kurulu, Filistin halkının bağımsızlık hakkına ilişkin tasarıyı 162 oyla kabul etti
content:
Fotoğraf: Basil D Soufi/Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0

BM Genel Kurulu’nda ilistin halkının kendi kaderini tayin etme ve bağımsızlık hakkını teyit eden karar taslağı kabul edildi.

İnsan hakları ve insani işlerle ilgilenen Genel Kurulun 3. Komitesi tarafından sunulan tasarı oylandı.

Oylamada 162 ülke, Filistin halkının kendi kaderini tayin etme ve bağımsızlık hakkını teyit eden tasarıya "evet" oyu verirken, 8 ülke "hayır" oyu kullandı, 8 ülke ise çekimser kaldı.

Lehte oy kullanan ülkeler arasında Türkiye başta olmak üzere tüm Avrupa Birliği üye devletleri, Kanada, Avustralya ile Güney Amerika, Asya ve Afrika'daki ülkelerin çoğunluğu yer alırken, ABD, İsrail, Arjantin, Paraguay, Mikronezya, Nauru, Papua Yeni Gine ve Palau aleyhte oy kullandı.

Karar, Filistin halkının İsrail işgalinden uzak, kendi topraklarında özgürce yaşama ve bağımsız olma hakkının devredilemez olduğunu teyit ediyor. Ayrıca bu hakkın koşulsuz, vazgeçilemez, müzakere edilemez veya uzlaşmaya konu edilemez olduğunu vurguluyor.

title: Solidarity reception for Rojava at New South Wales parliament
content:
The Federation of Democratic Kurdish Societies in Australia (FDKS-A), the Sydney Democratic Kurdish Community Centre, and the Sydney Kurdish Youth Association organized a solidarity reception for Rojava at the Parliament of New South Wales (NSW), Australia.


Speaking at the event, members of parliament expressed their support for the Kurdish people’s struggle for freedom, peace, and democracy. Representatives of political parties, civil society organizations, and members of the Kurdish community attended the reception.


Greens MP Abigail Boyd described the resistance in Kobanê as a symbol of international solidarity and the right of peoples to self-defense, affirming her party’s solidarity with the Kurdish people.


Labor Party MP Charishma Kaliyanda emphasized that Kobanê had become a symbol of courage, resistance, and, in particular, women’s struggle for freedom.


Liberal Party MP Justin Clancy also highlighted the significance of the Kurds’ struggle against ISIS for Australia and the wider world.


FDKS-A (Federation of Democratic Kurdish Societies in Australia) Co-Chair Gülfer Olan stated that the resistance in Kobanê was a struggle that concerned not only the Kurdish people but all of humanity, stressing that protecting the achievements of Rojava was a shared responsibility.


Baran Söğüt, spokesperson for the Federation’s Diplomacy Commission, commemorated Australian YPG volunteers

Reece Harding

,

Ashley Johnson

, and Jamie Bright, who lost their lives in the fight against ISIS in Rojava.


Michelle Harding, the mother of YPG internationalist Reece Harding (Bagok Serhed) who fell in Rojava in 2015, praised the Kurdish fighters for putting up remarkable resistance despite their limited resources. “I have enormous respect for them. Despite everything they went through, they managed to find solutions with the limited resources available to them,” she said.


The event also addressed the significance of the traditional floral-patterned headscarf symbolizing the resistance of Kurdish women, the Yazidi community’s solidarity with the resistance in Kobanê, and the Kurdish people’s struggle.


Speaking on behalf of the Reverend Bill Crews Foundation, Dr. Anjalika Wijesurendra reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining solidarity with the Kurdish people and their struggle for freedom.


The reception concluded with chants of “Bijî Kobanê” and “Bijî Berxwedana Rojava” and a musical performance.

title: “Tree of Remembrance” created for murdered women in Amed
content:
Since Friday, a “Tree of Remembrance” in Sümer Park in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) has commemorated women who were murdered in the city over the past two years. The Women’s Council of the Metropolitan Municipality attached the names of the murdered women to the branches of a tree to preserve their life stories in collective memory. The initiative was organized as part of events marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.


At the unveiling of the memorial tree, Rojda Çeçen from the Women’s Council Secretariat stated that violence against women was not limited to acts of violence themselves. “Looking the other way is also part of the violence. Confronting violence is therefore a shared responsibility of society as a whole," she emphasized.


Çeçen particularly commemorated two women who have been murdered in Sümer Park only recently. She said the pain of their deaths was still deeply felt. "The names attached to the tree represent not only individual victims of femicide but also lives cut short, voices silenced, and women whose memory must not be erased," she stated.


“Remembrance also means responsibility”


Özden Gürbüz Sümer, head of the Metropolitan Municipality’s Department of Women’s Policies, explained that the project had been jointly developed and implemented by the Women’s Council. She said the tree was intended not only to create a place of remembrance but also to encourage people to reflect on their own responsibilities.


“Sometimes we find it difficult to remember what we cannot see. With this Tree of Remembrance, we want not only to make these women visible but also to encourage people to take responsibility for what they see,” Sümer explained.


“May its roots strengthen collective memory”


Sümer continued: "In this way, the life stories of the murdered women are intended to become a lasting part of collective memory and the history of the women’s struggle. Remembrance must give rise to a sense of responsibility that strengthens solidarity and advances the struggle for a life of equality, freedom, and freedom from violence."


In closing, Sümer drew on the symbolism of the tree: “May its roots strengthen collective memory, while its branches reach toward a future free from violence.” She also pledged to continue the struggle against violence against women so that no more names would have to be added to the tree.

title: Kurdish women discuss shared political perspectives in Sulaymaniyah
content:
Representatives of women’s organizations from all four parts of Kurdistan gathered in Sulaymaniyah on Friday to discuss political developments in the region, national unity, and the future of the Kurdish women’s movement. Organized by the Platform for the National Unity of Kurdish Women, the meeting also serves as preparation for the third Conference on the National Unity of Kurdish Women. The central question is how women’s organizations can develop common positions amid political upheavals and strengthen their participation in decision-making processes.


In addition to representatives of women’s organizations, the gathering is attended by women politicians, activists, and other prominent figures from Kurdistan. In her opening speech, Şîrîn Tahir described the meeting as an important and decisive step in shaping the platform’s future work.


Tahir outlined three main priorities: assessing political developments in Kurdistan and the Middle East and their impact on women’s rights, critically reviewing the work carried out so far, and making organizational preparations for the third women’s conference. The aim, she said, was to bring Kurdish women’s collective strength and capacity for action into closer alignment across the borders of all four parts of Kurdistan.


https://rojnews.video/upload/videos/2026/11/w9XHyjDvqAHxEhNecCQM_20_5c6c0282c82d8f10f993c5ab1d3a7e1e_video_1080p_converted.mp4


Prioritizing national unity over party-political interests


During the first session, participants discussed the political challenges facing the Kurdish people and the impact of regional shifts in power on women’s rights and political status. It was emphasized that Kurdish women are internationally recognized as members of a single people, regardless of which part of Kurdistan they come from. “This shared identity must be matched by stronger political cooperation.”


The participants stressed that the national unity of Kurdish women must not be subordinated to party-political interests. Instead, they underlined, autonomous women’s organizing must take a leading role in developing shared political perspectives.


At the same time, participants warned against leaving the current transformations solely in the hands of existing, predominantly male-dominated power structures. They pointed put that, without women taking an active leadership role, there was a risk that political decisions would continue to be shaped by patriarchal attitudes. “The Kurds are not powerless in the face of the changes taking place in the Middle East. Through democratic struggle and collective political action, they can strengthen their rights and political status,” participants emphasized during the discussions.


Southern Kurdistan: Warning against political division


The political situation in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) featured prominently in the discussions. The participants strongly opposed any division of the region or weakening of its political status. In their assessment, such developments would primarily serve the interests of Turkey, Iran, and the Syrian transitional government, leaving the people of Southern Kurdistan more vulnerable to external interference.


The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) were therefore urged not to pursue their political differences at the expense of existing achievements. “Preserving the region’s political status must take precedence over party-political disputes,” the participants demanded.


The participants identified democracy, social unity, and political freedom as fundamental prerequisites for safeguarding these achievements. In this context, they also discussed a message from Abdullah Öcalan to the political forces of Southern Kurdistan, in which he had emphasized the formation of a democratic government and women’s participation in leadership as important steps toward overcoming the current situation.


The participants criticized the widespread exclusion of women from political decision-making processes. As a concrete initiative, they proposed forming a women’s delegation to hold talks with political parties and other political actors. The delegation, they said, would advocate for the protection of the political status of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq and the effective participation of women.


Rojava: Recognition of Kurdish rights in the integration process

title: Bakırhan: The goal of the peace process is democracy and equal citizenship
content:
Tuncer Bakırhan, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), criticized the Turkish government’s budget policies and outlined the objectives of the ongoing peace process at a meeting with civil society organizations in Mersin. The event was held as part of the DEM Party’s campaign, "Budget for Bread, Peace and Justice.” Bakırhan began by highlighting the social diversity of Mersin, where people of different backgrounds and faiths live together. He said the city, with its strong tradition of social and trade union struggles, could serve as an example for the whole of Turkey.


Budget not being used to meet the people’s needs


Referring to the budget deliberations, Bakırhan accused the government of spending tax revenues primarily on armaments, conflict-driven policies, interest payments, and companies with close ties to the government, rather than on the needs of the people. By contrast, he said, the DEM Party sought to prioritize the interests of workers, pensioners, women, young people, and low-income groups.


The DEM Party Co-Chair was particularly critical of rising child poverty, stating that many students could no longer afford their education expenses or were having to contribute to their families’ income. He described the rejection of proposals for free school meals in parliament as shameful: “One of the most shameful things in this world is being unable to provide even a single meal to children who go to school hungry.”


Bakırhan also addressed the current fund crisis. He demanded a full investigation into the irregularities, disclosure of who had received the funds, and reimbursement of the losses suffered by the affected workers, including interest.


“Peace is not a gift, but the result of social struggles”


Regarding the ongoing peace and democratic society process, Bakırhan stated: “Peace is not a gift, but the result of social struggles. The process must not be reduced solely to ending the armed conflict. What matters is establishing a democratic order in which Kurds, Alevis, and other ethnic and religious communities can freely express their identities and enjoy equal rights."


He appealed to political forces that have remained distant from the process, calling in particular on Yeni Party Chair Özgür Özel to reconsider his position. “A genuine and strong opposition is not one that runs away from peace, but one that moves toward it.”


Bakırhan also rejected the notion that the process would be complete once the armed conflict ended: “We will continue this struggle until democracy and equal citizenship are achieved. No one should therefore imagine any other outcome. Anyone who believes that the Kurds can be deceived at the negotiating table or turned into an instrument of another political agenda, or who thinks this is merely about a peace process, is mistaken. The goal is democracy and equal citizenship.”


Call for an end to government-appointed trusteeships


Bakırhan identified ending the state-imposed trusteeships of elected municipalities and safeguarding the rights of political prisoners as necessary steps. He called for the reinstatement of the dismissed co-mayors of Akdeniz district, the release of imprisoned politicians pending trial, and adequate medical care for prisoners suffering from illness. According to the DEM Party’s assessment, a peaceful resolution of the Kurdish question could save up to US$50 billion annually. The party states that these funds should benefit workers, pensioners, students, low-income families, and small business owners.


In closing, Bakırhan praised the public support for peace and democratization: “Repression and undemocratic practices come and go. But this hall, the will of the people gathered here, and their diversity will remain.”

author: Unknown
title: Resistance against solar power project in Arzoxlî on day 30
content:
The resistance against the construction of a solar power plant in Arzoxlî (Turkish: Kervanpınar), in the Sur district of Amed (Diyarbakır), has entered its second month. For 30 days, residents have been protesting against the energy project, which threatens their agricultural land and, consequently, their livelihoods. On Friday, numerous people once again gathered at the protest tent to continue the mobilization, which has been led primarily by women.


In addition to villagers, representatives of political parties, activists from the Peace Mothers Council, and members of civil society and environmental organizations took part in the protest. Chanting slogans including “We will prevail through resistance” and “Em axa xwe nadin” (“We will not give up our land”), the demonstrators marched from the village square to the protest tent.


“We will not bow to these companies”


Peace Mother Nezahat Teke, who also joined the protest, was particularly critical of the support the company was receiving from uniformed state personnel. “We will not bow to these companies. The women and men here must not be left alone in the rain,” Teke declared. She said the company could rely on military support in carrying out its activities. “This is not a matter for the soldiers, but for the company owner. Yet soldiers and police are supporting him. We mothers will resist until the end.”


Villager Güler Çiftçi also reaffirmed that the residents would not give up despite increasingly difficult weather conditions. “We wish the whole world had come out to support us today. We are fighting for our own land and our own water, through rain and drought, enduring hardship and difficult conditions. We will not surrender our land to anyone.”


Çiftçi accused the state security forces of siding with the company, saying: “The company has the state behind it. We do not want to see soldiers and the gendarmerie as our adversaries. We wish they would stand behind us. But unfortunately, today they are standing behind the company rather than us.” Çiftçi stressed that residents would continue to defend their living environment and the future of their children.


“Women are defending their livelihoods”


Halide Türkoğlu, spokesperson for the Women’s Council of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), praised the leading role of women in the resistance in Arzoxlî. Their struggle, she said, was directed not merely against a single construction project, but against the loss of the economic and ecological foundations of village life.


“The villagers’ resistance began under the leadership of women. Because when women defend their land, they are also defending their livelihoods and the future of their children,” Türkoğlu stated.


She stated that the government has deployed gendarmerie forces to surround the protest site rather than taking the concerns of the people seriously.


Türkoğlu criticized the fact that solar and geothermal energy projects, as well as mining operations, were threatening the livelihoods of rural communities in numerous regions of Kurdistan.


“While the alliance between capital and the government brings poverty into our lives, our natural environment is being destroyed day by day. Defending natural habitats is also a matter of fundamental rights: Our right to exist encompasses our identity, our language, and our natural environment. If anyone tries to take these away from us, we will never surrender them,” the DEM Party politician said.

author: Daron Letts
title: Lack of security guard rules could expose GN, professor says
content:
The Government of Nunavut could be sued if unregulated private security guards in the territory break the law, says a criminologist, who studies surveillance and security regulation.


That’s because Nunavut has no legislation that governs the training and certification of security guards.


“What are they waiting for? I don’t understand the rationale for not pursuing it and passing it into law,” University of Windsor professor Randy Lippert said in a phone interview.


The government does not appear to share that sense of urgency.


It has received calls to enact regulation during sessions of the legislative assembly in 2018, 2023 and 2025.


The latest call for regulation came from current Justice Minister George Hickes during the winter 2025 sitting of the legislative assembly, about 10 months before he joined cabinet.


He also highlighted the need for Nunavummiut to be hired in security roles.


“I want to encourage all entities of the government to consider working together on setting the stage of bringing forward legislation in the next government,” Hickes said as a regular MLA on Feb. 26, 2025, about nine months before he became a cabinet minister.


Last week, however, he declined to comment on the issue.


Justice Department spokesperson Stephen Shaddock said in an email earlier this month that the department

“is monitoring regulatory approaches in other Canadian jurisdictions.”


“However, there is no specific timeline for considering similar legislation in Nunavut.”


The Northwest Territories is the only other jurisdiction in Canada that does not regulate the private security industry.


But in Ontario, for example, the Private Security and Investigative Services Act requires companies to ensure guards have and maintain a valid agency licence. If security guards employed by the agency are charged for working without a valid licence, their employer may also face charges.


The licencing process includes a criminal records check and completion of mandatory basic training, which is at least 40 hours.


Ontario’s law allows people to submit complaints in instances where they believe a guard violated the act. The solicitor general’s office reviews those complaints.


Iqaluit’s Northern store recently

ramped up

 its security to include guards in tactical uniforms equipped with body cameras and what appear to be retractable batons.


The North West Co., the Winnipeg-based parent company of Northern, contracts the guards through Iqaluit-based Canadian Arctic Protective Services.


In an email earlier this month, the security company’s regional director, Paul Hunter,

 

declined to say whether the device that the guards carry is a baton.


A supervisor with Canadian Arctic Protective Services stands at the exit of Iqaluit’s Northern store with a body-worn camera in October. A University of Windsor professor warns the Government of Nunavut could be civilly liable if a security guard breaks the law because the territory is one of two Canadian jurisdictions without a law regulating the private security industry. (File phot Daron Letts)


Retractable batons and other instruments that may be used as weapons are regulated under the Criminal Code, said Shaddock.


“Organizations should ensure that equipment carried by employees complies with the law, as non-compliance may result in criminal charges and potential civil liability,” he said.


Lippert said that liability could extend to the government itself.


“If something bad happens, it seems like a lot of people are going to get sued, and it may well include the government,” he said.


When asked about Lippert’s warning, the Justice Department’s spokesperson said the department would not comment on “a hypothetical scenario.”


“In all instances where the Government of Nunavut is served with a lawsuit, the government will review the matter on its merits and respond accordingly,” Shaddock said in an email.

author: Jaharra Anglin Stubbs
title: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Unionize After Years of Fighting for Fair Pay
content:
On October 23, 2026, the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association was formally and voluntarily recognized as the official collective bargaining representative for the team’s cheer squad. For the first time in the NFL since the Buffalo Jills, an NFL cheer squad successfully unionized, highlighting the need for better protections for cheer team members.

For decades, the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders have been among the most recognizable cheerleading squads in professional sports. Despite their prominence and contributions to the team’s brand, members have historically received low wages for demanding work. Before a 400% pay increase for the 2025 season, some veteran cheerleaders reported earning just $15 per hour, in addition to flat fees for games and appearances. Even after the raise, questions about benefits and workplace protections remain.

The pay disparity became particularly visible in 2018, in afederal fair-wage lawsuit filed by Erica Wilkins, a former cheerleader. Wilkins claimed she earned no more than $16,516 in any year of her employment, while the team’s male mascot, Rowdy, earned approximately $65,000 annually. She also alleged that cheerleaders were not compensated for all hours worked, including rehearsals, training, and promotional activities. The lawsuit highlighted the significant pay disparities and lack of labor protections facing women in professional sports.

Although the Cowboys arevalued at $17B, making them the most valuable NFL brand, they were evidently more comfortable paying their male athletes fairly until recently. As Kelli Fingall, the cheer squad director, said, the raise to $75 was “60-plus years long overdue,” given the cheer team’s proven athleticism, ethics, and overall value to the brand and the NFL franchise, especially since it remains “one of the most talented dancers worldwide.”

Even though the Dallas Cowboys cheer team is a successful example of change, we must acknowledge that toxic, systemic gender inequity across the broader NFL cheer teams has long shaped cheerleading’s professional place in the NFL. In 1995, after the National Labor Relations Board ruled that the cheer team, the Buffalo Jills, could unionize, the squad was disbanded in 2014 due to severe wage violations, sexual misconduct, mistreatment, and other heinous violations.

Beyond the attempt to unionize, individual members across NFL cheer squads, such as Lacy Thibodeaux,sued their employers for violating numerous state labor and minimum wage laws. These instances of injustice show that cheerleading talent has been reduced to a casual skill rather than to dedicated competitive professional athleticism that deserves compensation.

Like all women, NFL cheerleaders deserve fair compensation for their work and should not be asked to work long hours without healthcare or enough to meet a standard of living. Although the Cowboys have acknowledged the cheer team’s unionization, the decision did not come from the goodness of their hearts; rather, it was a reaction to theNetflix documentary and the team’s threats to strike, which revealed injustices behind the curtain.

Union recognition is an important step toward that goal, but the NFL and its franchises must do more to ensure that fair treatment is standard across professional cheerleading.

author: Unknown
title: Илья Шакурский и «Цена свободы»
content:
«Цену свободы» фигурант пыточного «дела Сети» Илья Шакурский написал в сентябре 2025 года. Это текст о том, что на самом деле стоит за сухими строчками обвинения: пыльные обочины трасс, панк-гиги, споры о будущем, тишина зимнего леса и внутренняя свобода, которую невозможно запереть в бетонной клетушке.

Это место называется «следственные кабинеты». Я бываю здесь довольно часто.

Сижу в клетушке посередине комнаты, рисую что-нибудь на железном столике перед собой или просто смотрю в окно. Как правило, всегда в ожидании адвокатов, следователей, оперов или психологов. По большей части мне не нравится ходить сюда, особенно в кабинеты, находящиеся на левой стороне.

Окна здесь выходят не на волю, а на старый корпус СИЗО. Видны лишь арестанты в форточках, забирающие «дорогу» (верёвку с привязанным носком), мелькающие телевизоры в камерах и часть прогулочных двориков. Грустно… К тому же в кабинеты на левой стороне почти не пускают защитников. Здесь я могу встретить только местное начальство, приезжих оперов или казённые комиссии. Я никогда не знаю, кто сейчас войдёт в кабинет, но всегда испытываю волнение, так как ничего хорошего от моего присутствия на этой стороне следственных кабинетов не ожидаю.

В этот раз зашёл совершенно незнакомый мне человек. Рубашка, ветровка, брюки, аккуратная стрижка, красивые часы, чёрная кожаная папка. Всё ясно — следователь. Что ж, начинается игра. Он пришёл провести опрос по поводу моего заявления о применении ко мне пыток током. Его задача — минимизировать подробности, запугать опрашиваемого, скрыть факты за ненужными обстоятельствами, максимально постараться уличить заявителя во лжи. Моя — дополнять, исправлять, требовать записывать дословно и убирать то, чего я не говорил. Такое противостояние. Нюансы подобных встреч познаёшь лишь с опытом, но чаще всего такие юридические противоборства заканчиваются не в пользу опрашиваемого. В эти моменты особенно осознаёшь своё одиночество в борьбе с бетонной системой, которая нагло и лицемерно защищает себя от воздействия правды.

За всё время нашей встречи следователь, кажется, ни разу не посмотрел мне в глаза. Он уткнулся в заполняемый бланк и монотонно задавал вопросы, лишь нервно вздыхая при моих уточнениях и замечаниях. И только в самом конце встречи передо мной вдруг появился человек. Я увидел перед собой живое лицо, а не должностного робота. Я поймал на себе взгляд человека, способного видеть во мне живое существо, которое тоже может мыслить, чувствовать и говорить не только под запись. Меня ошарашил его вопрос:

Этого вопроса нет в перечне его документов — это личный интерес, вызванный его собственными мотивами.

Какими? Может, он просто хочет пополнить свою копилку историей с работы, чтобы за ужином было что рассказать жене на вопрос: «Дорогой, как дела на работе?» Или же он искренне пытался понять мой выбор — то, что движет мной и даёт смелости в подробностях рассказывать ему о чекистских методах пыток? Но от его вопроса веяло какой-то предсмертностью. Казалось, будто он уже знал, что я обречён, и перед моей участью решил узнать у меня о чём-то неофициальном, ценностно-философском. «Стоило ли оно того?» — вопрос, знаменующий некий финал, конец истории, где главному герою предстоит осознать ценность пройденного пути.

В кинематографе существует сюжетный приём, когда история начинается с финальной сцены. Итог известен, но что-то заставляет нас вернуться обратно, ибо только в развитии всей истории можно найти ответы.

«Стоило ли оно того?» — вопрос повисает в кабинетной тишине. Камера застывает крупным планом на лице главного героя, и из темноты погасшего экрана плавно всплывает основная часть истории, которая и привела его в это помещение.

«Когда одинокий рассвет нагло лезет в окно — не гони его…»

Интенсивный панк-рок играет в наушниках. Солнце на закате выплёскивает свои последние яркие лучи. Свет из щелей облаков обливает собой стены лесов. Впереди — неизвестность. Под ногами пыльный путь бесконечных обочин. Легковушки, фуры, «газели» и автобусы. Уроды сигналят и тычут в меня средний палец, выглядывая из-за руля. Девчонки улыбаются, но боятся остановиться. На примятой придорожной пылью траве валяются груды мусора.

Меняются цифры на электронных стендах с ценами на бензин у заправок. От маленьких кафе пахнет шашлыком и выпечкой. За спиной большой рюкзак. Музыка придаёт сил и бодрости. Большой палец поднят вверх. Пролетающие машины обдают ветерком. Я знаю, что скоро кто-то остановится. Так бывает всегда. Под Нижним Новгородом у старой …

author: CMI Argentina
title: El Senado sancionó por unanimidad la Ley de Discapacidad
content:
El Senado dio sanción definitiva a la ley de discapacidad con 71 votos a favor y ninguno en contra y a 40 días del vencimiento de la ley de emergencia que rige hasta el 31 de diciembre.


El texto acordado en Diputados y aprobado sin cambios en Senadores mantiene en forma permanente varios puntos de esa ley. Amplía la posibilidad de acceder a pensiones a las personas imposibilitadas de trabajar, fija que las pensiones por discapacidad serán compatibles con un trabajo formal aunque no se podrán tener ingresos superiores a dos salarios mínimos teniendo en cuenta el ingreso individual y no del grupo familiar. Además se mantiene el arancel único universal de prestaciones que será actualizado por el índice de movilidad jubilatoria.


La nueva ley también obliga a la Agencia Nacional de Discapacidad a pagar las deudas con prestadores en un plazo máximo de 90 días.


La senadora de Unión por la Patria, Florencia López, dijo que se logró porque se le pudo torcer el brazo al gobierno.


“Una plaza llena de familias y de personas con discapacidad, bastones blancos, sillas de rueda, con medicación, le torció el brazo al gobierno nacional”, remarcó. Y agregó: fue como David y Goliath, los más débiles, los más humildes, los más vulnerables, le torcieron el brazo al gobierno.


El debate en el Senado fue acompañado afuera del Congreso por una movilización de familiares, organizaciones y prestadores.


“Esta ley va a permitir dar los instrumentos, los elementos para que realmente podamos avanzar en las respuestas que las personas con discapacidad necesitan” dijo Pablo Molero, coordinador del Foro Permanente de Discapacidad.


Además agregó: “Ahora viene otra lucha, que es la del presupuesto 2027, que la semana que viene se va a tratar en diputados”.


Molero remarcó que es muy necesario que haya partidas presupuestarias para dar respuestas a los reclamos del sector sin que el Ejecutivo defina el futuro de las prestaciones.


El Senado también sancionó la denominada Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada manteniendo los límites a la extranjerización fijados en la Ley de Tierras y el capítulo que facilita los desalojos de inquilinos y de comunidades indígenas y campesinas.


También se aprobó que se trate la semana que viene la prórroga del Estatuto del Periodista reclamada por los gremios de prensa de todo el país y que se reúna un plenario de comisiones para avanzar con el proyecto de ley de Prevención de Ludopatía y Regulación de las Apuestas Online que tiene media sanción de Diputados.
