author: Aaron Ernest Cruz
title: Lakbayan Southern Tagalog children finally released
content:
Released Lakbayani children. (Photo from Salinlahi Facebook page)

The children were denied their rights to counsel.

The 15 minors arrested in barangay Sucat, Muntinlupa City on November 15 have been released four days later (November 19).

This follows the order issued by the Muntinlupa City Office of the Prosecutor on November 18 for the release of all those arrested.

The minors aged 14 to 17 were part of the Lakbayan Southern Tagalog that started their march from the University of the Philippines Los Baños on November 12 to join the protest on the arrival of US President Donald Trump.

The 15 minors were the last to be released from being held in Bahay Pag-asa in Muntinlupa City. There were a total of 20 minors among the participants of Lakbayan Southern Tagalog, who were arrested on November 15 during the police’s violent dispersal in barangay Sucat.

The five minors aged 15 below were already released on November 17 as they were found to have no criminal liability.

The more than 200 adults who were part of the Lakbayan were earlier released on the night of November 18.

This contradicted the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) claim on November 18, that all 236 delegates of Southern Tagalog were released. The 15 minors were only released in the afternoon of November 19.

“Despite days of delaying tactics and bureaucratic processes that kept the minors detained for four days after illegal arrest and parents waiting in distress – returning everyday and waiting outside overnight – with the pressure of child rights advocates, lawyers, and church organizations, the children are now free,” Salinlahi Alliance for Children’s Concerns said.

“As we celebrate this collective victory, we also continue to demand for the immediate release of the nine illegally arrested and detained protesters at the Liwasang Bonifacio last November 15. One of them is a minor and currently remains at the Manila Youth Reception Center (MYRC),” the group said in their social media page.

According to Salinlahi, the children were denied their rights to counsel as the Bahay Pag-asa Head blocked the lawyers and paralegals from talking to them.

Salinlahi stressed that these children suffered police brutality and their longer detention only makes their violations of their rights extend much further.

“Bahay Pag-asa is mandated to protect and rehabilitate children—not become an instrument for prolonging their detention and suppressing their rights,” Salinlahi said in a statement.

For the National Union of People’s Lawyer (NUPL) the Philippine National Police (PNP) must be held accountable for their brutality against activists who are only exercising their right to protest. “These findings expose the fundamental weakness of the PNP’s case. Having arrested and charged hundreds of individuals in one sweeping operation, the police could not even sufficiently distinguish the alleged acts of one respondent from another.”

Meanwhile, three students of the University of Makati (UMak) were also released on November 19.

The Taguig City Prosecutor’s Office dismissed the cases that were filed against the students. These are alarm and scandal under Article 155 of the Revised Penal Code and resistance and disobedience to an agent of a person in authority under Article 151 of the same code.

The Taguig City Prosecutor’s Office said in its resolution, “The evidence on record shows that the actions of (three students), were made specifically to voice out certain political and social grievances and not the purpose of causing general disturbance or public disorder.”

Lawyer Jose Topacio of the Alliance of Nationalist and Genuine Labor Organizations-Kilusang Mayo Uno (ANGLO-KMU) meanwhile pointed out that the three students were released only after six days of continuous confinement at the Taguig City Police Station, way past the time periods prescribed by Article 125 of the Revised Penal Code.

“We are also alarmed at the brazen displays of intimidation by the police, where the detainees were repeatedly told that the police intended to hold them for six days, that detailed files about them were being compiled since the Grand Hyatt protest on 10 September, and that their arrest should serve as a ‘lesson’ to them,” Topacio told Bulatlat in a message.

Topacio also noted how Taguig City police shouted at the visiting relatives of the students and repeatedly asked to move away from the station to other parts of the Taguig City Hall complex while conferring with counsel …

author: Esperanza
title: Danzar con la cámara: “A 26 pixeles de distancia” llega al 7º FestivalPICNIC de Valdivia
content:
Hacer de la boca una escena expandida por la medialidad es uno de los imaginarios posibles de Tecnocorporeidades, proyecto de creación artística liderado por Nirvana Sepúlveda y Loreto García, quienes trabajan la relación cuerpo-tecnología combinando danza contemporánea, performance y proyección en tiempo real. “No es nuestro propósito instalar un mensaje de cómo nos relacionamos con la tecnología, sino más bien provocar en torno a esta relación”.


Por Morín Ortiz.


Un proyector, una pantalla, un notebook, tres cámaras web, un micrófono, un foco led, dos aros de luz y tres cuerpos que producen movimientos y voces expandidas, componen el universo de “A 26 pixeles de distancia”. Obra de danza contemporánea de Tecnocorporeidades que, en 40 minutos, “produce ciberespacios eróticos, lúgubres y lúdicos, donde el cuerpo físico se disuelve en un cuerpo digitalizado que desborda los límites de lo real”, dice la sinopsis de esta obra para mayores de 18 años. 


Dirigida por Nirvana Sepúlveda y Loreto García, quienes se conocieron en el Centro de Danza Espiral para luego seguir su formación en danza en la Academia de Humanismo Cristiano, en Santiago. Desde entonces, se sintieron atraídas. Por el afán de investigar de Loreto García, quien además es socióloga, y por la desinhibida creatividad de Nirvana Sepúlveda, quien danza desde pequeña y practica burlesque. Entonces comenzaron a crear en contextos sociales marcados por las tomas feministas, la revuelta social chilena y la pandemia. Hoy la tecnología media la mayor parte del tiempo esta relación creativa y afectiva, porque Loreto vive en Temuco y Nirvana en Barcelona.


Pero el nacimiento de esta experimentación escénica tuvo lugar en Casa Varas de Temuco el año 2021, y luego en el centro cultural Ceina de Santiago, donde las investigaciones en torno a la proyección de danza en tiempo real devinieron en una performance, que hoy se convirtió en la primera de tres escenas que componen la obra. Recuerdan que por estos años las habitaban reflexiones pandémicas del cómo hacer contacto e insistir en el encuentro pese a las pantallas. “La danza, que piensa el cuerpo, tiene que pensar en este cuerpo que ya no es solo físico, sino que está expandido en múltiples redes imaginarias y virtuales”, señala Nirvana.


El nombre de “A 26 pixeles de distancia” es una cita del texto “Realidad virtual” del libro “Enciclopedia del amor en los tiempos de porno” (Editorial Cuarto Propio, 2014) de Lucía Egaña Rojas y Josefa Ruiz-Tagle. Esta y las oraciones finales “No soy real. Ya no me queda nada de humanidad, solo el deseo”, hicieron eco en Tecnocorporeidades por propiciar una visión expandida del cuerpo.


“Desarrollamos interacciones del cuerpo con la imagen desde una propuesta

cyborg

, que entiende el cuerpo como una figura híbrida que desdibuja los límites entre lo humano y lo más que humano y crea alianzas políticas basadas en el deseo por lo otro», comparte Loreto.


Más que una búsqueda discursiva, este trabajo escénico explora las operaciones técnicas mediante las cuales “producimos afectos y efectos con la tecnología. Un lugar experimental a partir de la relación cotidiana que tenemos con ella”. Proceso que les llevó a pensar “en el binarismo como mecanismos de producción de subjetividades y desde ese lugar, el proyecto Tecnocorporeidades nos permite construir otros imaginarios en torno a la sexualidad, al género, a las posibilidades que tiene un cuerpo”.


El equipo de “A 26 pixeles de distancia” lo componen Nirvana Sepúlveda y Loreto García en la dirección e interpretación, Yoko Pérez y Tiwa Labastida también como intérpretes, Nicolette Michael en diseño integral e iluminación, Samuel Martínez en asistencia técnica e iluminación, Carlos Contreras como realizador audiovisual y fotógrafo, Álvaro Núñez en composición musical, Matías Vergara en operación técnica, Lukas Julio en producción y Morín Ortiz en comunicaciones.


Con casi una decena de presentaciones autogestionadas en Santiago, Temuco y Collipulli


Tecnocorporeidades está en pleno desarrollo de un proyecto de Circulación Nacional financiado por el Fondo Nacional de Fomento y Desarrollo de las Artes Escénicas, convocatoria 2026. Con el que se presentaron en el Festival LOFT de Concepción y les tendrá en el Festival PICNIC de Valdivia y en la Carpa Trashumantes en Temuco.


Con un espacio de formación y una exhibición, llegarán hasta el 7º Festival PICNIC del Centro Cultural Bailarines de los Ríos, el jueves 19 de noviembre …

author: Jacob Hoffman-Andrews
title: Outage Chaos: Who Turned Off All The Computer?
content:
It's been a tough couple of weeks for anyone trying to

use email

,

fly

,

spend money

,

use an Apple device

*, or do

signals intelligence

. Technical service outages are nothing new, but why do so many big ones seem to be happening all at once? Are hackers, AI, and international conflicts to blame? And what can we do about it?


Since most service interruptions don't make the news, it's hard to get a baseline on how often we see them happen normally. But after a major incident like the

Microsoft cloud outage on November 12

, any smaller disruption is more likely to become a story as part of a pattern instead of an isolated incident. We would have heard plenty about the 

Air Traffic Control problems

 anyway, but the November 18 disruption to the

PlayStation Network

 might have gotten less attention. There might appear to be a spike or an upward trend in outages, but we can't easily verify that, and the increased coverage will tend to make it seem more significant and interconnected than it necessarily is regardless.


One boring reason we might see an uptick in problems right now is the date on the calendar. With Thanksgiving travel, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Giving Tuesday, and Surveillance Sunday (we assume) all coming up, organizations often schedule major system updates for the first three weeks of November. This helps them prepare for holiday traffic, and lets them shift the outage risk to the time before those dates when they may consider it far more important to maintain reliable service.


While none of these particular outages have yet been directly attributed to AI (

or to malicious hackers

), bank CEOs and the NSA briefed congress and

reportedly attributed

 at least some of them to rushed attempts to patch vulnerabilities found by AI. That’s understandable: all software updates carry risk, and companies and governments are having to deploy more updates, and faster, than they’ve ever needed to before. Some of those updates are to important infrastructure, where an outage would be very disruptive, but the impact of leaving vulnerabilities unpatched would be even worse.


Vulnerabilities are a type of software bug that affects security. Once a vulnerability is found in a given piece of software and disclosed, typically the software maker will release a patch fixing that vulnerability. That’s why so many update notes say things like “performance improvements and security fixes”

—

 the security fixes are patches to vulnerabilities.


Companies and governments that run infrastructure face a challenging tradeoff: deploy patches quickly or slowly and cautiously? Patching quickly is important to keep systems secure. But every software update runs a risk: any change to a deployed system can have unintended consequences that snowball into a disastrous outage.


This exacerbates a much deeper problem long discussed in the engineering culture of many, if not most organizations. Keeping networks, servers, and applications not just secure but resilient in the face of patches, reboots, and capacity changes requires an investment in staff, time, hardware, and processes for frequent maintenance, redundant systems, realistic staging environments, automated rollbacks, monitoring, and pre-deployment testing. These investments are rarely as attractive to decision

-

makers as a new product or feature, or at times, sadly, as layoffs.


This should come as no surprise when we think of our apps, web sites, airlines

,

 and bank cards as supported by electronic infrastructure. As in the more visible physical world, maintenance can only be deferred for so long before the costs become immediate and dramatic. We accept the cost of an occasional short term bridge closure to reduce the risk of a bridge collapse, and highway departments schedule road work nearly every night of the year to repair and prevent the worst potholes.


When this kind of work is endlessly deferred in the world of software, we speak of

technical

 debt

:

issues we already know about that aren't causing a big enough problem right now to divert us from other work, but that, if left unaddressed, can easily multiply and interact to cause outages or other complications

.

 This can show up as routine steps that have to be done by hand instead of automatically on a schedule, a programmer's shortcut that works well in one specific situation but is more fragile in general, an operating system six months (or years) overdue for a reboot, or a …

author: Sara Connors
title: Yukon court dismisses wrongful death lawsuit against Whitehorse shelter operator
content:
The Supreme Court of Yukon has dismissed a wrongful death lawsuit against the operator of the Whitehorse emergency shelter.

Chief Justice Suzanne Duncan said in a Nov. 6 decision that the lawsuit was brought after the one-year limitation period under the Yukon’s Fatal Accidents Act.

Josephine Hager, 38, a Selkirk First Nation citizen, died at the shelter on Feb. 1, 2023. Her father, Dale Joe, filed the lawsuit last October.

An inquest in April 2024 heard that Hager, who lived in a supportive housing unit at the shelter, died from a lethal mix of morphine and alcohol.

The lawsuit claims Connective, the non-profit organization operating the shelter, and five unnamed staff members were negligent in Hager’s death.

However, Connective argued in an application that Joe, who filed the suit more than two years after his daughter’s death, missed the one-year deadline under the act.

According to the decision, Joe said he wasn’t aware of the circumstances surrounding his daughter’s death and its potential wrongful nature until shortly after the 2024 inquest, more than a year after she died.

The decision also notes that his mother and brother died within a year of each other, adding to his grief.

An affidavit from Selkirk Elder and former chief Lucy McGuinty also states that traditional Northern Tutchone laws prevent those who follow them from interfering with matters of the deceased until a headstone potlatch is held, which she said typically takes one to two years.

The decision also notes that other jurisdictions, such as Alberta and Saskatchewan, give courts some discretion to consider personal circumstances.

Connective, meanwhile, argued that the act stipulates that the limitation period begins on the date of death, regardless of a plaintiff’s knowledge of the matter.

The organization also argued that even if Joe’s argument were allowed to proceed, the lawsuit was still filed more than a year after he became aware of the circumstances surrounding his daughter’s death.

The organization further contended that Indigenous customs or traditions provide no legal basis to extend or eliminate limitation periods.

It also noted that a headstone potlatch had not yet been held for Hager or Joe’s brother, which it said contradicts McGuinty’s statement that cultural tradition requires a headstone potlatch before the deceased’s affairs may be addressed.

Duncan said there was merit to Joe’s argument that the one-year limitation could begin when he became aware of the circumstances surrounding his daughter’s death.

However, she found that nothing in Yukon’s act allows a plaintiff’s personal circumstances to be considered grounds for an extension.

Duncan granted Connective’s application, effectively dismissing the lawsuit.

A spokesperson for Connective said in an email statement to APTN News that it was aware of the dismissal but had no comment.

Father disappointed lawsuit dismissed

Mark Wallace, Joe’s lawyer, said his client filed the lawsuit seeking justice for his daughter and was disappointed it was dismissed.

“(Joe) had really hoped that Justice Duncan would agree and let this go forward,” he said, noting his client was “quite upset by it.”

Wallace acknowledged that they knew there was a “reasonable chance” Connective would move to strike the lawsuit based on the limitation period, but said they hoped Duncan would agree with their arguments.

However, he said he didn’t disagree with the decision and that Joe wouldn’t be appealing.

“I think her interpretation of the law is correct,” he said.

Wallace said that while the outcome wasn’t what they wanted, Joe is hopeful the lawsuit will help raise awareness of the act’s limitation period for people in similar situations who might not be aware of it.

He also said he would like to see more flexibility under the act to account for personal circumstances, such as adopting wording similar to that in other jurisdictions.

The lawsuit is the 4th filed in recent years involving deaths at the shelter.

Two were settled last year, while another is still before the courts.

Sara Connors is originally from Nova Scotia and has a journalism degree from the University of King’s College in Halifax. After graduation she worked in South Korea for two years as an English language teacher and freelance journalist. After she returned home in 2019 she worked behind the scenes at CTV Atlantic in Halifax before joining APTN's Yukon bureau in July 2020.

author: Fraser Needham
title: Outgoing Green Party leader says Carney is the most ‘opaque, unaccountable person in politics’
content:
Elizabeth May says Prime Minister Mark Carney is perhaps the most challenging party leader she has had to work with in more than four decades in politics.


“Accountability is really important and Mr. Carney is the most opaque, unaccountable person in politics I think I have ever seen,” the Green Party MP said.


May stepped down as Green Party leader earlier this month, making way for former Kitchener, Ontario MP Mike Morrice to take over the party’s reins.


She will continue on as the MP for the riding of Saanich-Gulf Islands in British Columbia.


One of the reasons May voted in favour of the 2025 budget was Carney’s pledge to respect Canada’s Paris commitments on climate change.


With the Liberal government’s continued backing of oil and gas projects, it is now highly unlikely Canada will meet these commitments.


Carney, a former governor of both the Bank of Canada and Bank of England, has often been touted as the right leader at the right time due to the country’s ongoing trade issues with the Trump administration in the U.S.


However, May said his credentials may not be as suitable as they seem.


“He comes with a very impressive resume and a lot of people assume he’s an economist and a banker,” she said. “He’s really a banker. Economists are capable of saying let’s take a project like pipelines and before we throw billions of public dollars at it, can we do a cost/benefit analysis?


“Is there a market for diluted bitumen in other countries around the world? Is there a reason we want to violate Indigenous rights and bulldoze these things through with bills like C-5 and C-39? He’s not held to account very much.”


In spite of it all, Carney and the Liberals continue to ride high in the polls. May has a theory of why this is the case.


“It’s like when you are on a highway and all the traffic slows down because you are rubbernecking an accident over there. If we keep our eyes on the road in Canada, we can see some flaws with Mr. Carney but if we’re rubbernecking and looking at, ‘Oh my God, the White House,’ it’s really easy for Mr. Carney not to be held to the same standards that previous prime minsters would have been for their actions.”


‘There needs to be a guarantee that the accountability does fall with the government,’ says AMC Grand Chief Kyra Wilson. Photo: Todd Lamirande/APTN.


First Nations water


The head of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs says the organization has a number of issues with the Carney government’s First Nations Clean Water Act (Bill C-37) including the fact that it does not include access to clean drinking water as a human right.


“There needs to be a guarantee that the accountability does fall with the government,” Grand Chief Kyra Wilson said. “We always need to ensure that government is upholding the treaties. First Nations signed treaties with the Crown. It’s Canada’s duty and obligation to uphold those treaties. So, when we’re talking about safe drinking it’s not up to First Nations people to prove the case. It’s Canada’s obligation to uphold all of that.”


Wilson was in Ottawa this week to serve as witness before the House of Commons Indigenous and Northern Affairs Committee on Bill C-37.


She also said AMC takes issue with the fact the legislation was drafted without sufficient consultation from First Nations.


Arctic drilling


The minister of Northern and Arctic Affairs said oil and gas exploration off the coast of the Arctic will not move forward without the necessary consultation with Inuit organizations and environmental safeguards.


“We will be working hand-in-hand with the Indigenous groups in the north to understand whether we should move the Tariuq Accord (2023 co-management and revenue-sharing agreement for offshore petroleum resources signed between Canada, Inuvialuit Corporation and the Government of the Northwest Territories) forward,” Rebecca Chartrand said. “The governance is there, there’s still much work to do on making decisions.


“So, the decisions will rest on whether we have sound environmental assessments ensuring that we’re protecting the marine ecosystems and this comes directly from the early engagement meetings that I have held with the leadership in the north.”


The 2026 federal budget pledges $11 million over four years to support Arctic offshore governance which has led some to question whether or not the Carney government is going to lift the moratorium on offshore oil and gas activity signed between the previous Trudeau government and …

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Majority of reported ‘serious’ injuries to Indigenous children in Manitoba tied to sexual assault
content:
Warning: this story discusses child abuse and suicide


Manitoba’s youth advocate says more than half of serious injury reports involving kids are linked to sexual assault, and that 71 per cent of victims are Indigenous children.


“It’s pretty telling,” said Sherry Gott, the executive director of

Manitoba Advocate for Children and Youth (MACY)

. “The numbers are pretty high, 53 per cent of our reports are a result of sexual assault or sexual exploitation, and the majority of those are Indigenous children.”


MACY is a non-partisan advocacy organization funded by the provincial government.


Alongside investigative work, it provides advocacy and social services to youth and families, which can result in safety plans, placements and post-release mental health and addictions support for children and young adults (aged 18 to 20).


Since 2000, her office has published annual reports which summarize trends, data and updates with respect to youth in Manitoba, as well as the organization’s recommendations to the province.


In 2023, the organization created its Serious Injuries Reviews and Investigations program, in response to a recommendation from the provincial

Phoenix Sinclair Inquiry

, created to examine the circumstances surrounding the neglect, physical abuse and

eventual murder

 of the five-year-old girl in Fisher River Cree Nation almost a decade prior.


The inquiry resulted in amendments to provincial law, which aim to improve child welfare and investigations surrounding children both in and out of foster care.


According to the report, MACY received 506 referrals from April 2025 to March 2026. Only 300 of the referrals were able to be reviewed, according to the legal definition of a serious injury, according to the report. Five of the reviews were closed before completion because the youth died.


The report noted that the number of referrals received by MACY has been steadily growing over the last three years. The 2023-2024 report recorded 184, and 2024-2025 recorded 273.


Because of the demand, only 135 of the 300 referrals legally eligible for review have ended with complete serious injury reports, as of writing. Only 99 were assessed for potential investigation, and 36 of those assessments were reviewed further.


Just one case is currently being investigated.


Gott told APTN News that MACY doesn’t have the resources to keep up with the demand.


“There is a backlog, and we’ve actually redeployed some of our staff [from other departments] to do the work,” she said.


According to MACY, 53 per cent (71/135) of the injuries that received a report were a result of sexual assault, while 55 per cent of secondary injuries were also linked to the same cause.


Additionally, 25 per cent of cases involved drugs or alcohol; 22 per cent were linked to self-harm or attempted suicide; 20 per cent were bodily injuries, such as broken or fractured bones; 19 per cent involved gunshot or stab wounds; 15 per cent were head injuries; and accidental and “severe neglect” cases accounted for four per cent each.


Forty per cent of the injuries resulted in a hospital visit, and 35 per cent “were deemed life-threatening,” the annual report continued, and 71 per cent of all cases involved a youth who was First Nations, Inuit or Métis.


The report stated that, based on MACY’s data, 62 per cent of kids involved in serious injury reports have “experienced victimization in their lives.


“This fact alone highlights the importance of a targeted response and intervention by social services following any form of child victimization,” the report continued.


Additionally, “60 per cent experienced mental health concerns that were co-occurring, or combined with, substance use and suicidality.”


Gott recommended that the province should also pay attention to how many of the serious injuries occurred to a child in care.


“Either at the hands of caregivers, or foster parents, or their own families, so we need to highlight that quickly and implement some sort of strategy to support those children,” she said.


MACY also reviews and investigates the deaths of children, based on information received from the

Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME)

 every time a death occurs.


In 2025-26, the OCME recorded 238 official child deaths; 195 of which involved children 17 and younger, and 43 involved young adults (18 to 20).


Almost half of the deaths were natural (44 per cent), and 36 per cent were undetermined. In most cases, the …

author: The Canadian Press
title: Gitxsan Huwilp Government in B.C. wants train hauling stopped in territory after latest derailment
content:
The

Gitxsan Huwilp Government

 in British Columbia said lives and food security are at risk after two recent rail accidents on the 103-year-old track along the Skeena River.


The First Nation said in a statement that the latest derailment has reignited its call for the “immediate stop to all train hauling” in its traditional territories and fishing waterways, calling the practice dangerous.


Several railcars jumped the tracks on Tuesday, spilling diesel and sending some cars loaded with forest products into the Skeena River about 15 kilometres west of Terrace.


CN Rail announced the track had been repaired and train traffic resumed on Thursday, while the two crew members who were injured in the derailment have been released from hospital.


The company said environmental protection measures are in place in the river and specialized environmental response teams remain at the site, working to contain and recover spilled diesel fuel and removing derailed equipment.


The First Nation said it is the second such incident in eight months, after a mudslide derailed grain cars travelling along the river south of Prince Rupert in March, resulting in a spill of nearly 8,000 litres of diesel.


Hereditary Chief Toby Howard said the latest accident demonstrates the continuing risks posed by freight transportation through Gitxsan territory.


“A 103-year-old track has created dangerous conditions for the rail system in our territory,” he said in the statement.


CN Rail did not immediately respond to a request for a response to the nation’s calls to halt train hauling in the territory.


Howard said the nation’s hereditary chiefs have offered the provincial government assistance in identifying “the areas of most vulnerability on the line” but the Transportation Ministry has dismissed the offer.


“The hauling of any materials — dangerous, human or otherwise — must stop immediately until CN Rail can guarantee the rail line is safe,” he said.


The derailment is also “well within the reach of ocean tides, jeopardizing an entire ecosystem,” the First Nation’s statement said.


“We must ensure that every inch of the railway from Burns Lake to Prince Rupert is inspected, otherwise our Gitxsan people are not safe,” Howards said.


Read more:


Derailment in Gitxsan territory has the hereditary chief calling for a halt to all rail traffic


CN Rail said it appears a rock slide caused Tuesday’s derailment, which involved two locomotives and five railcars.

title: Nunavik communities elect new school board commissioners
content:
Nunavik communities have elected representatives to Kativik Ilisarniliriniq’s council of commissioners, with the new council set to serve a three-year term.


The election results were announced Wednesday. Representatives were elected in 13 of the region’s 14 communities, a press release issued Wednesday by Nunavik’s school board said.


The election in Kangiqsujuaq was postponed to Thursday for logistical reasons, communications director Jade Duchesneau-Bernier said in an email.


Several candidates were elected by acclamation, including Adamie Alayco in Akulivik, Nancy Palliser in Inukjuak and Sarah Aloupa in Quaqtaq.


Ten commissioners were elected in contested races, including Charlie Akpahatak (Aupaluk), Evie Mark Kalingo (Ivujivik), McCombie Annanack (Kangiqsualujjuaq), Peter Annahatak Timmons (Kangirsuk), Eva Kauki (Kuujjuaq), Jeannie Aragutak (Kuujjuaraapik), Jacqueline Amamatuak (Puvirnituq), Patsy Cameron (Salluit), Mary Berthe (Tasiujaq) and Noah Inukpuk (Umiujaq).


The newly elected commissioners will meet for the first time from Nov. 30 to Dec. 4. During that meeting, they will elect a president and members of the executive committee from among themselves.


Aloupa, who was re-elected by acclamation as Quaqtaq’s commissioner, is eligible to serve another term as president. She will remain in the role of immediate past president until the new council makes its selection.

title: Yazidi women’s organizations call for international search for missing persons
content:
Twelve years after the genocide committed by the terrorist organization Islamic State (ISIS) against the Yazidis in Shengal, the fate of around 3,000 people remains unknown. The Free Yazidi Women’s Movement (TAJÊ) and the Umbrella Organization of Yazidi Women’s Councils (SMJÊ) have issued a joint appeal to 54 state and international institutions and political officials, calling for the establishment of an international search and rescue commission to locate abducted women and children in particular and secure their release.


The letter is titled “We demand freedom and justice for those abducted during the genocide of August 3, 2014.” The organizations recall that around 6,000 Yazidis were abducted during the ISIS attack on Shengal, and numerous families are still waiting for news of their loved ones although twelve years have passed since. “Every family whose loved ones are missing has the right to know the truth. Every person who remains in captivity has the right to freedom. And every victim of the genocide has the right to justice,” the letter reads.


Uncertain fate following the dismantling of al-Hol camp


The women’s organizations expressed particular concern about the situation in Syria. They said numerous abducted Yazidis were held in Idlib and other regions in the past, and the ongoing political and military instability is making it difficult to search for them. Another concern was the dismantling of al-Hol camp during the Syrian offensive against the Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria at the beginning of this year. According to TAJÊ and SMJÊ, Yazidi women who had been unable to reveal their identities for fear of threats and reprisals were also among those held there.


Since the dismantling of the camp, TAJÊ and SMJÊ said, it has remained unknown where these women were taken and under what conditions they are currently living. The fate of other abducted Yazidis in Iraq and Turkey must also be clarified, they said and, in this context, referred to their campaign “For Justice and Freedom – Become a Voice for Those Abducted During the Genocide.” The campaign aims to prevent the crimes committed against the Yazidis and the suffering of their families from being forgotten as time passes.


Four demands to the international community


The letter focuses on four specific demands. First, TAJÊ and SMJÊ call for the establishment of a specialized international team involving the relevant states, international organizations, and other responsible bodies. The team would systematically search for those abducted, determine their whereabouts, and organize their release. Second, the women’s organizations demand that ISIS perpetrators be brought to trial not only for terrorist offenses but explicitly for genocide and crimes against humanity. They demand that the crimes committed against the Yazidis be prosecuted in accordance with international law.


As a third measure, they propose an international commission to investigate cases of missing persons. Scientific investigations, identity registries, and DNA analyses would be used to identify and locate abducted and missing persons and reunite them with their families. Finally, the organizations demand that states that have officially recognized the genocide against the Yazidis take practical steps to give effect to that recognition.


These include searching for missing persons, rescuing those abducted, protecting the rights of survivors, and prosecuting those responsible. “Recognition of the genocide is not merely a political and moral stance. It also entails far-reaching obligations,” TAJÊ and SMJÊ emphasized.


Letter sent to parliaments, governments, and UN institutions


The appeal was sent to a total of 54 government bodies, international organizations, and political officials. The recipients include the German Bundestag, the Federal Foreign Office, and the German Institute for Human Rights, as well as parliaments, ministries, and human rights institutions in Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Austria, Sweden, Luxembourg, Portugal, and Armenia.


Institutions in Australia, Canada, Ireland, and the United States, as well as the European Commission, the European Parliament, and several United Nations human rights bodies, were also contacted. Among the officials personally addressed was European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

title: YRK reports Iranian drone and artillery attacks on Serdeşt region
content:
Iranian regime forces attacked areas in Serdeşt district in Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat) with artillery and drones on Wednesday. According to the Press and Communication Center of the Eastern Kurdistan Defense Units (YRK), the attacks were concentrated particularly on the Mirava region.


According to the YRK, the shelling on November 18 lasted from 11 am to noon and was part of the Islamic Republic’s ongoing artillery and drone attacks on the region. The attacks reportedly caused damage to the natural environment and landscape. They also significantly disrupted the daily lives of local residents.


YRK underlined that the repeated attacks were fueling insecurity and concern among residents and making their living conditions and daily activities more difficult. The YRK reported that their forces had suffered no casualties or damage in the attacks.


Most recently, the Iranian regime carried out massive attacks on Serdeşt last week. In the ensuing clashes between the Revolutionary Guards and YRK units, guerrilla fighter Dersim Behar lost his life.


The YRK reported on Tuesday, November 17, that their units carried out two actions in the cities of Bane and Serdeşt regions.


According to the statement, specialized and professional YRK teams targeted a base of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in central Serdeşt on November 15. The base commander and one Revolutionary Guard were killed, while two other Revolutionary Guards were wounded.


On the other hand, another YRK unit killed an officer affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in Bane on November 16.


The YRK stated that both actions had been carried out to honor Dersim Behar’s memory and avenge her death.

title: Four lawyers remanded in custody in Izmir
content:
The police and prosecutorial procedures concerning the six lawyers, who were detained following raids on their homes on the morning of 17 November in Izmir, have been completed.


The six lawyers, including members of the Izmir Branch of the Progressive Lawyers Association (ÇHD), were transferred to the İzmir Bayraklı Courthouse. Following their statements to the prosecutor, they were brought before the Criminal Judgeship of Peace on duty, with prosecutors requesting their arrest.


Following their hearings, the court ordered the arrest of ÇHD Izmir Branch Secretary and lawyer Veysi Çetin, ÇHD members and lawyers Yemen Cankan and Erdoğan Akdoğdu, and lawyer Bahattin Özdemir.


Meanwhile, ÇHD member and lawyer Emrah Kanbay and lawyer Göksel Akbaba, who appeared before the court as part of the same investigation, were released subject to judicial control measures.

title: DEM Party to visit Abdullah Öcalan
content:
The Imrali delegation of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) will travel to the Turkish prison island of Imrali again in the coming days to meet with Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan. The delegation consists of members of parliament Pervin Buldan and Mithat Sancar, as well as lawyer Faik Özgür Erol.


The delegation last visited Öcalan on September 13. More than two months have passed since that meeting. An exact date for the upcoming visit has not yet been announced.


The announcement comes just days after new information emerged about Öcalan’s detention and working conditions. DEM Party Co-Chair Tuncer Bakırhan stated during his party’s parliamentary group meeting on November 17 that Öcalan had been moved to a residential area specially built for him on Imrali. Accordingly, his working conditions have also changed following the relocation. In addition, his secretarial support has been increased to enable him to work more quickly and effectively, Bakırhan stated.


The changes are linked to the ongoing peace and democratization process. In his speech, Bakırhan emphasized that, following the cessation of armed hostilities and the initiation of dialogue, the focus must now be on establishing the legal and political foundations and opening up space for democratic politics.

title: Hatimoğulları calls for strengthening local democracy in Adana
content:
Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) Co-Chair Tülay Hatimoğulları has accused the Turkish government of neglecting Adana’s economic development and weakening local self-government. At a meeting with neighborhood and village heads (muhtars) as part of the campaign “Budget for Bread, Peace and Justice,” she criticized the shifting of state investment incentives and agricultural policies that are accelerating the decline in agricultural production.


Hatimoğulları explained that muhtars were often the first point of contact for people affected by poverty, unemployment, and social exclusion. She remarked that women, unemployed young people, people with disabilities, and those without adequate access to social benefits, in particular, turned to them with their problems.


“Adana has lost its industrial base”


Hatimoğulları recalled that Adana had once been a major industrial and agricultural center that attracted workers from across Turkey. “The fertile lands of Çukurova provided a livelihood for many people. Industry was much stronger. But because investment incentives were shifted to other cities, Adana has lost its industrial base. Agricultural policies have also deprived the city of its agriculture. The plains of Çukurova, Harran, and Konya have the potential to meet the country’s food needs. Instead of utilizing this potential, however, the government is pursuing policies that undermine agricultural production,” Hatimoğulları said.


Elected mayors must be reinstated


Addressing government interventions in Adana’s municipal administrations, Hatimoğulları called for the reinstatement of elected mayors. She stressed that the arrests and removals from office not only disrupted the work of municipalities but also made it more difficult for muhtars to convey concerns from their neighborhoods to the relevant authorities.


The DEM Party Co-Chair continued: “The people of Adana elected Zeydan Karalar, but he is no longer at the head of the city administration. Although he was released from detention, he has not been reinstated. The elected mayor of Ceyhan, Kadir Aydar, was also released but has not been reinstated. Seyhan Mayor Oya Tekin is in prison. Following the operation against the Çukurova municipal administration, Emrah Kozay and other officials remain in detention. Can we still speak of local self-government and democracy under these circumstances?”


Hatimoğulları demanded that the affected mayors and municipal officials be allowed to stand trial without being held in detention and be reinstated in their positions. She also called for expanding the powers of municipalities and muhtars. “In the face of growing social hardship, they are often barely able to respond to the population’s requests for assistance. Real democracy does not emerge when everything is governed from Ankara. Real democracy emerges through the strengthening of local self-government.”


“Peace must not become an election campaign tool”


Regarding the peace and democratization process, Hatimoğulları described the absence of further news of deaths among Kurdish and Turkish young people as the most important achievement of the past two years. “This is enormous progress for us. We all know how much suffering and devastation each death caused among those affected. The fact that we no longer have to experience this is a major gain.” At the same time, she criticized the antidemocratic measures, police operations, arrests, and detentions for placing a strain on the process. She said the issue was the democratic and peaceful resolution of a century-old question which must not be subordinated to the interests of individual parties.


“Whoever tries to sacrifice this process for their narrow party-political interests, whoever fails to approach it sincerely and seeks to turn it into an election campaign tool, will be mistaken. No matter who they are. Because we regard this process as a genuine peace process. We want it to succeed, to ensure there is no turning back, and to prevent us from ending up where we started.” Hatimoğulları emphasized that the DEM Party had never viewed the process as an opportunity to gain partisan political advantages. She said this position applied equally to the governing parties and the opposition.


“We want the deaths to stop permanently. That is why we support this process. No party should reduce it to its own interests. We say this to both the governing parties and the opposition,” she stated.

content:
The Press Center of the People’s Defense Forces (HPG) has released the identities of seven guerrilla fighters from the Eastern Kurdish city of Merîwan who lost their lives in various areas of Southern Kurdistan (Northern Iraq) between 2011 and 2024. In a statement, the HPG paid tribute to their commitment to the Kurdish freedom struggle and extended their condolences to the families of the martyrs.


The HPG statement said:


“We remember our comrades Rênas Botan, Kawa Hewraman, Sîrwan Qendîl, Hewrê Kemanger, Sîrwan Zirêbar, Serxwebûn Hewraman, and Serkeft Hewramî, who fought as steadfast militants committed to the Apoist principle of self-sacrifice, with respect, love, and gratitude.

They rejected colonial borders and the order that denies the existence of our people, and assumed a leading role in the struggle in the mountains of Kurdistan.


Despite the advanced military technology of our time, they relied solely on the strength of human will, consciousness, and conviction, setting an extraordinary example of courage and determination. They fought fearlessly to defend the existence of our people and, through their selfless commitment, embodied the unyielding will to resist colonialism.


Through their actions and unwavering commitment to the freedom struggle, they became an embodiment of the determination on which our resistance is founded. Our fallen comrades, who have secured a permanent place in the hearts of our people, have thus become guides toward a free future, an expression of our struggle, and a guarantee of its success. title: DEM Party calls for timetable for parliamentary monitoring commission
content:
The Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) is calling for a binding timetable for the establishment of a parliamentary monitoring commission as part of the peace and democratization process. At a press conference at the party’s headquarters, spokesperson Ayşegül Doğan criticized the fact that it remained unclear when the commission would begin its work despite talks between Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş and the political parties.


Following the talks last week, Kurtulmuş had announced that the commission would be established “in the coming days.” Doğan described this statement as insufficient: “Instead of vague statements, a timetable should have been presented long ago. What are they waiting for to complete the preparations? Why is there a delay? There is nothing left to wait for.”


The DEM Party spokesperson demanded that the commission’s working procedures, responsibilities, and roadmap be made public. She also said it was necessary to clarify the political framework under which the parties would cooperate within the commission. She noted that the delays were also affecting coordination between the legislative and executive branches.


Call for the participation of all parties


Doğan emphasized that all parliamentary groups must be represented on the monitoring commission, and that broad political participation was essential to the success of the peace process. In this context, she criticized the decision by Yeni Party Chair Özgür Özel not to nominate any members to the commission. During the work of the National Commission for Solidarity, Brotherhood and Democracy, he had declined to participate in the delegation visiting Abdullah Öcalan. This was compounded by votes against the framework law.


“Now comes the decision not to participate in the monitoring commission either. It creates the impression that they want to avoid being perceived as supporters of the process at all costs. This does not reflect well on them,” Doğan stated. She stressed that the demand for democratization was legitimate and necessary but must not lead political forces to distance themselves from the peace process. Peace and democratization were inseparably linked, she underlined.


Doğan warned that the Yeni Party’s stance could widen the gap between the party and the Kurdish people. “The debate must not be reduced to party-political majorities and tactical calculations. We are in a process that must rise above such calculations and in which potential pitfalls must be identified in time. To end this war that has lasted for 50 years, everyone must be at the table. We call for the participation of all parties.”


“Sick prisoners must not be left to die”


Another major focus of the press conference was the situation of seriously ill prisoners. Doğan expressed her support for the indefinite vigil outside the Turkish Ministry of Justice, which is demanding the release of sick prisoners and guaranteed access to medical care.


She recalled the recent death of political prisoner Tuncer Sağlam and criticized the fact that applications for release from prison and suspension of sentence had gone unanswered. “If it is possible to save a person’s life but a decision is made not to do so, then that is a political decision,” Doğan said. She also cited the cases of Evin Zapsu, who is imprisoned in Kayseri-Bünyan Women’s Prison and has stage IV cancer, and Newroz Bozkurt, who is being held in Sincan Women’s Prison and suffers from chronic leukemia.


“The imprisonment of seriously ill people under prison conditions must end. We will not allow the right to life to be subjected to arbitrary administrative decisions, political calculations, and arbitrary practices. We support the sit-in protest and will stand in solidarity with the families until the very end. For us, this is a matter of rights and justice.”


Criticism of appointed trustees and political bans


Doğan also condemned an appeals court’s decision to uphold the 19-year-and-six-month prison sentence imposed on Sıddık Akış, the co-mayor of Hakkari. She pointed out that the ruling had been issued at a time when the legal foundations of the peace process were under discussion. The continued arrest and prosecution of Kurdish politicians, she argued, contradicted the stated goal of democratic reform. According to Doğan, what is needed is an expansion of the space for democratic politics rather than further restrictions.

title: GOP Rams Through Trump FCC Nominee Opposed by Free Speech Groups
content:
Democrats boycotted the vote as Trump’s other lame duck nominees caused headaches for the Senate GOP.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

As Democrats plan investigations into corruption and abuses of power, Republicans are working to shore up the president’s influence over the federal bureaucracy while they still can. But Senate Republicans are having mixed success as they attempt to speed through the federal nomination process for as many GOP-approved officials as they can.

Despite a boycott of the confirmation hearing by Democrats, Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted on November 18 to advance President Donald Trump’s nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs to serve on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). Thumann Severs is senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, and Democrats had called for an additional hearing to question her about internal records suggesting that she helped Carr pressure cable news outlets to change their content on Trump’s behalf.

“Today, Senator [Ted] Cruz greenlit a vote for an FCC nominee who not only provided false testimony to his committee, but did so to cover up her role in FCC Chairman Carr’s ongoing efforts to pressure and punish broadcasters that anger the president,” said Jessica J. González, co-CEO of the digital rights group Free Press, in a statement on Wednesday.

González pointed to internal FCC documents recently released to watchdogs under the Freedom of Information Act that show Thumann responding to emails about Trump and Carr’s jawboning of cable news outlets, including pressuring ABC to temporarily pull comedian Jimmy Kimmel off of late-night TV last year. Jawboning is the use of informal public pressure and veiled threats by government officials to cajole or coerce private actors, and the Senate Commerce Committee has advanced bipartisan legislation to rein it in.

Thumann is one of multiple Trump nominees that Republicans are attempting to ram through the confirmation process before Democrats regain majorities in Congress next year. Other high-profile Trump nominees failed to gain traction in the GOP-controlled Senate on Wednesday, including Jim O’Neill, a venture capitalist who is not a scientist but was nominated to run the National Science Foundation, despite vocal opposition from actual scientists.

Senate health committee Chairman Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana) abruptly blocked a vote on O’Neill, citing a nasty shakeup over childhood vaccines at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, where Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. installed O’Neill as acting director after firing public health expert Susan Monarez. Monarez later testified that she was pushed out after resisting Kennedy’s efforts to fire career scientists and change public vaccine recommendations to align with anti-vax ideology.

The U.S. faces a severe measles outbreak and has officially lost its measles elimination status due in part to lower childhood vaccination rates. Senator Cassidy has said he now regrets casting a deciding vote last year to confirm Kennedy, a longtime leader of the anti-vaccine movement who regularly spreads misinformation from his perch at the Department of Health and Human Services.

“I like Jim personally, but this time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Cassidy said as he blocked O’Neill’s confirmation.

Additionally, the White House dropped its nomination of physician and abortion opponent Heidi Overton for Food and Drug Administration commissioner. The move came as a disappointment to some Republicans, including Cassidy, who suggested on Wednesday that the nomination had enough GOP votes to pass. Reproductive health advocates feared Overton would undermine access to medication abortion, which she has baselessly asserted is “dangerous to women.” Overton also controversially played a role in the White House’s overhaul of the childhood vaccination schedule, and infamously stood behind Trump as he falsely stated that the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine could be “quite lethal.”

author: Unknown
title: Dünya Çocuk Hakları Gününde 5 çocuk işçi anlatıyor: Hakları yok, patronları var
content:
Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Bugün 20 Kasım Dünya Çocuk Hakları Günü. Başta bakanlık düzeyindeki yetkililer olmak üzere pek çok kişi açıklamalar yaparken bugün Türkiye’de çocukların karşı karşıya olduğu en büyük sorunlardan biri çocuk işçilik.

Adana’da sanayide çalışan çocukların anlattıkları, hem çocuk işçiliğin arkasındaki nedenleri ortaya koyuyor hem de yoksullukla artan çocuk işçiliğin nasıl kurumsallaştırıldığını gösteriyor. Kimi okulda başarısız olduğu düşüncesiyle eğitimden kopuyor, kimi ailesinin içinde olduğu yoksulluk nedeniyle çalışmaya başlıyor. 11 yaşında çalışmaya başlayan çocuklar, MESEM’e kayıt yaptırabilmek için 15 yaşını doldurmayı bekliyor.

Adana’da oto sanayi alanında görüştüğümüz çocukların hikayeleri; Dünya Çocuk Hakları Günü’nde çocukların içinde bulunduğu durumu gösteriyor.

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Sanayi sitesinde görüştüğümüz çocuklardan 14 yaşındaki Deniz, üç yıldır oto tamir işinde çalışıyor. Altıncı sınıfa geçtiği dönemde okulu bırakan Deniz, çalışmaya 11 yaşında başlamış. Nasıl başladığını anlatırken “Babamla konuştum. ‘Çalışmak istiyorum’ dedim. Sınavlarım kötüydü. Matematik de biraz zordu, yapamadım” diyor. Deniz, okulu bırakmayı derslerine bağlasa da kazandığı paranın büyük bölümünü ailesine veriyor: “Anneme veriyorum. Bana bir şey kalmıyor. 500 lira kendime alıyorum. Arkadaşlarımla pazar günleri AVM’ye gidiyorum. Yemek yiyorum.”

Deniz’in 15 yaşını doldurmasına bir ay kalmış. Yaşını doldurduğunda MESEM’e kaydolacak. 3 yıldır okulla eğitimi birlikte götürmeye çalışmış. Eğitimine devam etmek yerine mesleği sürdürmek istediğini söylüyor. Deniz’in ailesinde kendisinden başka çalışan çocuklar da var. Üç kardeş olduklarını, küçük kardeşinin dört yaşında olduğunu söyleyen Deniz, diğer kardeşinin de çalıştığını belirtiyor. Babası sanayide kaporta-boya işinde çalışıyor. Kendi kazancının eve katkısını ise “biraz” diye anlatıyor.

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

17 yaşına girmeye hazırlanan Utku da 14 yaşındaki kardeşinin MESEM’e başlayabilmek için 15 yaşına gelmesini beklediğini söylüyor. Kendisi beş yıldır aynı atölyede, öncesinde de iki yıl başka bir iş yerinde çalışmış. Utku, sanayiye yönelme kararını “Dedim, ‘Sokakta sürüneceğime gider sanayide sürünürüm daha iyi.’ En azından elimde bir altın bileziğim olsun, cebime para girsin” sözleriyle anlatıyor. Utku ayda 15 bin lira kazandığını, bunun yarısının MESEM tarafından karşılandığını söylüyor. Kazandığı paranın yarısını eve verdiğini, kalanını kendisi için kullandığını anlatıyor. Evde kendisi, kardeşi ve babası olmak üzere üç kişinin çalıştığını belirten Utku, 14 yaşındaki kardeşinin de 15 yaşına geldiğinde MESEM’e başlayacağını söylüyor.

15 yaşındaki Hasan da bir yıldır şanzıman tamiri işinde çalışıyor. Bu işe nasıl başladığı sorulduğunda “Ailem ‘şanzımancı ol’ dedi, biz de geldik, öğreniyoruz abi” diyor. Hasan da MESEM öğrencisi olduğunu, haftanın bir günü, perşembe günü okula gittiğini söylüyor. Haftanın beş günü iş yerinde çalışıyor, cumartesi yarım gün de atölyeye geliyor.

MESEM’deki eğitimini nasıl değerlendirdiği soruduğumuzda “İş. En çok iş abi. Pek okul gibi değil. İşe gidip geldiğimiz için ders çalışamıyoruz. Zaten hocalar da sınıfta bırakmıyor. MESEM’i de bitirdikten sonra çalışmaya devam edeceğim” diyor. Üniversite eğitimine ise “Lazım değil” diye cevap veriyor.

Hasan kazandığı paranın büyük bölümünü ailesine veriyor. 2 bin lira kadar kendisine ayırdığını, gerisini ailesine verdiğini anlatan Hasan’ın evde kendisi, 20 yaşındaki motor tamircisi ağabeyi ve çiftçilik yapan babası çalışıyor. Çocukların mutlu olup olmadığı sorusuna ise “mutsuz” yanıtını veriyor ve ekliyor, “Ülkenin durumu pek iyi değil.”

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Aynı kaporta atölyesinde çalışan Berat ve kardeşi Bilal’in anlattıkları da çocukların çalışma hayatına yönelmesinde aile koşullarının ve okuldan kopuşun etkisini gösteriyor. 15 yaşındaki Berat, dokuzuncu sınıfta okuyor ve MESEM’e geçmek için başvuru hazırlığında. Yaşını yeni doldurduğunu, dayısının iş yeriyle ilgili evrakların tamamlanmasını beklediğini söylüyor. Berat, ailesinin ekonomik durumunu anlatırken “Bir tek babam çalışıyor. O da yetmiyor. Mecburen çalışıyoruz” diyor. MESEM’de hem çalışıp hem okula devam edebildiği ve para alabildiği için bu yolu tercih ettiğini belirtiyor. Kazandığı paranın bir bölümünü kendi ihtiyaçları için kullandığını, özellikle kıyafet almak zorunda …

title: Pentagon, İran'la savaşın maliyetinin 48,3 milyar dolara ulaştığını açıkladı
content:
ABD Savunma Bakanlığı (Pentagon) yetkilisi Arthur Miller, ABD'nin İran'la savaşının maliyetinin 13 Kasım itibarıyla 48,3 milyar dolara ulaştığını açıkladı.

ABD Senatosu Silahlı Hizmetler Komitesi'ndeki oturuma katılan Donanma Müsteşar Yardımcısı adayı ve Pentagon'un mali kontrolör yardımcısı Miller, açıkladığı rakamın mühimmat harcamaları, teçhizat yenileme maliyetleri ve operasyon giderlerini içerdiğini kaydetti.

Öte yandan Miller, Senatör Richard Blumenthal'ın sorularına yanıt olarak söz konusu rakamın, İran'ın saldırıları sonucu hasar gören Ortadoğu'daki ABD tesislerinin onarım maliyetlerini içermediğini belirtti.

ABD Kongre Bütçe Ofisi (CBO), 1 Ağustos'ta yaptığı açıklamada, savaşın maliyetinin 38 milyar dolara ulaştığını bildirmişti.

title: Labor for Palestine National Network Solidarity with the Palestinian Trade Union Call for Global Action November 20-29, 2026
content:
Solidarity with the Palestinian Trade Union Call for Global Action November 20-29, 2026

The Labor for Palestine National Network stands in full solidarity with the Palestinian labor movement’s urgent call for global action to end complicity in Israel’s ongoing genocide and apartheid, from Friday, November 20, 2026 leading up to the International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People on Sunday, November 29, 2026.

As the Palestinian labor call points out:

“Our struggle for justice in Palestine is inseparable from the global struggle against systemic racism, exploitation, climate devastation and all forms of oppression.

“It is the duty of unions to ensure that the workers they represent—whether in ports, on ships, in businesses, or in government offices—are not involved, often without their knowledge and/or consent, in actions that involve complicity in atrocity crimes anywhere, including Israel’s war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide against our people.”

Zionism is racism, and both the Democratic and Republican parties have blood on their hands for their deep complicity in Israeli settler colonialism, demonizing Palestinian resistance, and attacking the Palestine solidarity movement.

Although US workers have the power to end bipartisan-backed Israeli genocide, US labor leadership, which is closely tied to the Democratic Party establishment, has been deeply complicit with Zionism for more than a century, and most unions have—at best—remained silent.

Major unions who have nominally called for a ceasefire and arms embargo fail to acknowledge the Palestinan trade union calls or the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) picketline, and continue to resist members’ demands to use workers’ power—at the workplace, in the electoral arena, and in the streets—to shut down the genocide down, which continues to grind on with no end in sight.

This breach of solidarity was conspicuous during the historic October 30, 2026 international dockworker strike in solidarity with Palestine, which shut down 113 ports in five continents and 22 countries—none of them in the US—and now again during November’s week of global actions.

The indifference of union officialdom is a betrayal of the most basic labor principle, “An Injury to One Is an Injury to All.” As the Palestinian General Federation of Trade Unions-Gaza reminded US unions in 2025: “True labor solidarity is demonstrated through actions, not just words, and we count on your awareness and determination to take concrete steps to end this tragedy.”

Now is the time to reaffirm and escalate more than a half-century of rank-and-file labor solidarity with Palestine, including groundbreaking statements by the League of Revolutionary Black Workers in 1969, Arab worker-led strikes and protests against the UAW leadership’s support for Israel in 1973, ILWU dockers’ refusal to handle Israeli Zim Line vessels since 2014, the UAW’s 2026 divestment from Israel Bonds, and other grassroots Palestine labor solidarity since 2023.

As the November 21 Bay Area Mobilization for Palestine and Against War points out:

“This call to action comes at the heels of the US midterm elections, when voters this month delivered a strong rejection of US support for Israel and its genocide in Gaza, the war on Iran, the militarized brutality of ICE, and Trump’s racist and authoritarian agenda. Our movement has made clear that Palestinian liberation is inseparable from all struggles against racism, exploitation, and oppression everywhere. Let’s mobilize to show the people of Palestine our unwavering support, and to amplify to those in power what people everywhere are demanding: Stop Arming Israel, and No to War on Iran!”

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Garbage truck fire caused by ‘suspected’ lithium-ion battery
content:
A garbage truck fire believed to have been caused by a lithium-ion battery prompted the City of Iqaluit to remind residents to take care when sorting their garbage.


The truck was on its regular route Wednesday when it caught fire while collecting waste on Joamie Court near Tundra Buddies Daycare,  a public service announcement issued later that day said.


“Crews responded quickly by unloading the waste onto the roadway to prevent the situation from escalating,” the announcement said.


While the fire’s cause has not been confirmed, officials suspect it was related to the improper disposal of lithium-ion, or rechargeable, batteries.


Lithium-ion batteries can spark fires when crushed, punctured or overheated, sometimes leading to explosions that can ignite nearby paper, cardboard and or debris, the announcement said.


The city issued a

similar reminder

 in July after a fire at the city’s landfill. As well, in August 2024, a fire

caused

 by a laptop left overheating on a bed caused damage to a Rankin Inlet home.


Iqaluit residents are advised to discard lithium-ion batteries at the safe disposal site at the city’s landfill.


The city is also creating plans for additional drop-off locations for hazardous waste, Coun. Kyle Sheppard said Wednesday in a Facebook post.

author: Chris Walker
title: Jeffries Staffer Created AI Program to Monitor Democratic Caucus Members
content:
The House Democratic Party leader’s office denies that Jeffries knew about the AI program.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

A staffer for House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) custom-designed an artificial intelligence (AI) program to monitor the public communications of lawmakers and different factions within the party’s caucus.

According to reporting from The Washington Sun, which unearthed the source code for the program in a public GitHub software repository, the staffer asked the AI tool to monitor statements and social media posts of House Democrats in an effort to improve messaging strategies for Jeffries.

The program, which the staffer called Caucus Pulse, was produced using Anthropic’s AI agent Claude. To help the program, the staffer, whose identity is not yet known, fed it tens of thousands of posts from Democratic lawmakers purchased through the social media site X.

The program itself explains its purpose as being an assistant to the staffer, describing them as a “research analyst in the House Democratic Leader’s research and writing shop.”

The Washington Sun reached out to Jeffries’s office, with the Democratic leader’s spokesperson Christie Stephenson assuring the publication that Jeffries (who is the presumptive next Speaker of the House) wasn’t himself aware of Caucus Pulse.

“A staffer in this office conducted a short-lived experiment with AI in a personal capacity, without the involvement of the Office of the Democratic Leader,” Stephenson said. “No official resources were used, and we’re addressing this matter internally.”

In public statements, Jeffries has spoken out about the rapid and unregulated expansion of AI.

“The explosive growth of artificial intelligence and the challenges that are therein presented — that’s not a hoax,” Jeffries said in September, referencing comments from President Donald Trump that described fears about AI as hoaxes conjured by the media or by Democrats. In that same statement, Jeffries called for “immediate” and “decisive” action on the issue.

The regulations Jeffries will push for if he becomes Speaker of the House, however, are yet to be determined. Notably, Jeffries has received significant backing from many AI industry leaders, including $150,000 from executives at Anduril, an AI-weapons company that contracts with the federal government, and $44,300 from Mehdi Allhassani, an executive at the AI surveillance company Palantir, among other tech-based campaign donations this past election cycle.

House lawmakers also formed a bipartisan “AI Safety and Innovation Caucus” this week, which will be charged with balancing AI safeguards while also “ensuring the United States remains a global leader in innovative AI technologies,” the group announced.

The regulation of AI and data centers was one of the top issues among voters in the midterm elections. According to exit polling data, 56 percent of voters described those two issues as a “crucial or major factor” in determining how they cast their ballots.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we must raise $16,000 before midnight. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Latest COP31 Text Drops Fossil Fuel Phase-Out and Embraces “Magic Technologies”
content:
“Saudi Arabia and some petroleum states have really won big time here,” says German activist Luisa Neubauer.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

As we continue our week of broadcasts from the global United Nations climate conference known as COP31, we get an update on the formal negotiations from German activist Luisa Neubauer. The latest draft text of the key climate commitments that countries are debating has dropped language about phasing out fossil fuels, but it does include an emphasis on carbon capture and storage — a largely unproven technology that critics say cannot be deployed at scale to curb emissions.

“We have much better solutions at hand, like renewables,” says Neubauer. “This is not going well. We are not doing fine. And if anything, after this conference ends, we need people to take the streets and fight for more justice out there.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh. We’re broadcasting from Antalya, Turkey, at the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: As we reach the final hours of climate negotiations at this global conference, negotiators have released a second draft text for the final outcome of this year’s COP. Global civil society activists have already criticized the text for stripping out hard-won language on accountability from Global North countries and legal anchors to protect the countries and communities most vulnerable to climate change.

AMY GOODMAN: Earlier today, Teresa Anderson, the global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International, said climate negotiations are, quote, “looking bleak.” She criticized the European Union’s climate chief Wopke Hoekstra.

TERESA ANDERSON: Before coming to COP, actually, the EU’s climate chief, Hoekstra, said any chance of a deal on new climate finance is “dead in the water.” “Dead in the water.” The more I think about it, the more shocked I am that he used that term, in the aftermath of Nepal, as El Niño floods are happening. I’m shocked that he chose that metaphor. When the next catastrophic flood happens, those words will haunt him.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: Democracy Now! also caught up with campaigners who’ve been closely following the negotiations here at COP31. This is Kirtana Chandrasekaran from Friends of the Earth International speaking alongside a protest for just solutions from wealthy countries in the Global North.

PROTESTERS: No false solutions! Real solutions now! Real solutions now! No false solutions! No false solutions!

KIRTANA CHANDRASEKARAN: I’m Kirtana Chandrasekaran with Friends of the Earth International. I was at the “divan” meeting last night, and the divan is supposed to be a roundtable for leaders, but there was no leadership in the room. And all we saw is the Global North countries abandoning their moral and legal commitments, country after country saying that “we are worried about breaching 1.5,” with no irony about how we’ve got here, which is 30 years of inaction on their part, and the solution for that being so-called clean electrification.

And what we can see happening now, under the guise of clean electrification, we are seeing many, many new gas plants to electrify data centers. We are seeing many, many new coal plants in the Global South, a massive push, and nuclear, as well. So, they say the words, but they’re not doing any of it. And so they talk about roadmaps, but what is in the roadmap? You know, they were supposed to mobilize $100 million. If you talk about clean electrification, it requires over $2 trillion of investment just for grids and electricity.

AMY GOODMAN: At another protest just this morning, a young activist from Nepal urged people to visit her country to experience what it’s like to live on the frontlines of a climate change-fueled catastrophe.

SNEHA RAI: I think everybody here knows about the 26th August, 2026, flood. … This is not a single disaster. I think this is the one disaster that you have reached to you on the further side of the world. But we have been facing this on yearly. Yearly, every year, we have been facing this. We don’t need hope anymore. We don’t need words anymore. We need actions right now. And Nepal is a mountainous country, you know, and we have been saying that we are resilient people. We are resilient, but …

author: S. Baum
title: Ohio Bill Threatens to Criminalize Drag and Gender Nonconformity, Opponents Warn
content:
Civil liberties and trans rights advocates say the bill has nothing to do with the purported aim of protecting children.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Ohio appears to be on the cusp of passing a drag ban. Transgender Ohioans and their allies are sounding the alarm.

“House Bill 249 seeks to limit drag performances to strip clubs and similar locations, making it a crime to perform in drag in other places where a minor may be present,” an ACLU of Ohio petition to stop the bill reads.

“This bill broadly targets anyone who performs exhibiting a gender identity different than the entertainer’s biological sex at birth. HB 249 also relies on notoriously vague legal standards used to determine whether content is considered obscene and/or ‘harmful to juveniles.’”

Dara Adkison, the executive director of TransOhio, told Erin in the Morning that if this bill becomes law, it would be “the most extreme criminalization of drag and perceived gender nonconformity in the country.”

In addition to traditional drag, HB 249 also specifically targets transgender and gender nonconforming performers. Those found to violate all or part of these measures could be tried for a misdemeanor or felony, which could carry jail time.

Although in theory, the bill applies only to “performances,” not everyday Ohioans, its ambiguity blurs the line between lawful and unlawful; the bill fails to even articulate what constitutes a “performance.”

“If I’m doing my grocery shopping down at Kroger, and I whistle to myself as I’m going down the aisle or hum to the music overhead, has that suddenly become a drag performance in the middle of the Kroger shopping center?” Arienne Childrey, a transgender woman and community activist, asked while being interviewed by Erin in the Morning. She said the bill isn’t about drag performance or protecting children as much as it is about criminalizing gender nonconformity.

Childrey has been following the progression of Ohio’s drag ban for a long while—since 2023, to be exact, when HB 249’s predecessor bill, HB 245, was proposed. That bill was sponsored by Rep. Angie King, Childrey’s own representative in the statehouse. When Childrey and others staged a protest, King responded by mocking demonstrators, arguing they were fighting for the “right to twerk and gyrate in front of your minor children.”

An Ohio drag ban was reintroduced in April of last year. It passed in the House in March 2026 and then stalled for months in the Senate. On Nov. 17, analysts at TransOhio noticed it was put on the legislative calendar for a hearing sometime during the week beginning on Monday, Nov. 23. An exact date and time has not yet been announced.

“What we have right now is vengeance politics playing out in Ohio,” Childrey said, referring to the aftermath of this midterm cycle’s blue wave.

“Their veto-proof supermajority evaporates after the new year,” she continued. “Come January, that disappears. So they know that they are ‘do or die’ this time around; otherwise, they have a two-year legislative cycle where they won’t be able to move something like this through if they were to try.”

The state’s Senate Judiciary Committee must now vote on whether to pass the “sub bill,” or substitution bill, which is an amended version of the text. It will then need to be heard before the full Senate and be reconciled with the House if there are further changes.

However, it is still dripping with the same anti-trans animus and ill intent as before, even if its GOP proponents try to brand it as some sort of middle-of-the-road compromise, activists warned.

For example, the sub bill removed the definitions of “biological sex” that it previously codified, but those were enshrined by HB 96 anyway; the newer version also added a section making it a felony if “the offender previously has been convicted of or pleaded guilty to two or more violations of this section.”

“The vagueness is actually more dangerous now,” Adkison, of TransOhio, told Erin in the Morning. “The sub bill INCREASES the criminal penalties for an offense that previously didn’t exist. Under this bill, gender nonconformity (even among cis people) will be scrutinized, and those who don’t look ‘male’ or ‘female’ enough will face potential prison time.”

“This is so clearly a violation of the First Amendment freedom of expression,” Adkison added.

content:

Olağan Kurultayı'na ilişkin ceza davasında Yeni Parti Bursa İl Başkanı Nihat Yeşiltaş ile Osmangazi Belediye Başkanı Erkan Aydın'a verilen 2 yıl 1 ay hapis ve siyasi yasak kararını Fomara Meydanı'nda yaptığı basın açıklaması ile protesto etti.
